ANY HUSBAND TO ANY WIFE. Let the swift years go swiftly by If only thou and .t are one: If only every setting sun Sees us together, eye tO eye, And heart to heart, and hand in hand: With kindred thoughts and hopes and fears; If only ray tears are thy tears And thy joys mine; if we but stand For ever by each other's side. Yen, let the years go as they will • Until thy heart and mine are still, fr 7 If only it be not denied That we shall never part till death. I could not say farewell to thee, Nor couldst thou say farewell to me: , We two must breathe our last long breath

" Together; we must go as one. Indeed I could not leave thee here, 0 wife, 0 love, who art so dear. ps' The mystic life that was begun When 'first I told my love, and caught Thy whispered words of love as sweet; - The life that's gone with flying feet - Through paths with all fair pleasures fraught; : The life that we are living still, Which.we have lived since that bright day When thou amongst tha flowers of May Breathed with a blush thy low "I will The life of wedded happiness • And pleasure, and of hallowed pain Wherein was nothing that was vain, And every wounding did but bless; i-- The life which we have lived so long, From hour toliour, from day to day, • From one May to another May, Like an unbroken, endless song; That life,shall never end. The sun That saw its birth shall never see Its ending.. As for thee and me, Goof moulded our two lives in one.

Landlady : "The coffee, I am sorry to say, is ex- hausted, ,Mr. Smith." "Border : "Ah, yes, poor thing, I wad expecting that! I've noticed for some time that it hasn't been strong." , ABOUT A SLENDER INDIVIDUAL—A Yankee, in describ- ing a lean opponent, said, "I tell you what, sir—that man doesn't amount to a sum in arithmetic; add hint up, and there's nothing to carry." The perfect lawgiver is a just temper between the mere man of theory, who can see nothing but general princi- ples,,and the mere man of business, who can see nothing p but artictilereirennistifnov. . "Doctor, said the grateful patient. seizing the physi- cian's hand, "I shall neverberget that to you I owe my life." "You exaggerate," said the doctor, mildly; "you only eve me for fifteen visits; that is the point which I hope you will not fail to remember." PLANNMAN'S RECENT EXPETHENCE.—FIannigan, rising •excitedly from the table after tasting an olive for the : *rat time: "It's sorry I'd be to disturb the hilarity of the matin', gentlemen, but I believe some joker has been saltin' the guseberries, bad scran to him?' In its refinement, its elegance, it graces and adorn- ments are seen the glory and perfection of life. It is the highest honour to be equal to them and capable of sus- taining them, and the greatest happiness to appreciate them properly and enjoy them rationally.• The path of truth is a plain and safe path; that ofl falsehood is a perplexing maze. After the first departure from sincerity, it is not id your power to stop. One artifice unavoidably leads on to another, till, as the iatricacd of the labyrinth increases, you are left en- tangled in your own snare. Hope is based upon faith, desire upon caprice. The former, is almost always calm and steady, moderate and reasonable; the latter is often impulsive and unsettled, extravagint and enreasonable—fer desire; With its present longings, anticipates only a momentary gratifi- cation', while hope, with its moral bearings i looks forward, to some permanent good. Where were you engaged last?" asked a San Fran- cisco lady of the new coloured cook. " Yefoughten• ter ax me dat, lady." "Well, I want to know, as it may tend to ("lye you character." "Wall, lady, I was engaged ter Bog Phillips, de triflingest yeller mon I ever seed. Why, lady, dat malt stole my yearrings and runned away! How many times was yerself engaged, lady ?" DUTCHMEN ON 'CHANGE.—Opposite the Palace is the Exchange—a handsome, modern building, resting on a . foundation of 3,469 piles. It has on the outside a fine lonic colonnade, and the interior hall is covered with glass. Between one and three daily a busy, crowd may be seen in this hall, and it is intereSting to watch the characteristics of the people as they transact their busi- ness. There is plenty of excitement, but it differs alto- gether from that to be witnessed at the Bourse in Paris, or in any other Continental city. Instead of the shout- ing and gesticulating to be found there, only low mur- murs and quiet whispers are to be heard in Aensterdam ; the eagerness, the hard bargain-driving,are just as great; but business is conducted with that solidity which characterises Dutchmen. A story is told of a Dutchman who was walking in one of the shady streets of his own city one day when a keg of gunpowder eiploded at a short distance behind him. lie held a pinch of Snuff between the thumb and forefinger of the right hand, and his spectacles in his left hand, and it is recorded that he duly sniffed the snuff and adjusted the spectacles on his note before turning round to see the cause of the uproar behind. hint A panic en 'Change in France reminds you of "Bedlam broke loose"; a panic on 'Change in Amster- 'dam reminds you of a Quaker's meeting. There is an •old Dutch joke concerning the Palace and the Exchange. MA:former has no handsome entrance-door, a conspipu- • eus`defect in the building; the latter has a huge porch austained by seventeen columns; hence the Palace is generally called "the house without a door," and the Exchange "the door without a house.—Fieen Cities of the World. Atecrirter COLLECTION or RIDDLEI—There is a curious little work the contents of which are said to have been collected by Hans Sachs, the Nuremberg cob- bler and master-singer, in 1517. This curious book was reprinted sOveraltimes in the seventeenth and early part of the eighteenth century, but' it is now sotnewhat scarce. It wee issued without place!of publication or publisher's name, in small form without cover. The book pretends to have IYeen prepared by Hans Sachs for his private • that he might make merriment among his friends, when Linking, and they were tired of his songs. It does 11,4atJ3' Altair' any anecdotes; it is made up of a collection .ddles more or less good, some coarse, and some pro- "; ; but the age was not squeamish. The title under ehich the little work was issued was," Useful Table- talk, or Something for all; that is the happy thoughts, good and bad, expelling melancholy and cheering Spirits, of Hilarius Hish-wash-Master-tiler at Kielenhausen." The hook consists of ink a hundred pages, of which 4-quarter are consumed by prefaces, introductions, &c., and about thirteen filled with postcript and index. The humours • of the book are somewhat curious; for instance, in the preliminary index of subjects it give—" IX. The reason why this book of Table-talk was so late in being published." When we turn to the place indicated for the reason, we find a blank. There is no such reason. There is a fulsome and absurd dedication to the " Ronotuatble and Knightly 'rileburner " who lives "By the icy ocean near Moscow, in Lapland, one mile from Podolia and three miles above it." Although we are not told in the place indicated why the little collection was not issued immediately after the death of Hans Sachs, nor ambng his works, we learn the reason elsewhere, in the preface, where we are told that the jokes it contained were so good that a rivalry ensued among them as to precedence, and till this was settled it was impossible to get the book printed. Here are some of the conundrums. ...-Question: After Adam had eaten the forbidden fruit, did he stand or sit down? Answer: ?either; he fell.— Question.: Two shepherds were pasturing their flocks. 'Said one to the other, "Give me one of your sheep, then I shall have twice as many as you." "Not so," replied the second herdsman; give me one of yours, and then we shall have equal flocks." How many sheep had each? Answer: One had seven, the other five. If the first • took a sheep out of the flock of the second, he had eight, the other our ;if the contrary, each had six.—Question Wl= is four times six? Answer: 6666.—Questi0n What , does a goose do when standing on one leg? Answer: Holds up the other !—Question: When did carpenters first proclaimthemsetees to be intolerable dawdles? Answer: When building the Ark they took a hundred years over it.—Question: Under what law are the soldiers? Answer : Can(nlon law. Some of the riddles have survived in the jocular mouth to the present day; for instance, who does not know this ?_Question: What Smells most in an apothecary's shop? Answer: The nose.—There is one conundrum which surprises us. The story was wont to be told by Bishop Wilberforce that he bad asked a child in Sunclav school why the angels ascended and descended • au Jacbb's ladder, whereupon the child replied that they did so because they were moulting, and could not fly. But this appears in Hans Sachs' book, and is evidently a very ancient joke indeed. In this collection also appears the very heavy riddle :—" Which is heaviest, a pound of lead or a pourid el feathers ?" Which every one knows, , •'but with an addition, which is an improvement. After the answer "Each weighs a pound, and they are equal in weight," the questioner says further: Not so—try in Nrftter. The pound of feathers will float, and the pound of lead will sink."—,-Question: How can you carry a jug of water in. Our hands on a broiling summer day, in the full blaze of the sun, so that the water shall not get hotter? Answer: Let the water be boiling when you fill the jug.—Question: How can a farmer prevent the mice from stealing his corn? Answer: By giving them corn.—Question : A certain man left a penny by his will to be divided, equally among his fifty relatives, each . to have as much as the other, and each to be quite con- tented with what he got, and not endy any of the other legatees. Flow did the executor comply with this testa- mentary disposition? Answer: Be • bought a packet of fifty tin-tacks with the Penny, and hammered one into the back of each of the legatees.—Chambers's Journal. div.p: How many peas are t ere in a pint 7—One Contentment is a good thing nntil it reaches•the point where it sits in the shade and lots the weeds grow. There will never exist anything permanently noble and excellent in a character which'is a strafiget to the ,exer-

cise of resolute self-denial. Efe that is taught to live upon little owes more to/hie father's wisdom than he that has a great deal left him does f 4 his Father's dare. ThoseNwho quit their proper character to assunie kvhat does not belong to them are for the grater part ignorant of both the character they leave isnd of the character

they assume. , Smith (to a friend aim apfdied for a position as letter- carrier) : "Think yes got the persishon ?" Als friend : "Got it? No. The first question they axed ma.was how fur it was from London to Constantinopul ,I.told 'em if that was goin' to be the round, rd give it up." Mistress: "I did not call you, Jane. I wishe4 to speak to Henry, the new butler." Jane (the Irish housemaid) : " Excnse ine, mum, but Henry couldn't oome. He belaves there's a big escape of gas in the cellar, an' he's just shtarted down wid the candle to hunt for it," "Describe some effects of the poceeding.,s under Queen Mary," said a member of the Schopl Board in an English towns The glib'anower was r*led off, " Manx eir the bishops were deprived of their sees.' Or ortilf gentle- men asked the meaning of tine statement. Aftbr a long pause, one boy put up his hgzad and said, "Had their eyes

put out." - The worker who looks with satisfaction on the cons- I fort that his labour is affording, or the beauty that it is creating; 'Ors the strength and sustenance that it is providing for those who will profit by it, is„.in so. doing, cultivating in his own heart the benevolent spirit that delights in diffusing happiness: There is indeed hardly any part of the character which may not be strengthened, improved, and trained by daily labour, if wise thought and carefuleffort be turned in the right direction. THE Youso CCCECOO.—A cuckoo laid it egg in a wagtail's.nest,,in the ivy on a house, which is a very unusual place for a cuckoo. The wagtail, of course, brought it no and when it was old enough to get out of the nest it used to sit on a lawn-tennis net, and ea4l for the wagtail to feed it. The wagtail had to get .a great many flies and worms for it, as the cuckoo was a good sized bircl;And still the wagtail would go on. feeding it, though it' had to stand on its shoulder in otder to do so.—" Little Folks" Magazine, February.

I- SRAMfftili VEGETABLE—An Indian mantle or praying insect, a little less wicked, though no less cruel than the spiders; deceives the flies who come to his arms under the false pretence orbeing a quiet leaf, upon which they may light in .dafety for rest and .refreshment. Yet another abandoned member of the Same family, relying boldly upon the resources of tropical nature, gets itself up as a complete orchid, the head and fangs being moulded in the exact, image of the beautiful blossom, and the arms folding treacherously around the unhappy insect which ventures to seek for honey in its deceptive jaws. Happily, however; the tyrants and murderers do not alwnys have things all then' own way. Sometimes the inoffensive prey turn the tables upon their torturers with distin- guished success. For example, Mr. Wallace noticed a kind of sand-wasp, in Borneo, much given te devouring crickets; but there was one species of 'Cricket which exactly reproduced the features of the sand-wasps, and mixed among them on equal tends without fear of detec- tion. Mr. Belt saw a green leaf-like locust in Nicaragua overrun by foraging ants in search Of meat for dinner but remaining perfectly motionless all the time, and evidently ,mistaken by the hungry foragers for a real pieee of 'the foliage it mimicked. Sa thoroughly did this innocent locitst understand the necessity fp.t. remain- ing Mill, and pretending to be a leaf under all,advancit that even when Mr. Belt took it up in his hinds it neve; budged an inch, but strenuously preserved its riga leaf- like attitude. As other insects sham dead," this inge- nious creature shammed vegetable.—Cornltill Magazine. ifiCOC-HOISTING no VIRGINIA.--SUddertly there is a great 1 commotion in the wooden valley beneath, and in a few 1 seconds you might be in Leicestershire spinny, so busy and joyful are the little pack with their tongues. "That's a fox, any way," says the doctor to the sorrel mare; "and likely as not, a red." Two small farmers, jogging down the road; pull pp their horses and yell with the peculiar shrill scream that is traditionally as much a part of Virginia fox-hunting as the familiar cries of the British hunting field are with us. The doctor, though his voice is not what it was thirty years ago 'catches the infection, and, standing up hi his 'wooden, leather-capped stirrups, hallooes at his bounds in what he would call "real old Virginia fashion." "The , dogs are out of the wood, and are strealdn' it up the broomsedge field yonder--dawg my skin if they ain't!" This is ;too much for the doctor. "Pull down the fence, gentlemen, for God's sake! and we'll push on up to the old Mathew's graveyard on top of the hill. We shall see right smart of the chase from there. I know that old fox; hell go straight to 'the pines on Squire Harrison's quarter place." The four or 'five top rails are tossed off the snake fence; but the doctor can't wait for the remaining six. The long spur is applied to the flank of the: sorrel mare, the apple switch to her shouldet. Amid aicrashing and scattering of rotten chestnut-rails, the doctor, cloak and spectacles, saddle-bags, pills, medicine bottles, and overalls,' lands safely m the' —corn-Stalk ' 'field upon the other side. The two farmers follow through the fearful breach he has .made, and they may soon all be beard upon the opposite lii4 cheering and yelling to the hounds, which by this-time are well out of reach & such encouraging sounds. Neither the country, nor the !horse, nor the doctor is adapted for riding to hounds; nor, as I have before intimated, has,, the latter any idea of doing so. The good man wants I to hear as much as possible—to see as much as possible I —of the chase; but when he neither sees nor hears a great deal—which, when a strong red fox goes straight away, is generally the case—he will still take much delight in collecting the details from other sources. If 1 his hounds eventually kill their fox half-way across the I county, friends and neighbours, who-became accidental 1 witnesses of various stages of the chase, and each of whom , did their share of hallooing and cheering, will send round 1 word to the "old doctor,' or "call by" the next time 1 they pass his house, and cheer his heart with praises of 1 his dogs. The doctor will probably have bandaged Mrs. 1 Gubbins's leg, and be half way home by the time the ' death-scene takes place, in some laurel thicket possibly miles and miles away from thesartiet,where we left our friend bursting through the/epee. Not more than half-a-dozen, probably,"`or'the fourteen or fifteen . hounds with which the deetrir started, will assist at the finish. Two cat thteei of the pup- pies will have dropped out early in, the dar; and come home hunting rabbits all the way. Three or four, more are perhaps just over distemper,. and will fall in their tracks, to come limping and' &tiding "home at noon. Rambler and Fairfax, bower, having assisted at the finish and being perhaps the most knowing old dogs of the lA, will have trotted round. .t old hl4 Colonel• Peyton's close by. They are mighty' icnotookthies rtgry—f or Virginia hounds won't touch fox's flesh—sna wnito mefindy the outside collecting chips, they succ.eed in sliPlAng log kitchen in the yard and abstracting from the top of the stove an entire ham. The 'Said ham was just pre- pared for the Colonel's supper- but Hi fox-hunting all is forgiven. So after a little burst of wrath he reckons they are the old Idoctor's dogs, shuts them up in the granary- and gives them a cake of cornbread ap.iece.—Blabktroeclo ' Magazine for February, 1887. If undue pressure has been exercised upon her by her father, and she dislikes the other man, and issiestperaikely fond of you—the first two contingencies being fotaskic, and the third improbable—l dan't see why I, more 'any one else, should throw moral stones at you forl wanting to elope. Of course, I take into consideration that you are both an honourable man and by no means a poor one; able, in fact, to atone ,hereafter for any irregularity in the present. But I really cannot follow you whep you coolly propose that I should play i the principal part n your little comedy : that I should run away with your beauty, and bring her up fgom the country, only W. band her over, with a -mock ilaterrie.l blessing, to you in town. Hang it all; it is too pre- posterous! A line must be drawn somewhere, Marston, even in obliging a ftiend ; and though- I. won't cut you if you choose to run away with another Man's Asecie,l must really leave you to manage your domestic affairs in your own way." ' ' gut, my dear Gunter," exclaimed 'Marston patheti- cally, "I was just going.thel-plain to you that it is quite impossiblelor me to act for myself in this matter, lam so well-knowri- deism at Evenden, wherd'Mise Custance lives, that I couldn't even pass through the station in an express train; disguised as a Cherokee Indian without , being recognised. -If I were to go down myselto fetch Nelliel: away all sorts of complications would arise and the planwould be spoilt, to a dead. certaiety..,,Whireae i . it wouldn't give you any real trouble, and you would lay me under the greatest poesible obligation. At any rate, you won't refuse to listen, like a good fellow, to the scheme that Nellie and kigive worked out for you." ! . "Upon my vrarcl,'- you'ie a pretty -pair !"...t•To talk in that tranquil manner of a nefarious plot, in which all the loaves and fishes are to be yours,"and all the burdeniis to fall upon a third person! 'Well, go on." "It is beautifully simple. You see, Evenden ns a sta- tion at which-two goods train, up and clown, meet. If you are so inclined you can arrive at Evenden at 11 30 a.m.,lhave a bun and a glass of water, and ;return to town by the 11 35. What could be more convenient than ~ this? for, of course, all you will bevel() do will be, in- stead of consuming the bun and water, to go to the . waiting-room, where you will find a young lady heavily veiled, in a bonnet trimmed with yellow flowers. You will conduct.;her to a, earriage in the 11 354 which you will Thad waiting in the station, and I'shall meet the pair of you on arrivaPhere. :CeiuldienStthing be more simple and complete? Youpn no risk, ;you syaste:yery little time, you make the aerstutintance; of„ a *arming young lady, and you frustrate the absurd 'designs of :a wrong- headed and 'grssping parent. ..4w* .an opportunity of occupying your. time pleasantry and usefully doesn't occlir every-dist? Positively -y.ou •otight to be dOwnright t grateful to me instead o:i f treasts. to make yourself dis- ...4sii:r li: _ aggseaV .e." -*A "My dear fellow, I don't want to be disagreeable ; and if 'lUallY there i 9 nothing more ffistagonethan'what you , say, I don't knew that I very much miadolending you a ' hand. When yea/ first suggested elopemUttitl had a dim vision of rope-ladders and a dog-cart, a ttearful young woman too frightened 'told° anything but•cry, and a raging parent accompanied by the jilted • Vother fellow ? bringing up the rear, 'With! pistols and,aprneecution for abduction. Your idea though tamer, is more practical; 'and if it can be coniatably carridd out betweea break- fast and lunch, I'm your man. But, f say, Marston, it mustn't occur again; you know." A- "0, dear, .no I One -elopensent in a lifetime is quite sufficient for a fellow of my simple tastes." , The Jack Gunter of the-above conversation was a fine young bachelor, with nothing particular: to do, and a sufficiency of money .wherewith to do it.. A Treherne by birth, he had taken the name of Gunter or coming into a property, to htife:` refused which.iyould have made him a pommel]. He had no relations to speak of, except one-brother slightly older than hikself, to whom he was devoted,' but' as th whose. 4%Ureabouts he was as a rule profounehy ignorant. For Henry Treherne was one oi these erratic spirits who, like Ulysses, "cannot ' rest from 'travel : Vonei day he would turn up suddeerysfrom America? and a fortnight inter Jack Guntv would see in a sporting paper a letter from him describing some exceptionally good day with the Norwegian salmon. In spite, however, of this spas- modic intercourse, the breithers were always ow the best of terms, and usually contrived ;',to have pleasant meetings at.' least tdrice a year. ' With -Charlie Mar- ston; too, 'it svoidd, seem from -the converse- ' . don recorded above, 'that ' Tack Gueter was on , , a footing of more than common intimacy; but ' this was hardly the 'Case. Although acquaintances of long standing, and thrown a good deal together, the two, men were by no Itleatla very intimate, and neither had until: to-day unburdened himself to the other regarding his private affairs. Under these circumstances Marston's request might seem., a strange one; but he had always had a great regard for Gunter as the soul of good- nature, and moreover as-the possessor of a peculiarly chivalrous. and trustworthy disposition. pActing on an impulse, he had resolved to lay 7the whole matter before Jack, taking' care to -.place especial stress upon the ease and smoothness with which the-1 operation cotild be carried out. As we have seen, this line Of areal/tent proved convincing, Jack being, more- over, suddenly seized with the idea that!the incident, would prove intenSely amusing to Hew:: who loved a good Story, and Who, for all he knew; might turn up at; any moment. The elopement was entirely successful. About half- past ten one wintrymorning Mies Nellie Custance left. her father'e house, Which lay about a mile out of Even- den, with the expressed intention of visiting the local dressmaker. Very neat and prettyfild Miss Nellie look in her ulster and hat, with a becoming flush on her , winsome face. At soinething to eleven Miss Nellie entered the dressmaker's house, and at sonsething.pastt issued from it much altered, being now attired in a bonnet. with yedloy, flowers, an entirlydifferent dress, and a new jacket. Her face was hes; Xy velliscl; and on her way to the station she failed to attract any of the respectful recognition usually accoißed to Lawyer Cns- tance's -pretty daughter. Miss Nellie arrived at the station about twenty-five minutes past eleven, took her . ticket,, and' retired to the general -waiting-room. In a few, mintrteir time a large gentlemen , acrlearecl, and carried her off to the 11.35 up train. The morning was fine, the train was a fast one, and after the first awkwardness was over, Jack and Nellie became excellent frietids, . 'lndeed, it lilig with a distinct feeling of regret that-the former surrendered his Charge to Marstbh, who, vsag waiting with ill-concealed impatience on the arrival platform. It was, however, easy to- see from; Nelliet's ' face that, grgteful as she might 'betoJack for the good service he had rendered, she was not very loth to quit his protection for that of her enamoured Charles. J'ack returned to his rooms srather low-spirited, as tender-heartedbachelors are wont temporarily to be when they have just seen a friend carry off a charming bride. Moreover, for some 'obscure reason:he:was beginning to feel dissatisfied with the *part he had him- self played in this business, well regulated and successful though it had been. Running away with a girl on one's own account is, aproceas which to as esgtain extent is- hallowed by precedent; and has, betides, a flavour of romance which is not altogether displeasing. 'But thie acting" as 'proxy ' for another man was a different matter, and now that it was over, Jack- became rather- offended with himself for having acceclN so readily. to Marston's extraerdinarwrequest. Of ' course, the in- cident a little embellished would make a good story for Ilenry,butJackbegan to think he would not care to have it generally known. Perhaps it would be as well, at any rateSto ask the Marstons not to mention' to any tone for the present the details of theelopement. Acting on which reflection; Jack sat down and wrote 4 feWlines to Charlie, which he despatched by hand to the hotel from which-he knew the 'Marston would start that afternoon oripiir wedding trip. • ' -' Lunch and a cigar brought about a more comfortable frame of mind; and Jack was pondering over the- ad- - visability of, a stroll, when, bY one of those' curious coincidences- which happen Jauch oftener' in real life than in fiction, Henry Treheme =arched unconcernedly into the room, took a chairt,' remarked that it was cold, end inquired pleasantly after his brother's health. He seemed in excellent spirits and much more carefully, dressed than 'usual,. a fact duly noticed by Jack,. as he greeted him with impulsive fond- etess. . "Why, what's happened to you, old chap?, You are- looking as fresh as a daisy,and as neat as if you had lust come out of a bandbox! Off to Paris this time; k sop- pose, instead of Greenland,or Madagascar, or some other 1 lof your usdal haunter ' - '. .-, " No," replied Henry, quietly; "I am not going to I tratel ag,ain just yet. 'I think 'tit settling down for a bit, ;lack, and have come to talk my plans over with you." '..'" Capital t -and when you have done that, I have a 'lstifiry to tell you—the tee of my morning'S doings, which I think will rather interest you. But sit-closer to the tire; Harry, ond have a drink." ." The, two brothers had just Settled down- to a cosy chat When the door opened, and Charlie • Marken put In his shSeheesaelaniddg, j.tooanc.kchoeims7vmegacuttlfithetO6 belstahcrtempane;l±. :gem.. bias' over owhvaaedsr I answer to his note. Of course neither he nor Mrs.' ' lliealw aa r r called,Yiat i. n g in a cab at the doOr—to give Jack a- verbal Marston would ever breathe a word of Jack's share in i the elopement. "Thanks, very much," said Gupter, ,MuCh, relieved; "the only: man I propose telling is my brother Henry, - who has past turned up in his usual sudden fashion. By the way, I don't think.! have ever told yen about him; Such a good scgt; you positively must. come in and make his acquaintance." ' "I really can't, my dear Gunter. Couldn't leave my wife alone for another instant. Having run away. once, I don't know how sooh she mayn't take to it again." 1 "But why not ask her to come up, too? I know the; ttain by which you are going, and it aloeent tits* for another half-hour. Far better wait here, than_ in that dirty station. Come, I insist upon it; I certainly have a right to be treatedas a friend -of the •faroily, and my- brother is my alter ego." . ... .• . , . , . With which words Jack 'hurried Charlie downstairs,' and a minute later was leading Mrs. Marston into hie sitting-room. Henry was looking out of the window, but turned to meet the new arrivals.' Poor Nellie had turned deathly pale, ind-Was clinging for support to her husband; and her husband and HenryTreherne'were glaring at one another lik two stage villains in a, duel with swords. - -.A VOYAGE TO lIIELBMINE. By RAWCLIFFB. :2V-A melancholy interest attaches ,to the following diary, as the writerrdied inanaedlately after copying it for the press. 'edit* of thiet jouritil feceived it the other day_ from Victoria. Australia, and along with it was a note _ . . . . .
, --, 7 i frern the sister-in-law of the writer, saytng that Ile.died on the evenOg of the day that he had fisished his`dfory. It should be added that Ntr: Rawelitfe bad gon6 otfrto Ass- _ _ . .
tralla in the last stage Of consumption. as"a Itst chance el

r arresting the disease. , Ha was well-knows and highly esteemed in Blackburn as a workman,w'no was skilful with his pen both in Prose and .verse.] , "Having for A long time been afflicted with that, what. I call teriible, ate qe, consumption, and . lutting,, after struggling with it so long, being advised by the doctor to go out, if. possible, ,to Australia as the only hope of prolonginglife,!l, paaed by many friends, made an effort; and started on the voyage. , • , ,•• • "The good ship Garonne, one of the Borg ,Mail' steamers of the Orient Line .M Which sailed,' was announced to sart on the let Sept., 1886; and; with the great bulk of passengers, I got aboard of her at the stated time; but, from whatever cause, the authorities kept us in the port of London until the 3rd. Well, the time passed over though to :me- slowly, but, perhaps, that may be accounted for 'through my unhealthy condition. "I thought I had dons, well to secure an enclosed cabin berth, for which .I gave £23, brit found out my mistake,- for my quarters and my food were no better than those of the steerage passengers, which cost only £16,161:At length we make,- as start, and everyone seems-ready to accept sea sickness and afl the rest of annoyances -as well as pleasures incident to 'an! .podean .voyage. We start,--li 25. am. the te-ir! day' the - weather iloe,:with rather .a- 'stiff breeTe. -Art tmany.seem quite jubilant When they age. reauroff. I havetead of people weeping at kiSing the sight of land, but I failed to find-any of this class on the Garonne; all seemed light-hearted, and all went 'Merry as a marriage pew good ship sped along, and scion we were, to the naked eye, out' of sight -of land until si.l4 o'clock, when the min, gave us a magnificeview of, Doves Male. k I could not help aoggetrelislnek
Oh, the white:chalk. cliffs of • &Nei: hoyr, beautiful you

are Unto the anxious voe4ger'wliaelees you from afar— . I Not frowning, no,,blit 2miling on our good ship as we Pass Along the pleasant waterereNch are green as Brin'S grass! ' _ 1 ,) ' "'Sailing all- nigheewe atriv •ed at Plymouth at 12 15, p.m, and, after receiving ,a few more passengers, owe- stoning a delay of two hours, off we speed kgam. ' 'Now we rough it through the Bey of, lliscaY. As I Write (Sunday, Sept. sth), 7 30 a.m., we are waiting for the Irish stew, coffee, and bread andebutter. The waters of the bay are very envy indeed,- so • angry that one can scarcely stand up on deckhel am free as yet from sea- sickness, but have got notice,. as I am very poorly and so weak that I .can. hardly .get up . the-hatchway, rk4 'take it cool.' 11 a.m.—l have just bean to the Catholie Chapel, or place set, apart for, the Catholics aboard to . worship. There were four, Irish priests; threasiaters of mercyeand a congregation of about 40. „ It-seemed-e 0 me like holding service or. • sacrificing mass under dime epie,iee,,for they used, in lieu .of smell bell, a half-pint glass and a erusher, which, I must say,, did their Work remarkably well. Coniitigemit of the chapel, I find' the water to be blowing. over, top-deck, and many women going sick. I:find by conversation that we have about a soore of men aboard who really belong to the Austra- lian-colonies, having simply been paying-visits to the old country. Without exception you could get nothing from them but praises for the colonies, and were ready to defend all and everything belonging to them at all hazards. "Sept. 6th, 11 a.m.—Have now had a day's sea-sick- ness, and, what with being without food, and hiving so much waste on me, I feel completely done-up. We are not yet through the bay, and the air 'is so thick that the fog-signal-has to be kept going—belching worse than a factory "buzzer." Three o'clock p.m.—Fog! fog!! fog !! ! nothing but fog I must, however, be on top- deck, however foggy or cold it isonorderto keep breath- ing as easily as possible. The pea-soup we had to dinner I rather liked; it has been the only food I have partaken of with any degree of relish since coming aboard. From Plymouth I Sent a leeter home, and hope to send another on leaving Naples.' It is, I find, a strain upon the affections to' part thus—probably for ever—but while there is life there is hape, and a great many people live almost on it: "Tuesday Morning, September 7th.—Had a 'rather rough night. The ship melted all the time, and is still rocking like a eradle. One half of the seals are sea sick, I amongst the number. I have crawled npwards to. the top deck, and, after vomiting aped deal, am just able 'to make a few notes. What a jingling of pots and pans ' and tins tumbling about in all directions, all through the' night. The sailors say that we are not far from the Spanish coast. .10 a.m. After some drizzling rain, and an angry sea, the sun peeps out, and with still a good stiff breeae, we sail past Lisbon. Those on deck seem livelier, but a rattnany of us seem but half awake. Now we pass Cape. t. Vincent, and huge romantic rocks all I alone the coast, . with no houses save and except two lighthouses and a Monastery, standing close to the edges of the cliffs. Aa we slowly passed the first lighthouse the ship's colours were hoisted, ancompaniea by the buzzing noise from the engines, such as we hear at short intervals during e thick fog. Some- time elapsed before there appeared a response, and an Irishman beside me said, "Ah, he's not at home ; or why does he not come nut ? Ah, there,. I see his head out of the window !" This was correcteand.immediately a flag was peen ,from the lighthou.se, when the ship's colours were hauled down again. . "Wednesday morning, Sept. Bthr-I find that whilst we have been sleeping we have passed the Straits of Gibraltar, and are steering ahead up the Mediterranean, the weather in the early morning (seven o'clock) being quite warm, she sea- calm, and the- day likely- for be- coining very hot. The crew just now are busily en- gaged putting or fixing up the awnings to keep, off the scorching sun. 530 p.m.—The day' throughout has been, hot, but now as-evening comes on, with_ a calm sea, how pleasant !—bat the joys the sweetest are the fleetest. After havingtime to look round me ancbconverse with a great many of the voyagers, .I begin to think we have aboard as good a class as ever sailed the blue seas. Many of the ladies and theirymlng daughters pa.gs in a use- ful way4helr time. viz: e—by knitting or sewing; while the gentlemen play. cards, dominoes, or draughts. After twilight has closed in the Carnival commences. Music,. instrumental and vocal, songs sentimental and comic, some in one place, and Others in another, blenchtogether in a sort of wild cadence, reminding one of the witches in the Kirk of " Tara.o'-Shanter " immortality. The revelry is alvrays kept .np until ten. Many a tints, while laid in my berth, .have I been moved to tears by some old song. When .the sea was rough, coming through the Bay of Biscay, otie Platy sang" Oh where is my boy to night?" and I must leave you to judge how Pfelt. Thursday, Sept. 9tlse—After a fair night's rest I find we are still scudding along the calm, blue Mediterranean, the weather all that one could wish. What comical things those eea porpoises are! Here- there are hun- .reds leaping about three or four feet out of the water, as if they were practising diving. I have seen porpoises before, but never it such large numbers, or its such close Proximity. According to the lee We have the 'last. 24 hours travelled at the rate of za miles, and the day be- fore 304 miles; so, barring foggy weather,, and being obliked to stop in the Suez Canal, we shouldatverage per 24 linurs 300 miles. . "Friday, Sept. lOth.—Another sunny day,. with a fresh breeze and a calm sea, as we pass just before dinner the Sardinian coast, and all seems well aboard. Cut off from the rest of the world by the deep Waters,. all on board seem to draw closer together, for NIW are as one fanully, and, every day, are becoming .to know each other better.. We meet together very .often and in a familiar manner, and not one, from starting, has ever been known to leave the house, so domesticated have we become!. As for tramps, a thing is unheard of, and bu:glars here have no foothold. Saturday, Sept. llthelase been. qniteean extraordinary day on board the Garomne—quite a grand holiday or- gala, so to speak, and for all who could go on deck there was something more to look at than the broad expanse of waters. All the day we were sailing on the calm waters amid sunny weather, gliding; by romantic castles, monasteries, lighthouses, &c., built on the jagged rind butting rocks. We passed the island of Sicily, and, at a little before 2 p.m. we dropped anchor neat the foot of Mount Vesuvius; which was burning mid emitting large volumes of smoke. A salute of one gun. was fired ' on account,l suppose, of our ship; bearing the Royal Mail. I, of course, shall net attempt to describe my ideas as I first saw Naples with its magnificent bay and its still more magnificent surroundings—its white- fronted buildings standing in • such a pieturescene position. The cleverest descriptionist could not convey to ,the mind even a faint idea of the- whole scenery of the clas6o city as seen from the water.. We were anchored in the bay three hours, and a good many took advantage and went in the boats ashore, bringing beck baskets of fruit, such as peaches, tome- OeSe grapes, lemon, &c., as well as little trinkets as ilheivenird Of their' short visit. As for myself, I was afraid of being left among the Neapolitans, so; like the majority, I remained aboard, and was much amused'by watching, from the ship's Side, the dealings of those there with the vendors of fruits, fancy baskets, caskets,

Mr. Bradley was standing not more than a foot from the telephone when it began ringing: 'lnstantly applying the instrument to his ear, and calling "Hello !" he heard some one's voice faintly back . "Hello! .Is that Mr. Bradley ?" . " Yes," he replied. "Who are you?" - "Is it Mr. Henry A. Bradley, of Cohort Hill?". „ . . . '• "Yes, sir, that is, my name and residence. Who are you?" . - ~„ . . . "You inust not be 'surprised, Mr. Bradley, but I ani a burglar in your house on Colton Hill?" • "What on the living earth do you mean ?" . "Just what I say—a burglar in your hotrie on Colton Hill, and talking with you here at the telephone. You are necessarily excited by this information, but try to ' cpmpose yourself," the squeaking voice went on. "Great Heavens!, CorApose myself i You, infamous scoundrel, what are you doing in My house?" - - • "Precisely what I have said, Mr. 'Bradley. I au h professional burglar—l really hope you will take this quietly. It will be to your advantage, you know; 'Will show you that." -. - "I shall take it quietly, you poor sinner, by starting a squad of police up the hill after you in less than, ten minutes. Say your prayers for strong legs, for -you will need them more than you :ever did before." - "You cannot do it; sir. Listen to me, and I will show you that I know all about the situation. In the first Plakk., your heuse is the only one on this hill;exeept Mr. Boyd's, immediatelyacross the street, and heAsaway in the country for theaummer. .In the second pMee,, the , nearest inhabited house is half a mile- distant,'. at the foot of the hill, -..,and the nearest telephone,- except the one , in. your, neighbour Boyd's, is at Winchester, five ' miles off. ' Now, 1 know yo e might 'ring Up the Win= &ester telephone, but it is a long way off, and besides; tarps, is .p.o squad of policemen there. I should not otider'if the town"s.'sirigle, gearldilinlwbre-aiteepoine- , whert3 lira darner:- 'Don't pin-tee-that I knew all abofit , thelriadi,and thitt.yon harVbetter lieopersuaded-tc...take .it quietly?.',, ' '• . • • t,. 0,, l• . . • ~ __ ; "What id teq.ue,uce do you want, anyho* 1" queried ' Mr., B IfT, ..Ikliaring the question with which, the, 1 burglar lad ended. {i) ' "For o e matter, to assure you that lam perfectly well'peitted itrall ybur affairs, which Will take-but'a few 'words. You are by present occupation, Mr. Bradley; 1 treasurer of :the Nonontauk-Woollen .Mills-.-" . "That's correct enough." 1 "—And the 30th of every nienth you go outitf: the milis-With tentliousandAollais..in greettbariks tote up in a bundle,- like groceries, for pay-day.".. ~-.1.-" yes; we Pay our employes monthly.", . . "You iided net be at thetroxible,of answering; : I:Will go right through Neith the facts of the case. As I,.say, the 30th ofbevery iSionthyou go out to' the mills. Well, the 30th came yesterday; but' you missed the Lowell express, which you usually take, and you had to post- pone your trip until to-day, So, you took the local train.watea.d, and you came mit to Cel;*id Hill, bringing the inenoyhenie with, yod. Then in the main, when sitting at supper, you told your wife, that yoli disliked carrying the greenbacks so much about, and that you would leave them in the house until this afternoon, when you would call for them on the way to the : mills. • Have I been correct ?" " Possibly ;. but I 'must tell you that money is not there. It wili he a !great. disappointment to; you, butt brought it into the, office this morning." - ' "Well, well, I will try to bear it. But listen to the rest of my tale:: After sapper_ you apPeared to hide those greenbacks in someplace upstairs, and,tliis morn. ing, for some reason, when you started for Boston with your wife, you did not leave flee bundle which you brought. home with you yesterday..ow .am I to understand ' that?" 1 • . -- r - '"By, the use oi your. reasoning 'faculty, :There are' many ways'of carrying money." , "My_n•easoning.'faculty is just what_ troubles me; the more I reason,, the more I am convinced that the money is here in this house. Of course you will never admit it without some inducement, and I therefore have a plan to propose for the adjustment of this whole matter—on a basis of mutual benefit I mean. I will now state it. My name is Smith, by-the-way!' "Very well, Mr.fimith. I cannot say that lam glad to make your ,acquaintance. I must say that our preseut relation seems tome very unconventional." - . e "Unconventional, Mr. Bradley, yes,' but not without. its conveniences. - Just see. . Though a burglar in this house, I sin able, by means of the latest refinement Of civilized invention, to converse with the very owner hinl-` seff,who knows all its nooks and corners.. And you also,' the owner, are presont at an ocCerfence of great import.' once to yourself. instead of remaining ignorant until all. is over, as nivallyhappens." •. . " Oh, Well, if you: talk in that way. Pray how and. when did you enter my•house, Mr. Smith, and how am ,I to know that you are, ;in fact, talking with me Iron* there, and not from gome other point on the line ?" "I entered at the rear kitchen 'window ris soon as I 'saw you and Mrs. Bradley stertdown the hill. You can easily makeaure of my presence' here by Listing me some question about the room," - "Very well. There is a small picture over the tele- phone. , Can you describe it?" "I can. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 415 p.m. CONTINTIOUS RAILWAY Basirm.—EarlDatawanacalled attention to the circular of theßoard of Trade with re- gard to continuous railway brakes, and asked if it was the intention of Government to takeany steps to enforce the requirements, and moved for a return of the number of servants in the employ of each company who are regularly on du..3, for more than 12 hours consecutively. —Lord &Aster or PEssron had nothing to add to the reply he had preiriously given. The Etoard of Trade felt the importance of the question, and did not intend to relax any effort to bring moral pressure to bear upon railway companies to induce them to increase the brake power necessary for the safe-conduct of trains. He had no reason to suppose railway companies insensible to that moral pressure, and since the last Board a Trade circular large extensions had been made of brake power to trains. Be had no objection to grant the return asked for. The motion was agreed to.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Lord Imam/Inc called attention to the urgent neces- sity for farther legislation in order to deal with the dis- order and lawlessness existing in Ireland. He aSserted that the people of England were nbt aware of what was going on in Ireland, and that many of the loyal class in the latter country asked whether there was; any Govern- ment except the Land League. He called for the sup- pression of that League, whatever the results might be. That step would dissociate the priests from an organisa- tion in which they were acting as local leaders. Tlavtn2 observed that the plan of -campaign was put in opera- tion on the 23rd of October last, he pointed out that no action was taken by the Government, either to proclaim its illegality or announce an intention to put it-down, till the week before Christmas. As to remedial legisla- tion to follow the restoration of law and order, he recom- mended doing away with dual ownership in the land by the extension of Lord Ashbourne's Act, emigration when it could be carried out with the will of the people, and reproductive works; but he held that if the Union was to be maintained law and order must be at once re-estab- lished._

Lord Basaotnont, while admitting that the crisis was* grave one, was allowing the Government their own time to act in the direction indicated by Lord Inchiquin. Having denounced the aims of the Nationalist Land Leagurers, he asked whether it was true that Sir T. Esmonde, who had been engaged in carrying out the plan of campaign, had been appointed High Sheriff of Waterford. Lord Mmr-a-row was convinced of the necessity of dealing with the Land Act of 1831, and held that dual ownership by Statute was impracticable. He was much disappointed at having heard from Lord Granville no denunciation of those who were endeavouring to confis- cate the property of the landlords. Lord DE Ros concurred with those who thought that legislation was required for the protection of the property of landowners in Ireland.

Lord CADOGAN did not think a desultory conversation such as that raised by Lord Inchiquin was calculated to strengthen the hands of the Government. He denied that there had been any neglect on the part of the Government in carrying out the law, though the plan of campaign was published in a newspaper on the ;3rd of October, no overt act in furtheranee of the conspiracy was committed for some time after that date. Sir T. Esmondes had been appointed by the Lord Chancellor of Ireland because his name was the first on the list of those returned to his noble and learned friend as eligible to-serve the office of High Sheriff of the county of Waterford ;' but he had no doubt that if sines his appointment the bon. baronet bad committed a breach of the law he would be dealt with for having done so. He quoted statistics to show that actual outrages had decreased in Ireland, but referred to the queen's speech at the opening of the session to show that the Govern- ment were not insensible to the gravity of the situation, and were determined to bring forward measures which wouldstrengthen theirpowers, now inadequate, of dealing with that situation. _ _ _

Lord Fr=azkatia did not doncur in what had been said in condemnation of the Act of 1881, because he re- garded the principle of security of tenure established by that statute as one of great value. He entirely con- curred with those who advocated the firm maintepauce of law in Ireland; and, referring tek the calumill• and vituperation to which the Judges there were subjected; he spoke of the bad effects which the language used about those learned personages must have on the minds of the people who read it in newspapers, which were their only sources of information. Their Lordships rose at 7 10 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Moun&z.

He would cause inquiry to be made into any specific allegations. SIR H. DRUMMOND WOLFF.—Mr. S. WILLIAMSON asked whether her Majesty's Government weie considering the propriety of speedily putting an end to the burden on the taxpayers which Sir H. D. Wolff's mission imposed, —Mr. W. H. Swim said Sir H. D. Wolff was engaged in the conduct of difficult and delicate negotiations at Con- stantinople on Egypt, and it was not therefore the inten- tion of her Majesty's Government at present to termi- nate his mission. IRISH LAND PURCHASE.—Mr. W. H. Syrrryr, replying to Mr. J. Ellis, said that under Lord Ashbourne's Irish Land Purchase Act £1,64t),405 had been advanced and applications for advances amounting to £383,764 were now under consideration. AMENDMENTS TO THE ADDREBS.—MT. SHAW-LEE/3,7RD asked Sir R. Paget if he intended to proceed with his amendment to the Address on the condition of agricul- ture ?—Mr. W. H. Sierra appealed to the hon. gentletnan not to press it, and to the House to allow the business of the session to proceed with the least possible delay.--Sir R. PAGET said he would not move his amendment to the Address.—Mr.SllAW-LEFEVRE said he had an amendment On the hon. baronet's amendment. If the latter was withdrawn It would be a'-question with him whether he should move it on report.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: ADDRESS.
div.p: THE ADDRESS.

The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed Mr. ESSLEMONT drew attention to the grievances of the Scotch leaseholders, especially -those still subject to the law of hypothec, and moved an - amendment expresslng regret that it is not proposed to inquire int 9 their excep- tional position. Mr. ANDERSON seconded the amendment, and appealed to the Secretary for Scotland to Shorten the discussion by granting an inquiry; but Mr. HALDANE protested against the .amendment as causing needless waste of, time. .If the subject required discussion at all it should' be raised by a separate motion or bill. Mr. A. J. BArAroun declined to accept the amendment, remarking that if the facts alleged were known to exist inquiry would be superfluous, quid if granted it would only raise hopes which could not be realised. He declined to assent to the breaking of contracts by Act of Parlia- , liament, and peinted'out that if the principle was once' admitted it would be impossible to draw the line at Con- tracts between landlord and tenant. .

Sir G. BALForre and Mr. WALLACE spoke in support of the amendment; and Mr. SIIIREA.WILL justified legisla- tive interference with contracts if moral reasons required it.---Mr. M. Stewart and Sir A. Campbell defended the action of Scotch landlords, and Mr. A. L. Brown dwelt upon the evils which had resulted from the law of hypo- thec.—Mr..l. C. BOLTON sympathised with the Scotch farmers, but thought the case of the leaseholders had been much exaggerated, and saw no moral or legal rea- son to justify Parliamentary interference.—Mr. BAR- CLAY contended that the importance of the question fully warranted its discussion, and pointed,to the Crofters Ant of last pear as a precedent for further legislation on land tenure in Scotland.—Mr. C. GRAY spoke against the amendment; and Mr. Beuce,also speaking against it, argued that to put an end to leases would have a detri- mental effect on Scotch agriculture.—Mr. Id`LAAsu canvassed the objections to leases, which, he contended, were as advantageous to tenants as to landlords. bat thought that an inquiry into the subject mightlave beneficial results.—Dr. Ctanx treated thp subject from the economical point of view; and Mr. C. PARKER, while doubting whether the case of the leaseholders Was so serious as had been alleged, advocated an inquiry, which, he thought, would open the minds of thote who were net acquainted with the system of land tenure, and might induce landlords to be lenient with their tenants. —Dr. M`DoNALD insisted that an ample case for in- quiry had been made out.—Sir D. CURRIE was against the amendment, believing that such an interference was not desired by the Scotch tenant farmers, although he thought they required relief in other respeots.—On a division the amendment was negatived by 198 to 96. Sir G. CAMPBELL next moved his amendment, submit- ting that the affairs of the realm have outgrown the capacity of the House, and calling for a Ministerial measure by which the special affairs of Scotland and other parts of Great Britain may be relegated to bodies representing the several parts of the kingdom.—Mr. FRASER-MACKINTOSH seconded the amendment ; and after some remarks from Dr. Cameron and Mr. J. O'Connor (Tipperary), Mr. A. J. BALFOUR, enlarging upon the meagre character of the proposal and the inco- herent form in which it had been submitted to the House, pointed out the impossib,ility of giving due con- sideration to so import.aut a subject at such a period of the debate.---filr. E. H.ARRINGTON and Mr. Huarriza also spoked—The amendment was then withdrawn, and the debate adjourned on the, motion of Dr. Cebtanotr. After other business, the House adjourned at a 9s„
