GORST said that there was no report from General Stewart after the 28th of November, but previous to the 24th of December the whole of- the military reports as to the ruby mines' expedition were included in the papers already pub- THE SCOTCH CRosTens.—Dr. Cameron took advantage of the debate on the address to raise discussion on the posi- tion of the Scotch crofters, his amendment proposing to represent to her Majesty that recent events in Skye and Thee, and the general administration of justice in the High- lands, had caused serious concern to the people of Scotland, and demanded a full inquiry. When speaking had been maintained on this theme for an hour or two in a thin House the crofters' friends became somewhat irritated at the small degree of interest they Inspired on the Ministerial side of the House. A motion for adjournment was made and even I carried to a division in order to remedy this state of things, I and the Lord Advocate, hurrying in from the dining-room, I found himself suddenly called upon to make excuse for not I himself carrying on debate. In due time ho did reply with a spirited defence of Scotch justice, and the contention that there was no conceivable use for inquiry. The debate was ultimately adjourned and the House adjourned at 20 mins sites to one. HOUSE OF COMMONS.---Wasseestar. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. THE SCOTCH Ceoprzes, &c,—The debate on the Crofs ters Question was kept up until nearly the close of the site, ting, without eliciting any concession from the Government, the Scottish Secretary adhering to the resolution announced. by the Lord Advocate to refuse idquirv. The amendment was negatived by 253 votes to 136. Mr. Sexton's motion then to adjourn the debate led to a mildlv-worded but on- I mistakably earnest protestation from the Leader of the House against the further continuance of the discussion—at all events at this stage of the Address.—Mr. PARNELL re- plied coldly with the reminder that serious things were tak- ing place in Ireland, and that if the First Lord of the Trea- sury did not consent to the adjournment it would have to be accomplished in the ordinary way.—The thing thus said, was done by Mr. M. Kenny, who talked till the hour when debate on Wednesday is adjourned by operation of the Standing Order.—The First Lord of the Treasury gave notice of his intention to move for precedence for the con- sideration of the Procedure Rules after the debate on the Address. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tarrnsislor. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a smarter after four o'clock. Loan Duturavere's Resmitesamea.—The Earl of Dna- RAVEN explained why he had felt it incumbent upon him to resign his appointment as Under Secretary for the Colonies. He had not resigned on a matter connected with colonial policy. He regretted that they had felt it necessary to say that they must apply to Parliament for further powers as to Ireland. The reason law was not respected in Ireland was not because of its origin, but because it was not carried out. But the main point which influenced him was that of economy, and he felt that no inquiry would produce any good and permanent results unless retrenchment was made a condition precedent of any overhauling of the pub- lic accounts.-The MARQUIS of SALISRuRY said he was unable to understand the points of the noble earl's objection to the Irish policy of the Government. The only method of effect- ing public economy was to carefully examine all the items of expenditure and the object to which that expenditure was devoted. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes after five ' o'clock. „„sseSaHOUSE OF COMMONS.—DatmsaaV. • The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Isis AAIBLESIDE RAILWAY BlLL.—There was a lone de- bate on the motion of the second reading of the Ambleside Railway Bill, the rejection of which was moved by Mr. BRYCE, who described it as a contractors' line, and said it had no support from the best part of the inhabitants of the district.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. H. H. HOWARTIL—Upon a division the second reading was carried by 189 to 177. • LIE TRIAL IN DUBLIN.—Mr. DILLWYN moved to ad- jouru the House in order to call attention to a matter of de- finite and urgent importance—viz, the irregularities which have taken place at the trial at Dublin.—The SPEAKER declined to put the motion, on the ground that there was on the paper a motion standing in the name of M. Sexton for the first of March to call attention to the effects of the system of jury packing pursued by agents of the Govern- ment. PROCEDURE.—Mr. Sumer moved that the consideration of the proposed rules of 'procedure have precedence of all orders of the day and notices of motion on every day on which the consideration of those rules may be set down by the GoveraMent.—Mr. RICHARD moved as an amendment that Tuesday next be excepted from the operation of the motion when the question of Disestablishment in Wales would come up.—The amendment was rejected by 261 to 150.—Mr. PARNELL asked the Government to except from the motion Wednesday next, which the Irish members had Secured for a bill for including leaseholders within the Land Act of 1881.—The amendment was rejected by 242 to 107, and the motion relating to the rules of procedure was agreed to. • THE ADDRESS: CLOSURE APPLIED.—The debate OR the Address was resumed by Mr. Distort, who said he had left the court at Dublin to appear before the House to impeach the manner in which that trial was being conducted. The

at my a. -. ...era in April, , _net Mr. Hedgcock endorsed on the back of the invoice the state- ment which appears thereon at my request. Sworn this 11th day of February, 1887.—Grzonom HAZLEHURST, dis- trict auditor. In some further evidence which he gave, Mr. Hazlehurst said th t, knowing the object of the altera- tion, which was to make a payment legal which in itself was illegal by flux of ime, he called upon the master for his explanation, but he disclaimed all knowledge how the erasure had taken place ,and said that he could afford no further information about it. That was all that passed on the first day. On the next day he was so diseatisfied with the want of explanation that, knowing the Guardians were meeting, he determined to bring it before the chairman of the Board. When, at an interview held in the adjoining room, the master again disclaimed all knowledge of the affair. He (the auditor) on that occasion called the chair- man out of the Board-room. He could not give the words used by-Mr. Mackey.—ln reply to Mr. J. C. Sutton, Mr. liazlehursr said that before the discovery of the erasure by his clerk no communication whatever had been conveyed to him with regard to the account.—ln reply to Mr. Jeans, Mr. Hazlehurst said he could not give the exact words used by Mr. Mackey when he said he knew nothing about the era- sure. He added that it was not a common occurrence to find alterations in accounts.—Mr. JEANS : IS it usual to kick up such a row as this on every occasion ?—Mr. Hann- HIIReT : I cannot say that.—Mr. JEANS: I suppose this would be a trifling offence but for Mr. Mackey denying it ? Mr. HAZLEHUBST : By no means.—Mr. JEANS: Of course altering the account is a mere trifle ?—Mr. HAZLEITURST : There is a design in this alteration.—Mr. JEANS said be happened to have in his hand a letter which came from Mr. Sutton's office. He then read the letter, which was dated 2nd February, 1880, and was addressed from Mr. Sutton's office to Mr. Mackey, the initials of the writer "W. E. being given. It ran as folloWs :—" Will you please get in and pay to the treasurer any accounts due for atones (except barrack steees) as the Union funds are limi- ted at present. With regard to an old balance of 8s 9cl due to Mr. R. Heaton, an invoice account, perhaps the easiest way to deal with it will be for you to pay it through your petty cash as an invoice account. With regard to the claim I of Mr. Bromley (1636dt, the Local Government Board will only allew 4s 6d, and 143 6d should have been paid before the 31st December last, so if you pay that amount to Mr. Bromley through your receipt and payment book, you had better get him to date the receipt before the end of Decema ber last. It should be charged in receipt and payment book as invoice account. I enclose two small accounts from Mr. J. C. Wright." He (Mr. Jeans) begged to submit that that was an equally enormous offence to the one they had under consideration.—Mr. SUTTON: I should like to see the letter. —Mr. JEANS said he did not make any imputation on Mr. Sutton. The letter was written by one of his clerks.—Mr. Sut- ton having read tho letter, remarked that it was written before Mr. Hazlehurst's time as auditor.—Mr. JEANS asked what had been the result in other cases in which he had made a similar discovery as that with regard to the erasure in the account.—Mr HAZLEHURST said he was not aware that he had ever hunt case of such designed erasure as that one.— In answer to Mr. Sutton, Mr. Hazlehtirst said the action he had taken with regard to the erasure had certainly not been upon the suggestion of anybody. Mr. GEO. KAY, the chief clerk of the auditor, next gave evidence, which was corroborative of that of the previous witness. When Mr. Mackey, he said, was called upon for an explanation as to the account, his reply was to the effect that he knew nothing whatever about it.—ln answer to Mr. Sutton, Mr. Kay said that prior to his discovering the era- sure, no suggestion or communication whatever had been made to him with regard to it by anyone. He had no pre- vious knowledge of it whatever,—ln answer to Mr. VoiseYs witnesa said he had been in this district five years, and he had before seen erasures in accounts. He bad seen half-a. dozen sucherasures, but he should not like to swear that he had seen twenty.—ln answer to Mr. Jeans, he said he had never seen a similar alteration to bring accounts within dates, Tha Rev. G. F. Roberts, chairman of the Guardians, and Mr. Ratcliffe, a member of the Board of Guardians, next gave evidence, both stating that they were present on one of the occasions when Mr. Mackey was asked if he knew any- thing of the erasure, and that they understood him to say that he knew nothing about it. Mr. 8. Sutton, assistant ckerk, gave similar evidence. In answer to Mr. Jeans, Mr. Sutton added that he had no knowledge of the alteration in the account previous to its discovery by the auditor, and he had never been to Mr. Hedecock about it before he was sent by the auditor. Mr. B. Shearer, relieving officer, spoke ' to having heard the auditor ask Mr. Mackey if he knew anything about the erasure, and Mr. Mackey replied to the effect tiaat he did net. Mr. Henley they asked Mr. Mackey if he wished to give evidence. Mr. Mackey said a great injastice had been done to him in that matter. There had had been misrepresenta- tions to the Local Government Board, of which no proof had been called that day. From the position he was in he did not see how he could speak out with any degree of safety to himself. He had been persecuted there for years. and worried almost to death. After some further conversation, Mr. Mackey decided to be sworn, when he stated that he was present at the audit on. the 191 h January, 1886. He produced his books and invoices. The invoice produced was amongst the others, and Mr. Kay called his attention to it, and the auditor asked him if he knew anything about it. He replied that he would say nothing about it. There was nothing else passed in reference to this question on the 19th January. On the 20th the auditor called him into the Board-room, and called the attention of the chairman (Mr. Roberts) to the invoice. The chairman looked towards him (Mr. Mackey), but did not ask him any questions. He (Mr. Mackey), however, added that he would say nothing about it. He did not think anything else passed. His reasons for giving those answers were that he believed the matter would be reported to the Local Government Board and he would reserve his defence until be heard from them. —Mr. Henley asked how did he (Mr. Mackey) know that the Local Government Board would ever know of the era- lure; and why did he not give an explanation to the auditor when he was willing to explain to the Local Government Board ?—Mr. Mackey: Because I once before gave the auditor what I considered very satisfactory explanations in

regard to another matter' which was, however, reported over and over again to the Local Government Board.— In, reply to Mr: Voisev, Mr. Mackey said he knew of ar erasure when the auditor spoke to him about it.—Mr. Voisey : Had you been a party to the act of doing it yobrself ?--Mr. Meaccv— Certainly not. It_was done without my knowledge or before I knew anything about it. Mr. VorsEv.—Then when you rtplied to the auditor on the 19th Br 20th you did not in- tend to deny this actual knowledge? .Mr. MACKEY.— Certainly not. Mr. 134csmunsr.—In the case of this :era- sure not having been detected would you have considered it your duty to have it pointed it out? Mr. MaCKEY.—I be- lieve I should have done so. The INSPECTOR.—Then why did you not do so? Mr. MACEBY.—I was waiting an oppor- tunity to do so.—Mr. HENLEY.—Yon had opportunity to do so on two days.—Mr.Maciorc.—The note Wad then taken and I thought it weuld be reported.—Mr Volsci: asked who made the erasure.—Mr. MACKEY replied it was made by Mr. George Webster an inmate who some time ago attempted to commit suicide. _ _ _

The Imintoroit soon after concluded the inquiry. He Intimated that he would report the matter as soon as possi- ble to the Local Government Board. The thing had dragged on for a very long time and it would be better for all parties that it should be decided one way or the other, as soon as possible. (Hear, hear.) He would take care that they had a speedy answer. The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS moved and Mr. Voisey seconded a vote of thanks to the Inspector for the manner in whith he had conducted the Inquiry, and the proceedings termina- ted.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF • GUARDIANS. •
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF • GUARDIANS. •

A meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Black- burst, Jolley, Derbyshire, Isherwood, Harrison, Gibson, gilshall, Ba'harry, Humphries, Wright, Ratcliffe, W. Houghton, Clarke, Grange, Jones; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton, (assistant clerk) ; GMeokey, (workhouse master).
THE SCHOOLS. The Medical officer reported that the health of the children at Padgate Schools was good.
SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that school fees had been allowed in 110 cases, four of which were new and 106 old.—Mr. BrAcarrtrusx moved the adoption of the minutes. —The CHAIRMAN remarked that there had been a decrease in the number of school fees allowed. The time before there were 125 and the time before that 185.—The minutes were confirmed. VACCINATION.—SATISFACTORY REPORT FROM NEWTON.

The CLERK submitted a number of vaccination returns for different townships in the union. The return for New- ton showed that between the Ist January and 31st Decem- ber, 1885, the number of births were 657; there had been 541 children successfully vaccinated; unsusceptible to vaccin- ated, 1; dead 53; postponement by medical certificate, 20; removals to districts known, 6 ;removals to places unknown, 25; unaccounted for, 11.—Mr. RATCLIFFE thought this re- port showed how little use prosecution was. If they deal. with people in a mild way they got them to vaccinate, but when they prosecuted and sold people goods other peoplt sympathised with them and were determined not to submie to force.—The CITAIIMAN said he should be very glad it they could do away with prosecutions altogether in vaccinf ation cases.—Mr. RATCLIFFE : I think it is a very satisfac- tory report; it showed that prosecution had not answered.- -Mr. CLARKE : I hope, Mr. Chairman the time will soon come when prosecutions in these cases is done away with.— The subject then dropped. RESIGNATION OF THE WORKHOUSE MASTER.

The CLERK referred to a letter that had been read by Mr. Jeans at the Local Government Board inquiry, relative to the workhouse master's case on the Friday previous, and having read some correspondence which took place at the time the other letter was written, and of which it was rust a part. His clerk, Mr. Evans, wrote the letter in question, and he had called upon him for an explanation, which he thought in fairness ought to be read. He then read the following statement, written by Mr. Evans, viz: . .

, "With reference to the letter, deed February 2nd, ma, which was referred th at the Government Inquiry on Friday list, and which was written by me in your name. I desire to make an explanation. Owing to the irregular manner in which the workhouse amounts were then got in many of them were allowed to run beyond legal date of payment. Conse- quently, we had to apply to the Local Government Board for orders enablitv• us to pay, and that course had been followed in this case. Upon this occasion three accounts were thus treated, viz.: IL Moss, £l4 7s lid; T Hutchinson, 21 lOs Od; and D. Bromley, 165 6d. The Local Government Board them- selves have only power to allow payment within twelve months of incurring the debt, and consequently att.:sok out 12s of BronVey's account and issued an order for the payment of the rest. This order was dated December 29th,. 1879, and limited the period of payment to December 31st. That day being Board thy we drew Messrs Moss and Hutchinson's ac- counts, and requested the mister to pay Bromley's at once through his oetty cash. This he neglected to do, hence my commu&cation of February 2nd. Had the Master done his duty in the first instance by collecting the accounts at the proper time, or in the second instance by paying the account on December 31st, as requested, no such communication would have been ne,essary. The whole matter was explained to the auditor, the order ot the Local Government Board pro- duced, and the at.count passed —Tour obedient servant, W. Evens."

Mr. MACKEY said he should like to have a copy of the statements just read in order that he might reply to them. —The CLERK then stated that he had received the follow- ing communications from the Local Government Board. The first of these communications was addressed to the clerk, and ran as follows : " I am °treated by the Local Government Board to transmit to yen for the inft,rmation of the Guardians of the Warrington Union the enclosed c)pv of a letter which the Board have this day addressed to Mr. G. Mackey requiring him to resign the office of master of the Workhouse. The Board requests that they may be informed whether Mr. Mackey has placed his resignation in the hands of the Guar- dians." _ _ _

The "enclosed copy" alluded to above as having been- I sent to Mr. Mackey was as follows : .' Local Government Board:ignitehall, til.W.,lsth February, 1887.—Sir,—I am direoted by the Local Government Board to state that they have received from their Inspector, Mr Healey, his report upon the official inquiry held by him into the charge against you of having made false statements to the District Auditor. The Board have also received a copy of the depositions of the witnesses examined at the inquiry. The Board are satisfied from the evidence that such false statement was in fact made by you on two consecutive days; and they must, therefore, desire you forthwith to place your resigna- tion in the hands of the Guardians. The Board direct me to add that unless you at once adopt this course they will be under the necessity of issuing an ordor under seal removing you from office.—l am, s:r, your obedient servant, (Signed) EDMUND WODEHOUSE, Assistant Sedretary."
The Clerk added that Mr. Mackey had sent in his resigna- tion, and read it as follows

Union Workhouse, 76, 2,,3857.—T0 the Guardians of the Warrington Union.— Gentlemen,—l beg to tender you my resignation as master of the Workhouse, the same to take place according to arrangement. I shall not have much to regret at leaving only that which I brought with me over 17 years ago, and which money cannot buy.—l an, gentlemen, your faith- , ful servant, G. lii.scirsy. _ .

Mr. BLACKHURST moved that the resignation of Mr. Mackey be accepted.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded this proposal.— The motion was then adopted unanimously.—After a little conversation it was decided to hold a committee meeting of the whole Board to take into consideration the appointment of a successor to Mr. Mackey. MR. AiACKEY ON HIS RESIGNATION.

Mr. MACKEY having asked to be allowed to make a state- ment, explained that Mr. Jeans was not instructed and did not represent him at the inquiry on Friday. In fact, had he I - had a legal man the result would have been very different. j Hs (Mr. Mackey) sat down passive and quiet as a protest against the inquiry being limited in the way it was. He sat in silent protest, and asked no questions. If the wit- nesses had been cross-questioned as to their words, there would have been a very different result; be had no hesita- tion in saying that. He should ask the Board to be allowed to make a reply to the statements previously made by the clerk.—The CHAIRMAN said the statements would be in print, and Mr. Mackey would then be able to make a reply. —Mr. MAcarßy said they were going into print for the pur- pose of misleading the public. Those things had been going on a long time, and in fact he had been persecuted thdre for years. He did not blame the Guardians because they had been prejudiced against him; they had not heard his side at all. He had been attacked from meeting to meeting in his absence by the clerk, who had misrepresented him in every possible way.—Mr. DAB.EYSHIRE: I think that is not the case.—Mr. MACKEY (to Mr. Derbyshire) : I have some- thing to say to you. Proceeding, Mr. Mackey said. he felt , very keenly not so much for the loss of the situation, but I on account of his character. He was then proceeding to address the clerk, when the CHAIRMAN remarked that they could not allow it.—Mr. MACKEY: You can allow me to be sacrificed by a clique; Mr. DaTbyshire is 6ue of them, I am sorry to say.—Mr. GIBSON: I move that Mr.. Mackey be ordered out of the room.—Mr. MACKEY : You will not order me out of the room; I will not leave the roem.—Mr. Grissom: You will leave it if the Board orders you.— Mr. MACKEY: 1 have a good deal more to say.—Mr. GIB- SON : Tell the truth then.—:llr. MACKEY replied that he was telling the truth. For four or five years he could not do wrong but the clerk had turned against him, and he then could not do right.—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Mackey had been given every latitude and every opportunity of saying anything that was to his advantage, but his (the chairman's) o i pinion was that t would be better for Mr. Mackey if he did not speak at all, but if he thought there had been any injustice done him he had full opportunity of I communicating that injustice to those who haedealt with the case, that was the Local Government Board. There I had also been every opportunity afforded Mr. Mackey by the press to contradict any statement that had been made in the press to his detriment.—Mr. MACKEY said he contra- dicted the statement in the minutes that he admitted bay- in z made the erasure himself.—Mr. BIACKIIIIRST : That did not affect the case.—Mr. MASKEY said it did •affect the case, because he had written to the Local Government Board to say it was Webster who made the alteration, and then they said he told a lie.—Mr. BLACKIIIIRST thought Mr. Maokey had a great deal of fancy grievances about him. He had formed his opinions and it appeared that nobody could turn him.—Mr. MACKEY said he wished his cTievances had only been fancy grievances--Mr. BLACKHURST : I am certain of it —The CHAIRMAN said that was a painful epis- sode, and he was glad it had come to an end. He was very

I sorry in many respects for Mr. and Mrs. Mackey an& their family, but he did not see how the Board could- have acted , more fairly.—Mr. Mackey : Ido not blame the Guardians What he complained of was the unfairness of the letters written to the Local Government Board. The CHAIRMAN said those letters had been investigated by the Local Government Board.—Mr Macurav said they had not: he had never got a copy of them, and a question had never been asked with regard to them.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he had not had the slightest feeling against Mr. Mackey, and he had given his evidence as truthfully as his memory would allow at the inquiry. He believed that had Mr. Mackey come forward in the first in- stance and thrown himself on the mercy of the Board things would have been different.—The conversation on this sub- ject having dropped for a while, Mr. DARBYSHIRE afterwards said that he thought the Clerk had acted in that matter honestly and straightforwardly from the beginning to the end. He thought it Mould be known that they did not at- tribute any importance to the imputations which Mr. Mackey had made against the clerk.—The CHAIRMAN men- tioned that they had passed a vote of confidence in the Clerk in connection with that matter, and he thought that was sufficient—Mr. HARRISON could not see any advantage in continuing the subject:—The discussion soon after drop- ped. •

div.head: AN APPOINTMENT.
div.p: AN APPOINTMENT.
Mr. and Mrs. R. Williams, of 24, Erwood-street, Warring- ton, were appointed tailor and parent respectively of No. 1 home at the Padgate Industrial School at an annual salary of £4O.
THE COIINTY RATE.

Some particulars with respect to the county rate were read by the CLERK, showing that the county rate proper was £315 15s 3d, being a decrease of £157 17s 9d upon the last rate. The total of the county rate for Lancashire was £2,051 17s M. against £2,446 lOs 93 for the corresponding half of last year, being a decrease of £394 13s 4d. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.
RUGBY RULES. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

IThe encounter between these two teams at Warringtm, On Saturday, was witnessed by about 4,000 persons, and was in every respect a successful and pleasant game. The Rangers broagbt a strong team, while on the other hand Warrington were weakened by the absence of Gilbert, Davies, Hough. Appleton, and Rigby. The home captain lost the toss, and the visitors conseauen- tly chose to play with the sun in their favour. Frank Turner kicked off, Ratcliffe re-playing by a kick to touch. The same player immediately afterwards put in a smart run, but afterwards W, Dillon, Ashton, and Hayes broke away, and Barnes helping them by a good screw kick took play to tine. The little centre then made his mark, Frank Turner taking the piece, a minor resulting. W. Dillon charged the kick out, and dribbled nicely, and Jolley seemed certain of scoring when he sustained an injury to his leg which necessitated his removal from the field. Fair Turner at first, and later on Unsworth, took Jolley's place at three- quarter, thus leaving Warrington with fourteen men to fight out the battle. By good play on the parts of the brothers Haselham, Galley, and Barrow, play was taken to half way, Barnes relieving to touch. Ratcliffe at the centre get hold, and Massey rushing up, brought him down, but not retaining his hold the Ranger very quickly regained his feet, and after a very fine run got in and scored a try fer the visitors, the kick at goal being unsuc- cessful. The Warrineten forwards worked well together, and took play to the visitors' 2.5. Haselham (Harry) broke away, but was well stopped by Speakman. Barnes next passed to Turner, who gained ground by a well-judged kick to touch. The ball from now until the call of half-time travelled rapidly from end to end, Speakman, Massey, and Barnes on one side, and Taylor and Ratcliffe on the other, putting in some excellent work. In the second half Frank Turner came through a scrimmage, and Massey and Little- wood took the ball on the latter getting the try, Speakman , kicking a goal. The.game still continued to be very fast, each side having an equal share of the game, and when the referee blew his whistle, after the game had been in progress for 70 minutes, Warrington were declared the victors by a goal and a minor, to a try. Throughout, but especially after the visitors had scored their try the game was very fast, the home team apparently being determined not to come off second best, while the Rangers seemed equally remolute to maintain their advan- tage. There was some stiff forward play of which the War- rington men had generally the advantage, but on the whole the game was an open one, the Rangers at times showing some very creditable passing. Amongst their backs Rat- cliffe was particularly smart and needed a good deal of look- ' lug after, and for some of his feats he was warmly applauded by the spectators. Of the Warrington players Barnes as usual shone conspicuous both in defensive and offensive de- partments. Massey also was in hie best form, and put in some dashing play. Behind the pack Speakman as usual did well. Antrobus, who took Gilbert's place, worked hard, but didn't seem to appreciate the virtues of passing as touch as might have been wished. Boardman, in his new position , las back, di,d not do badly, and with some practice may do I very well Indeed in this difficult place. Amongst the for. I wards Ashton play4'd a vigorous game, and Hayes, Little- wood, and the two Turners were well to the fore. With re- gard to the visitors, in addition to Ratcliffe, the brothers Haselham, Galley, Taylor, and Parkinson, should also be mentioned.

Teams:—Manchester Rangers: C Hammond, back; W G Sabin, B Parkinson, and H Ratcliffe, three-quarters : S S Taylor and R Harrison, half-backs; H Haselbam (captain). Harry Haselham, W Galley, Wilson, E Mee, Barrow, Jones, Pollard. H Harnett, forwards. Warrington : Boardman, back; Jolley, Barnes, and Massey, three-quarters; Speak- man and Antrobus, half-backs; Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, W Dillon, W Hayes, R Littlewood, E Dillon, C Unswortb, W Povey, ferwards. Referee, Mr Parry.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

We are glad to see Fair. Turner's name again down to play for his crmuty. It is quite evident that whatever faults he may have made last time have not been so bad to prevent the committee from giving him another trial, and this time not on the reserve, but on the team. We can only wish him success, knowing that he will do his best to up- hold the reputation of his native town. The match ma Saturday last was a splendidly contested one, and it is the opinion of many that the Rangers are as good as any team in Manchester. The Warrington suppor- ters like to witness the play against such teams as this, as they are sure to see a fine open game, and not one of those where packed scrimmages so much prevail, and which are so monotonous to the onlookers.

Massey was in rare form last week, and we hope that be may be so for some weeks to come. Riney was unfortu- nately hurt, and will this week be unable to play, but we hear that he is mending nicely, and perhaps will be all the better for a fortnight's rest. Warrington meet ATall to-day, and being short of Barnes, Massey, Jolley, Gilbert, and W. Dillon, who are on the sick list; of Turner, who is playing for the aunty ; and with , Rigby unable to play, they wilt, have a very lively time of it. Appleton, we notice, is again at his position of full back, and no doubt he is the proper man in this position. Harry Ashton, the Warrington captain, has taken the right step to keep his team in form, as we understand he has this week" personally conducted" h:s "merry men" on some long walks. If this sort of preparation is kept up, barring accidents, the chances are that the cup will find its abiding place in Warrington for another twelve months at least. • , The Yorkshire and Cheshire county teams encountered each other on Saturday, on the ground of the Halifax F.C. Lockwood stool out from the Yorkshire team, Fawcett, of Marmingham, taking his place. There was also a change in the Cheshire team, L. Holden, of Birkenhead Park, taking the place of Liege, of Sale, and going half-back, Hughes being placed in the forwards. Final score :—Yorkshire, 2 goals, 3 tries, 9 minors; Cheshire, 1 goal, 3 minors. The following team ha e been appointed to reprelent Lan- cashire in the match against Nomersetehire at Whailey Range to-day, viz.:—S Roberts (Swinton), back ; V Slater (Salford), E Flower (Broughton), and J Valentine (Swin- ton), three•quarter backs ; J Mills (Swinton) and J H Payne (Broughton), half backs; C Anderton (Free Wanderers), T Banks (Swinton), U C Chapman (Liverpool Old Boys), H Eagles (Salford), A T Kemble (Liverpool), H H Springmau (Liverpool). A Tegdin and R Seddon (Broughton Rangers), and Fair Turner (Warrington), forwards. At the spring general meeting of the Lancashire County Football Club the following fixtures for next season were accepted :--Nov. 5, East v. West Lancashire, in Lancashire; Nov. 12, Lancashire v. div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATORDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. DatiNKENNESS.—DanieI Crosby was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly on Town Hill on Friday night.
MoNDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alder- men Harrison and Burgess, and Councillors Greening and Francomb.

11116CELLANEOCS.—Thomas Walsh was charged with hay. ing been drunk, and with begging, in Butiermarket-street, eR Saturday evening. Fined 5s and costs, or seven days' im- prisonment. —Mary Walsh was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Liverpool-road on Saturdiy evening, and was dismissed on prorHising to leave the town.—George Lomax, charged with begging in Horsernarket-street ore Saturday evening„ was dismissed with a caution.—William. Rutter was charged with I,eing drunk in the Market-place on Saturday, and was ordered to pay the lock-up fees.— Margaret Fleming, an old offender, was brought up for be- ing drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, on Satur- day night. She was sent to prison for seven days,—Elea Smith, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street on Saturday night, was fined 5s and costs.— James Walsh was charged with being drunk in Irlam.street on Saturday night. He went to the police station and de- manded to be locked up. Fined 55 and costs.—Mary Pren- dergast was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly in Dial-court. She was ordered to nay 35 61 costs.—For similar offences Joseph Ellis, John Dagnall, John Mannion. and Jane McCabe were each t ned 5s and coats.—William Featherstone and Samuel Shaw, for committing a breach of the peace by being disorderly in Bridge-street, were bound over in their own sureties of LICI to keep the peace for six months.
TIIESDIY.—Before Alderman Sutton and Mr. E. J. Guest.

CAUGHT BY THE LEGS.—Alice Daniels was charged with having been on the premises of Mr. John Platt in Lythgoe's- lane, during the previous evening for an unlawful purpose. —lt was stated by a man M charge of the premises that about half-past ten on Monday night he was informed by , his son that some One was in the building, having broken a I pane to get in. He waited for a while and then saw some one coming out, whom he caught by the leg and arm. and found to be the prisoner. He let her off on her promising to go home, but during that night she was again caught on the premises by a policeman.—Prisoner said she had gme on to the premises to spend the night because her husband was "drunk and very nastv."—She was fined 5s and costs, and ordered to pay the cost of the broken pane. DRUNKENNESS —Jane Riley, a young woman known to the police, was sent to prison for a month with bard labour for having been drunk and disorderly the previous evening, In Dial-street.

A COSTLY Darmr.—John McDonough, a young man liv- ing at 7, Old-road, Latchfo-d, was charged with having stolen a bottle of porter, valued at 31.—0 n the previous afternoon the cart of Mr. Liddle, of the King's Arms, Buttermarket-street, containing a number battles of porter, was standing in the yard of the Norton Arm, Latchford. A policeman was passing at the• time, and saw the prisoner come out of the yard, and, on seeing the officer, try to put something in his pocket, which, however, missed the pocket, fell and broke on the street. The officer then saw it was a bottle of porter, the prisoner picking it up and drink- ing the remaining contents. He thereupon took the prisoner into the yard, and after Mr. Liddle had been called ont, it was found that a bottle had been stolen —A fine of 5s and cost, in all 4s, or a month's imprisonment, was im- posed.
iVEDNEBDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclongh and Captain Reynolds. - . . . _ _ _

BEGGING.—John Quinn, Manchester, and John Clarie, Liverpool, were ch irged with begering, tae former in Knuts- ford-rd., and the latter in Buttermarket-at. They were dis- missed on promising to leave the town. TILIIRSDAT.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, and Mr. John Platt.

BEGGING.—John McGuire was charged with begging in Buttermarket-st., on the evening previous. He was dis- missed on promising to leave the town at once. Fainev.—Before Mr. John White (in the chair) and Dr. Gornall.

A NEIGHBOURS' Row.—Sarah Taylor and Sarah Green, both residing in Victoria-street, summoned each other for assault on the previous Friday.—Mr H J Longton appeared for Taylor —Mrs Taylor alleged that Mrs Green struck her on the eye. discolour;ng it; and Mrs Green said Mrs Taylor bad thrown a bucket and a "top bar "at her. Sel'eral wit- nesses were called, one of whom said the women "got hold of each other like cats."—Each party was bound over to keep the peace for six mouths.

FATHER AND Sos.—Thomas Llcker, a young man, was summoned by his father, James Locker, for assaulting him on Sunday night last. The parties live at Latchford. The father stated that his son came to his house and created a disturbance. He asked him to leave, but be would r.ot do so. The defendant rushed at him and knocked him down.— The defendant promised to pay the costs, and the case was dismissed. WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

- - WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. P. Stubs and Mr. Z. Armitage. DRUNKENNESS.—Thomas Walmsler, Great Smiley, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk in the highway at Great Sankey on the sth inst. , NOT UNDER CONTROL.—A. number of persons were SLlM- mooed for not haying their dogs under proper control, in the neighbourhoods of Sankey and Paclgate. (t.c. The fol- lowing were ordered to pay costs :—Michael Read, Henry Hine, Thomas Morris, and Thomas Efulme; and the following were dismissed :—Daniel Woodcock, William Philip Smith, Harry Lewis, Thomas %Worthington, John A. Holmes, William Greening, and Joseph Allen. USING A GUN WITITOUT A LICENCE.—JetTIeS Harrison was summoned for using a gun without baying a licence, • and was fined 203 and costs, or a month's imprisonmer.t.

LYMM PE rIY SESSIONS. FRlDAY—Before Messrs. Peter Stubs, Henry Stanton, and C. Lister. • DRUNKENNESS —Samuel Gibbons, who did not appear,was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly at Broom Edge on the sth inst. He was fined 25 Oh and costs.—Mary Whitehonse, an elderly woman, summoned for having been drunk and disorderly on the sth inst.; was dismissed with a caution.

ALLEGED Assam:rs.—Thomas Dickson, fustian cutter, Lynam, was summoned by Ellen Gilbert, wife of Edward Gilbert, fustian cutter, for assaulting her on the sth inst. Complainant said that defendant struck her three times on the side of the face and on the nose, and she ft! down in- sensible. Defendant denied having committed the assault, and called evidence to prove that the complainant created a disturbance. The Bench ordered both parties to be bound, craw to keep the peace, and each to pay costs.—Stephen Gibbon was summoned by Robert Loather, who complained that defendant assaulted him on the 9th inst. lie was fined Is and costs-21s 61 in all. SACRILEGE BY A Boy—Edward frazondale (11) was charged with stealing a box containing 33 in money from the Zion Chapel, Cherry-lane, Lymm, on the 6th inst.— John Knowles, one of the trustees of the chapel, said that be saw a "weekly offerings" box safe in the chapel shortly before six o'clock on the evening in question. At 7-30 the same evening the box was missing.—P.C. Dutton said that on the Sunday in question he received information of the robbery, and on Monday be saw the prisoner, who admitted having stolen the box, and who had jast hidden is 4d near the dam. The box, which was brolscn, was found in a garden.—Prisoner was ordered to recaive six strokes with the birch rod.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr James Reynolds. MISCELLANEOUS.—WiIIiam Santley was granted permis• sion to sell at the Union Vaults, Reath-road —Martha Hayes, Canal-street, was fined 103 and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the et'a February.

EammTION AT MaiicnEstan.—Thomas LeatherhatrOW, who at the recent Manchester Assizes was convicted of the murder of Catherine Quinn. ?. woman whom he lived with in Pendleton, was executed in Strangeways Gaol, on Tues- day morning. James !Jerry was the executionzr, and the hanging was witnessed by the ceStomaty gaol officials and several reporters. To the last he maintained the indiffer- ence which characterised him from the beginning. A drop of four feet was allowed, and death was probably instanta- neous. The farewell interviews with his relatives were of a painful character, KAY'S COMPOUND OF LINSEED. Aniseed, Benega, Tolu, witu Chlorodyne. 91d, Is lid. 2s 9d. of COemists.— Advt.

Tux Stilt Or IRELAIID.—The Dublin Commission was occupied the whole of Tuesday in selecting a jury to try the plan of campaign conspiracy case. The Crown ordered 2F, jurors to stand aside, and the accused exhausted their six challenges and failed in challenging others. On Wednesday on the trial of Mr. Dillon and other members of Parliament being resumed at Dublin, the Solicitor-General for Ireland Stated the case for the Crown, and promised to put in an affidavit sworn last year in which Mr. O'Brien admitted being editor of " United Ireland." The case was again ad- journed. Evictions on a large scale commenced on Tuesday on theostates of Lord Cork, lying to the west of the Dingle, opposite Olenbeigh. The sheriff, with a large force of police commenced operations amid great excitement. The resistence offered was slight. On Wednesday, at Birdhill, near Limerick, on bailiffs and the police endeavouring to carry out evictions on the Twiss estate they were stoned. Several charges were made on the crowd. Ultimately the evictions were abandoned. John Byers, an Emergency man, who was attacked on Tuesday in county ' Clare, died pn Wednesday from his wounds, and so strong a feeling exists in the district that down to a late hour the friends of the deceased man could not procure a Coffin. • On Wednesday, armed with pikes and sticks, a crowd of about a thousand men stopped the work of -sc. lotions, at Ballyfearitter, and the movements of the police during the daYo„p were!fr touch es h hcihnedaepredt, F 'louse in the City for Japanese ware,rg lass. etd a, and laucy goods. div.head: TIIE 'EXAMINER,
div.p: TIIE 'EXAMINER,
BAT-UIWAY, FEBRUARY 19, 1887.

GEORGE MACKEY, Master of the War- tri,„ng, ton Workhouse, has been compelled to his post. He is being made to suffer , ; heavy- penalty for what, on the face of it, ;7eetnsa light offence. But he has himself to blame for being put in such an unpleasant ,eosition ; if he had acknowledged, in the instance, the mistake that had been ri_acie, the probabilities are that he would h,"ve been reprimanded, and that nothing e would have been heard of the matter. b"tead of doing this, however, he has made worse by running himself into a corner I,lhtb. ,tatements which cannot be reconciled. ti Local Government Board have come to thy' conclusion that Mr. MACKEY has not told e Coal truth ; and this, rather than the ori- lativ,„ offence, is the cause h of the impe- ` Communication which as lead to a Of ;11Zriation. To begin at the beginning oatd & which has been somewhat comp 11 GoeVe ~."'hY side issues, the Auditor to the Local , ient Board had his attention called Clerk to an erasure in one of the cle,"°llse accounts. It is a rule of the i:,-;,k.,overnment Board that accounts must .egtcl within six months of their being sent th it has occasionally happened, when, datt„--gh oversight, an account has got out of /hi i ' that it has been re-dated. This s me- the ' Of Course; the proper thing is to report c,7v,ersight to the Guardians or to the i qe()esT. overnment Board. In the case n it seems that an inmate of the i 'louse, who has since -died, was n the of assisting the laster ; and, finding loi,;,,account of HEDGCOCK'S had run be- %ie"u the term, he erased the date, and put k later date to b.:ng the account within t4tPrescribed period. The erasure was de- dtiedr when the accounts came to be ttalted, and Mr. MACKEY, as Workhouse 111R-13ter, was asked for an explanation , ieglad of offering one, he alleged, accord- the ' statement of the Auditor, that h the othing about it. This naturally put ditor on his mettle; and so, later on, tio -6411 asked Mr. MACKEY for an explana- eoa;parld this time in the presence of the tth,;:rllati of the Board of Guardians and 44,7, oletribers of the Board. Again, Mr. otaa-„"Y disclaimed any knowledge of the and alteration. His explanation to Mr. 4, who conducted the inquiry on Fr- hi Istle;"'as that he had not asserted that e nothing of the erasure; what he had .t verw,as that he would say nothing about . t°Lt.tonately for Mr. MACKEY, his statement 13, tVs vital Particular is not borne out either of thge,Auditor, 'or, his clekk, or the members teeo!Poard who were present when, in the cled. inStancean 'xplanation was deman - af4lrel•Tbe disinteres i fed witnesses agree n knowi,rig that Mr. MACKEY disclaimed all edg• of the 'erasure and alteration. to s:lasked by the InSpector why he declined that LaillYthitti about the alteration. seeing rePly 'new wno h‘acl done it, Mr. MACKEY'S Plariatiw.aB that he preferred to make his ex- Itt h " to the Local Government Board. litre c).w absurd to take up such a position ! housel an auditor sent to audit the Work- Col3rs'e acccaults, and when, in the ordinary have "%of as to 0( hi them, duties, he asks for an explanation , the Workhouse Master would PeoPle b • ei love that he ref uses to make

one—not to screen himself for the moment but rather because he thinks it best to say nothing till he can explain to the Local Go- vernment Board. Further, when the question was put to him, on Friday, whether, in the absence of the erasure having been detected, he would have considered it his duty to point it out to the Auditor, Mr. MACKEY said he believed he should have done so. But this was more even than his friends could swallow. It caused Mr. VOISEY, who had interested himself in the Workhouse Master's behalf, to remarksthat "Mr. MACKEY was a very bad one to manage his own case." Indeed, he has managed it so badly that it is due to that, and not to the alteration of the account, that he has had to resign. Even the gods cannot help him who fights against himself. Mr. JEANS and Mr. VOISEY both , did well to show that no harm could be done to anyone by the alteration of HEDGCOCK'S account; but, on.the other hand, Mr. HENLEY took care to remind them that the inquiry was strictly limited to the charge against the Master of having made false statements to the Auditor. The outcome of the inquiry is that the Local Government Board believe that Mr. MACKEY has made false statements ; hence the demand for his resignation under a threat of dismissal. Without wishing to offer any apology for lying—even to the extent of lightly regarding it as "an intellectual mode of gettinc, out of a difficulty "—we cannot but think that Mr. MACKEY has been visited with a too heavy penalty, considering that for seventeen years he has managed the Workhouse with credit to himself and the Warrington Union. The lesson is, undoubtedly, a severe one, and it is to be hoped it will not be lost on other public servants who may be tempted, in however small a degree, to deviate from the straight line of rectitude.

THE dispute between the glass bottle- makers of St. Helens and Messrs Lyon and Co. has been settled in a way which is creditable to all the parties concerned. There has been something of concession on each side, and neither party to the dispute can therefore claim a victory. The em- ployed have gone to work on the old terms, and the employers are left at liberty, after all, to make use of foreign workmen, if the vacancies are not filled up by local men. This state of things is to continue—a sort of truce it may be called—for two months, anti in the meantime the masters and men of the whole district are to arrange a classi- fied price list, " including terms for the learning to make, and subsequent mak- ing of the turned seamless bottles, and the continuous working of such bottles as the masters may require." Assuming that a satisfactory list of prices can be prepared, it can hardly be doubted that it will effectu- ally remove the bone of contention. There can be no question that it is desirable for English workmen to keep themselves abreast of improvements in bottle making as in every- thing else, The seamless bottle is in de- mand, and the best way to keep the foreigner out of English worshops is for the English workman to put himself in a position to equal or beat the foreigner in competition. Of course, if a fresh process or new mode of working involves greater labour, there should be higher wages ; the bottle-maker 1 has just as much right to get the highest price for his labour as the manufac- turer has to get the best price for his bottles. English workmen are per- haps a little too conservative as to methods of working ; they do not-adapt themselves readily to a new thing. One reason may be that it takes time to get expert at a new way of work- ing, and in the interval there is a risk of pro- duction and wages being alike on a lower scale. But in the case in question all this is to be taken into account in preparing the classified list of prices. There does not ap- pear, therefore, to be any rock ahead; and. with the exercise of good sense and forbear- ance on both sides, the settlement which has been come to will be of such a character as will tender it unnecessary for the tuture to call in the aid of either Swedes or Norwe- gians—or the borough police.

_ "TOUCH AND GO." The Warrington magistrates have rightly made an example of two senseless young fellows who overloaded an ass, and then beat it so terribly that it "died through the illtreatment it had received." It is the brutal man who is brutal to his beast; but happily there is such a thing as law and punishment, as these young roughs will realise whilst they ruminate in gaol.

Quite a number of cases were dealt with, at St. Helens on Monday, arising out of at- tempts to defraud the railway company. There are smile people who seem to think that to cheat a railway company is a failing which leans to virtue's side. They require to be taught in an impressive manner thai: honesty is the best policy, and, if there is no better plan for doing this, the magistrates must pile Ossa upon Pelion in the way of fines.

"The young Princesses of Wales have I taken to dress-making, and show considerable aptitude in the cutting-out and fitting branch." They might set a worse—a much worse—example. Many of our young ladies would be much better employed if they would take to making puddings and pinafores, instead of accomplishing something and nothing in the way of "accomplishments." Better to darn stockings than get an indifferent reputa- tion as "blue stockings."

William Broughton, of Earlestown, has been brought so often before the magistrates that he has lost count. He knows he has been to gaol a good many times, "and all for nowt but being drunk." Poor fellow! He has been -born out of his time. He should have lived in the good old days" when the toper gloried in the announcement —" Drunk for twopence. Drunk and clean straw for fourpence." In this instance, the charge was' zos and costs," and there was no promise even of "clean straw."

Hurrah! In India prisoners are being re- leased and 'debts are being paid by way of celebrating the Queen's Jubilee. But—ah, these " buts "—perhaps it will be as well not to get either in debt or in gaol in this coun- try. England is not India.

Blackburn is going to signalise itself by trying to raise £25,000 for a Technical School. As much as £7,000 was promised at the first meeting. Warrington is in the dumps as to the Jubilee; there is no sight, as yet, of as much as £7OO. Some folk ate wondering, by-the bye, if the big-wigs felt hurt when Alderman Har- rison said the people who attended the j Jubilee meeting in Warrington were chiefly of j one class. It is pretty well known that that class was not the " upper class." Nobody

div.head: EXAMINEX_.BATUBIAY, FEBE UARY 19, 1:887.
div.p: THE EXAMINEX_.BATUBIAY, FEBE UARY 19, 1:887.

doubts that ex-mayors and aldermen, and even common councilmen, are brimful of loyalty ; but it is a little odd that, when a Town's Meeting was called on the subject of the Jubilee, they were for the most part "con- spicuous by their absence." Alderman Har- rison seems to want to know how it was, and we quite sympathise with him.

It is something, howeyer,.to know that the "small fry" who were present—numerous though they were—were absolutely unani- mous in suggesting that the Jubilee should be celebrated by making the Library a Free Lending Library. Alderman Harrison, as chairman, tried to " come round " them in various ways and in various speeches—it is a way he has as a chairman—but his elo- quence was wasted. They were not to be wheedled off the track; they knew what they had set their minds on hence their unanimity.

It was very shocking, however, of Council- lor Roberts to suggest that if the Library were not freed the ratepayers might take the matter AT at the next municipal election. Whoever heard of ratepayers having any right or voice in such a matter ? The duty of the ratepayer, as •the name implies, is to pay rates ; nothing more. As for the idea that Town Councillors are expected to repre- sent anybody but themselves—it is prepos- terous ; it is Socialism gone mad. Indeed, it is not too much to say that it amounts to "threatening language," and as such must be "put down--put down, you know."

The Rev. George Bond, in an attempt to defend the indefensible proceedings of the Widnes School Board, states that the School Board teachers have larger salaries than those paid in Voluntary Schools. "with the excep- tion of one gentleman who does such a lot of Church work as fully to earn his salary." What a charming confession! This school- master "fully earns his salary " by doing a " lot-of Church work;" and Dissenters who also are taxed to pay this salary are thus made to contribute to the support of the Church.

Why don't teachers strike against this sort of thing ? It is degrading to them to let it be understood that their engagement to teach shall include "a lot of Church work." The Government grant is not for any such purpose, as they well know. Let the parson do his own work—he is paid for it. " A lot ot Church work" fdrsooth, and the Rev. George Bond thinks this is a just way of earning one's salary as a. teacher! It is time that we had Free Education—that all schools were put under public Boards; the taxpayers are being robbed.

• The Runcorn Board of Guardians have appointed a committee to " watch the ex- pendique of the county magistrates and of the Bridgewater Trustees." They are all but helpless, and they know it; for, some time ago, the magistrates took £75 from tl-e Run- , corn Union as a hontribution in aid of the improvement of the Dee Bridge, and didn't so much as say—" By your leave." It is a monstrous piece of injustice that we should still have this kind of taxation without repre- sentation. Our systvn of county government is a bad system; it is barbarous in the ex- treme.

The chil- dren were beyond the control of their parents, and wandered about the streets instead of attending school. • WASTE OF WATER 4T WIDNES.—EIiAOeLtI Littler, of the Main Top Hotel, Mersey-road, was summoned to appear be- fore the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday, to answer a charge of wasting the water of the Local Board.—Mr. J. T. Allen, the clerk, prosecuted, and stated that there had been a large quantity of water wasted in the district. In this cast on the 20th January water was allowed to run through the tap into the urinal all night. The excuse made was that the servant had forgotten to tarn the tap. A fine of 71 and coats Ss i3d was imposed. STONING A CONSTABLE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. EL Gras- kell, sen., and Mr. G. Pilkingtoni at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Catherine Mathews made her 41st appear- ance. to answer two. charges of dlnnkenness, and a charge of veisting the police. At a quarter past ten on Monday night P.C. Chambers served the woman with a summons at her house in Caroline-street. Siva followed him into the street, curbed him, and stoned him. For the attack on the constable she was sentenced to a month's bard labour, and a fine of 5s and costs was imposed for the drunkenness.
-- - WARNING TO WIDNES liITECKERS.-At the Widaes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Rimmer, butcher, Waterloo- road, was charged with havinz caused an obstruction of the _ .

footpath. P.C. Cummings deposed that en the evening of the 4th inst. there were three-quarters of heef, five sheep, and several other pieces ef meat banging outside; the de- f. ndant's shop and projecting two feet over the footpath, which was only six feet wide. On the 9th inst., Constable Charles Potts deposed, one half of the footpath in front of the defenda, Vs shop was taken uP by a number of large boxes, and people bad to go into the roadway. The defen- dant's manager bad been previously warned.--r-The defend- ant stated the boxes were lying in the gutter, and denied ibere• was any obstruction.A line of ss, and costs Us 61,
. . - was imposed. . THREE BY SUNDAY VISITORS AT WIDNES —At Widnes. Police Court on Monday. John and Catherine Molloy, man . . . . . . ,
and witP, of 62, lieaumont-street, was charged with flaying stolen a shawl, worth Bs,..the property of J iseph Mills, lodg-

ing-house keeper, 2, Oxford-street. Un Sunday night, die pritioners went on a visit to the house of Mills, and during their stay were left in a room for a few mioutes- After their (I,parture the shawl, which Mrs. Milli had been wear- ing, was missed, and it Was subsequently found immersed Ii a bowl of dirty water in the back "yard of the house of the prisoner's. The male prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, was discharged; but the woman, who acknowledged the theft, was sentenced to 14 days' hard 151300!. STABBING AFFRAY AT RUNCORN. At Honeorn Petty Sessions, on Monday,' Michael McDonough, a young man living in Pryer-street, was charged with maliciously wound- ing .10bn Gallagher, a young man employed ass labourer at Weston. The prosecutor deposed that on Ss:Under night he was in the house of the prisoner's brother-in-law, William Donovan, having some beer, when the prisoner entered, and had also a' glint of the liquid Later an angry wrangle took place, ark! the prisoner threatened to put a knife he flour- ished in his hind into Gallagher, or another labourer named Thomas Keogh. Gallagher closed with the prisoner with the prisoner with the object of wresting the knife from him, but whilst struggling on the floor the prisoner stabbed ' him in five places. Dr. McDougall deposed to examining the wounded man at his surgery at midnight, two hours after tbe affray.. There were two cuts on the top ef the head, anOther Aar the outer corner of the left eye, running inwards, and a fourth wound was on the back, about Inches to the right of the spinal column. Had this latter wound gone in a straight direction, the chest wall would have been penetrated, and a vital part • probably injured. P.C. Charles Potts apprehended the prisoner at midnight, and on searching his house he found in a tool box in the scullery a knife, the haft and blade of which were wet with blood. When charged with the offence the prisorer,stated ,he knew nothing about it. He had not had a knife for two years, as he had no use for one, because he smoked thih tobacco. The prisoner was committed for trial. The room was well filletd. Mr.

BRUNSWICK IMPROVT.MENP CLASS, RTJNCORN.—At the ordinary meeting of this society, last Wednesday evening, there was a short paper read on "Providence," by Mr. Daniel Bisbrown. The essayist gave seneral instances of special providence which had come under his particular notice. A protracted diecuseion ensued, in which many members took part. THE LATE Alas Citantys TAYLOR —At FarDwOrth Wee- leyan Chapel, on Sunday evening, the Rev. It. Barden, j superintendent minister, of Widnee, occupied the pulpit, and during the course of his remarks made special reference to the lase Mrs. Charles Taylor, of Farnworth, who bad been a member of the Wesleyan body for upwards of 30 years. There was a crowded congrenation. Ponntart CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The series of popular concerts arranged by Mr R. Plertmint was resumed on Mon- day evening, after being discontinued a few weeks. A fairty good audience assembled in Bethesda schoolroom, and had the pleasure of listening t an admirable entertainment, to which Messrs F. Dennett, W. Blackledge, George Booth, and Miss Keath contributed. The Mill Brow military band ale* performed several selections. MOTHERS' MEETING. FRODSHAM.—The annual tea in connection with the Frodsham and Five Crosses Mothers' Meetings took place in Trinity Wesleyan ScAlroom, Frodsham. About 200 members partook of the rejnast. A 1 public meeting was held afterwards, and addresses delivered I by the Revs. E. Mosscrop and F. F. Eiltnnnds, and Mr. J. H. Lee, of Liverpool. From the report it appears that dur- ing the past year the total receipts have been £72 14e Si, ' which had been expended in the purchase of sewing , materials, aca. BETFIESDA CONGRECIATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—The ! annual sermons were preached on Sunday morning and ; ' evening by the Rev A J Basden, of Sandi:tenth There were good congregations at each service. On Tuesday evening the annual tea party took piece in the Lecture Hall, and a' good number of persons sat down to an excellent repast ' prepared and dispensed by the ladies of the congregation, Subsequently, instead of the usual Meeting, a pale of work was held, and proved highly successful. The articles ! I offered for sale were those remaining from the recent bazaar 1 in aid of the Manse Fund. and realised £lB. WIDNES OPERATIVE PLUMBERS.—'Fce annual dinner of 1 the members of the Widnes Branch of tire United Operative I Plumbers' Association took place at the Norton Arms. Lugs- ' dale-road, on Wednesday evening,. Upwards of 50 persons , were present. Mr. James Marsh took the chair and the vice-chair was filled by Mr. John Dungan. The chief toast ; was "Success to the association, Executive Council, and the Widnes Lodge," proposed by the chairman. Mr. Cherry, general secretary of Sheffield, and Mr. Pettigrew. of the Executive Council responded. During the eveuieg Messra. Geo. Chatwood and John Stephen Thomas were each pre- sented with an emblem of the association. DITTON CHURCH SCHOOLS—An ent rtainment of a novel and interesting descrimion took pitce at Ditton on Friday evening week in aid of the school funds, and judging from the large audience the managers would derive subs antial ' help in their educational work as a. result. The Rev. C. W. Wooll, MA. (view), presided. Miss Payne. of Brookfield, initiated the idea of giving a SiriGS of " lablcarex Tivants," or 'living pictures," and the programme might be described as a collection of pictures with the human frame. The sub- jects were allegorical, historical, dramatic, ad realistic. Mr. I Joseph Snspe Eccles (St Helens) presided at the piano, the scenes were arranged by Miss Payne and Messrs Sergi, Hill, and Lewis, and much assistance was given in the making up by Mr. Harry W. Cookson, of Widnes. Gnsusegrig COMPETITION AT WIDNES —The tie between the Widnes and Runcorn tivmnaaiums' in the first round of the competition for the Liverpool and District Challenge Shield, offered by the National Physical Recreation Society, ! was decided at the Baths Alsembly Room, Widnes, last night week. Mr. J. Beckett, of Liverpo -1 Gymnasium, ; officiated as judge, and after an exciting contest declared ; Runcorn club the winners by 25 points The scores were— Dumbbells, Runcorn 82 points, Widnes 64 ; barbells, Run- corn 84 points, Widnes 66 ; parallel bars. Runcorn 50 points, , Widnes 61. The teams were constituted as follows :—Run- I corn : T. T. Burrows (champion), W. Collier, J. Rhodes, T. Hancock, W. Catterall, A. Wells, W. Garrett, and H. W. Handley. Whines: R. Evans, R. Johnson, T. Forshaw, G. Evans, J. Wright, E. F. H. Taylor, W. Duggan, and W. I Roberts. THE JUVENILE RECHABITES OF Rostcoing.—The annual meeting of the Excelsior Juvenile Tent of the Order of Rechabites was held on Tuesday night at St. John's Pres. I byterian Snhoolroom. Tea was pronided for aboat 60 per- sons. An entertainment Was subsequently given, when the chair was occupied by the Rev. E. Hall. The report read by Brother Evans showed that in the Tent there were 129 members. Nine had, however, "lapsed," and three had been transferred to the adult Tent. The total worth of the Tent was about £3O. An address was also delivered by Brother Sharpies. of Manchester. Recitations were given by Brothers Walter Hague, J. Minshull, W. H. Povey, and W. Faulkner. A guitar duet was given by Mrs. Warburton and Miss Richardson, as well as several selections by the St. John's Chapel choir. During the evening Brother R Evans , was presented with a handsome floral album by Brother • Sharpies, on behalf of the Union Tent, who wished in this medest manner to show their appreciation of the zeal and - ability displayed by Brother Evans in the cause of Rectum- • bitism, and in recognition of his six years service as supers I intendent of the Juvenile Tent. Brother Evans &Anew- 1 ledged the unexpected gift in an appropriate speech. There are performing elephants, and why not trained cows? Messrs. T. and J. Ker- foot, farmers, of Winwick, secm to have had an eve to answering this question. They sent two heifers on the highway to go home themselves; but the performance was inter- fered with by an unappreciative policeman, who turned the animals back, and followed the matter up by summoning the owners to the police court. The training of those heifers has been stopped, and nobody can say what the world will miss in consequence. Magis- trates do not encourage budding genius.

There is bother with Egypt ' • as Mr. MC- Minnies once said—Moses had bother with Egypt. We want to leave, and yet we can't leave. It has cost us so much to get hold that we shall go on spending more rather than give it up. We are like the young fellow who admitted to his young wife that smokinz was a bad habit, and that he ought to give it up. "But then," he said, "think, my dear, what it has cost me to learn to smoke— it would be all thrown away." Logic of this kind is unanswerable.

The election at Burnley is exciting a great amount of attention. Both parties have made nice calculations which prove, in the judg- ment of the calculators, that their man must win. The Conservatives say there are Tories who would not vote for Mr. Rylands, but they will vote for a Tory like Mr. Thursby. On the other hand the Liberals contend that there are a great many Liberals who voted last election for Mr. Rylands, but they can not be brought to vote Tory— Unionist though they are; There is something in both contentions.; but—well, we will not prophecy; we will hole that Mr. Slagg will win.

Peters, Fr Hartland, F. Cave, J: Dennett, J. Whitfield, John Davies, J. Goulding, H. B. Shores (secretary), 4c. The Chairman said the sooner we handed over the government, with proper precautions, to the Irish themselves, the sooner we should have that union between the people of the two countries which all true patriots earnestly desired.—Mr. E. K. Muspratt moved "That this meeting desires to record its un- abated confidence in our great leader, the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, and to express its firm con- viction that the only method by which a just, safe, and permanent settlement of the Irish question can be obtained is by passing a measure of self-govern- ment for Ireland, based upon the easential prin- ciples of Mr. Gladstone's recent bill; and that, until the settlement is effected, much-needed legislation on the land and other subjects is entirely prevented." Neither the land question, Mr. Muspratt said, nor the question of mining royalties, nor many other questions exceedingly interesting to the mass of the people of this country could be dealt with until we got rid of the Irish difficulty.—Mr. F. H. Gossage seconded the motion.—Mr. Percy and the Rev. R. A. Armstrong spoke in•support of the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. F. Cane, seconded by Mr. F. Hartland, a Tote of thanks was stcordyd to the visitors, and a similar compli- ment having been paid to the Chairman, on the motion of the Rev. R. Yeatman, seconded by the Rev. D. Davies, the meeting terminated. NEW MAGISTRATE.—Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Wid- nes, was on Wednesday placed on the commission of the Peace for Lancashire by the order of the Chancellor of the Duchy. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.—YeSterdfiy at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. James Rey- to4s, John Craig, 45 years of age, was charged with attempting to commit suicide. About a quar- ter past seven on the previous night the prisoner was rescued from tl4e Weaver Canal 'at Weston Point by some boatmen who happehed to be in the vicinity. To P.C. Dale, who apprehended him, he said be jumped in the water because he had been out of work so long, and was tired of life. He ad- ded that he would not have jumped in at the gpot- where he did had he known help was so near. In the cell, previous to appearing before his worship, the prisoner declared to P.C. Sutherland his inten- tion to drown himself as soon as liberated. He was remanded to Knutsford gaol for seven days. A TICKETLESS TRA.VELLEIL —Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court on Monday, John Stewart, a labourer, of Warrington, was charged with having travelled from Liverpool to Widnes, on the London and North-Western Railway, without a ticket. On Sun- day night, at a quarter past eight, the prisoner attempted to 'pass the „Aicket collectors along with ' the passengers from the Liverpool train, but he Was promptly asked for his ticket. He gave Chester and Liverpool alternately as his starting point, . but could not produce a ticket from either place, and at last said he did not know where he came from. A penny was all he had in his possession.— A fine of .10s and costs as imposed, or 14 days in default. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room of the lVorkhouse at Dutton, on Tuesday after- noon. The chair was occupied by Lieut.-Colonel Ashton, and there were also present Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Speakman, Aaron, Stokes, Hadfield, Brandreth, Farrell, Campkin, Lewis, Warburton, 11. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy-clerk). TEE SIIPERA.NNUATION QuEsrrox.—The Deputy-Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board acknow- ledging the receipt of one from the Guardians informing them of the death of Mr. Jones, late Workhouse master. The Local Government Board sanctioned the payment to the legal heirs of the late Mr. Jones of such amount of his superannuation as was due to him at the time of his death. In regard to Mrs. Jones. as they had not received a medical certificate to the effect that she was incapacitated front continuing her duties, her case did not come within the Statute, and they were unable to direct that the superannua- tion should be made to her. .Under the especial circum- a'ances the Board would feel inclined to allow the Guar- dians to grant Mrs. Jones a reasonable gratuity.—Mr. Bad- field: Are we to understand from that tbat Mrs. Jones could have retained her position ?—The Chairman: It seems very much like it.—Mr. Hadfield: We understood at the tiros that she was bound to resign with her husbard.—The Clerk said that, under the Orders, she could not have staved.— Mr. Aaron: I should give it her; never mind the Local Government Board. (Laughter.)—The Chairman: The position is that Mr. Jones's representatives get the superan- umation due at the time of his death, and that Mrs. donee gets nothing.--Mr.Campkin: Perhapi they mean that there is nothing against her taking another place.—The Chair- man: It seems hard lines that she should be compelled to resign, and then have nothing allowed.—Finally it was resolved to inquire as to the state of Mrs. Jones's- health. and communicate further with the Local Government I Board.
FRAUDULENT RAILWAY TRAVELLING.

EXTRAORDINARY CASES. Before Dr. E. P. Twford, Alderman J. Mcl3ryde, and Lieut.-Colonel H. Pilkington, at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, William (lowborn. a contractor, living in floade-stre.t, Hirdlev, was summoned for travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Wigan to St. Helens without having paid his fare and with intent to avoid payment. Mr. Preston, solicitor to the railway aim- panv, prosecuted. Evidence was given by Ticket-collec• tor Wilding, Foreman-porter John Forshaw, and Detective James Henry Parkins, showing that on the 28th January the defendant arrived by a train from Wigan. He walked along the line towards a stoneyard belonging Mr. Mellor, and on being followed and spoken to about his ticket he at first said be must have lost it, but ha afterwards admitted that he had not had one. The Bench fined the defendant 40s and costs. _ . .

A SCIENTIFIC. DISCOVERY.

If anyone had informed Queen Elizabeth in her palmiest days that she could have been seated in her palace in Lon- don and conversed with Sir Walter Raleigh in his North Carolina home, receiving a reply from him within an boar's time, she would have declared it to be a miracle; and yet, had she lived in the present day, this apparent miracle would most readily have been witnessed, and not seem at all strange Sr uncommon. The truth is, new principles are ooming into existence, and the operation of many laws unknown in the past, are becoming fully understood in the' present. In no way does this fact come more forcibly to the mind than in the care and treatment of the human body. Million of people have died in past ages from some insignificant, or easily controlled cause, which is thoroughly understood now and readily handled. Coneumption, during the entire past, has been censidered an incurable disease, and yet it is demonstrated that it has been, and can be, cured, even after it oas had a long run. Dr. Felix Oswald recently contributed a notable article on this subject to the Popular Science Monthly. He regards cane sumption as "pulmonary scrofula." The impurities of the blood, produce a constant irritation of the lungs, thus destroying their delicate tissues and causing death. His theory shows conclusively that con- sumption is a blood disease. It has its origin, primarily, in a deranged condition of the kidneys or liver, the only two organs of the body, aside from the lungs, that purify the blood. When the kidneys or liver are diseased they are in a sore or lacerated state, which communicates poison to every ounce of blood that passes through them. This poisonous blood circulates through the system and goes to the lungs, where the poison is deposited, causing decomposition of the finely formed cells of the lungs. Any diseased part of the body has contaminating power, and yet the blood, which is the life of the system, is brought into direct contact with these poisoned organs, thus carrying contagion to all parts of the body. The deadly matter which is left in the lungs by the impure blood clogs up. and finally chokes the patient. When this is accomplished rapidlv it is called "pneu- monia." or "quick consumption," when slowly, "consump- tion," but, in any event, it is the result of impure blood caused by diseased kidneys and liver. These are facts of science, and are vouched for by all the leading physicians of the day. They show the desirability, nay, the necessity, of keeping these most important organs in perfect condition, not only to insure health, bat also to escape death. It has been clearly shown, to the satisfaction of nearly every unprejudiced man, that Warner's SAFE Care is the only known remedy that can care and keep in health the great blood-purifying organs of the body. It acts di- rectly on these members, healing all ulcers that may have formed in them, and keeping them in a condition to purify and not poison the bloat. This is no idle statement nor false theory, but one that can be substantiated. Miss Weg- man, of 67, Brondesbury-road, Kilburn. London, NAV., was given up to die by her physicians. For years she had a terrible cough, accompanied by night-sweats, chills, and all the well-known symptoms. She spent a season in Southern Europe, but found no relief. She save, "I finally conclu- ded to try Warner's SAFE Cure, and in three months I gained twenty pounds, recovered my lost energy, and my health was fully restored." The list can be prolonged in- definitely, but enough has been said to prove to every Suf- ferer from pulmonic tronbles that there is no reason to be discouraged in the least, and that health can be restored. The remedy can be bad of all chemists at 4s 61 per bottle, or direct of the proprietors, H. H. WARNER AND Co., 47, Far- ringdon-street, London, E.C.
