div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c. "Four Winds Farm," published by Messrs. Mac- millan and Co., London, is an excellent story by Mrs. 3folesworth. author of the "Cuckoo Clock, &e. It is a capital idea to make fairies, or attendant angels, of The Winds, and it is well worked out. The work abounds in what may be called proee poetry, although there is no attempt at fine writing, while the inci- dents are so varied and strileing that the reader's in- terest is never allowed to flag. The illustrations are by Mr. Walter Crane, who is himself a poet and an artist, and it is needless to say that they are admir- ably executed. "Four Winds Farm" is wholesome and pleasant reading for either old or young. The current volume of the Camelot Classics, publish- ed by Mr. Walter Scott, London, is "Leigh Hunt's Essays," and a good shillings-worth it makes. It is edited by Mr. Arthur Symons. who furnishes an in- teresting sketch of Leigh Hunt's life. These essays are the beat of the writer's work; and that is to say the book is delightful from beginning to end. In the "Great Writers" series by the same firm, we have the "Life of Samuel Taylor Coleridge" by Mr. Hall Caine. The editor is to be commended for the clear insight which he gives into the character of the poet. Ile makes many things plain which have hitherto been scarcely intelligible, so that the reader feels that he knows Coleridge after reading the work. The bibliography which follows the life has been carefully prepared, and is therefore very valuable to the student Allan Ramsey's poems are issued by Mr. Walter Scott as part of the "Canterbury Peels." The poems are selected and arranged by Mr. J. L. Robert- son, M.A., who supplies a sympathetic biographical sketch of the famous author of "The Gentle Shep- herd." There is. too, a glossary of the Scotch words words used by the poet. The volume, like all the rest of the shilling works issued by the firm, is neatly bound in cloth and well printed. " Whitaker's Almanaek," compiled by Mr. Joseph Whitaker, F.S.A., grows year by year more valuable as a work of reference. The almanac for 188718 a goodly volume of over Goo pages, an addition having been made of some i6O pares, and it is reilly a wonder- ful shillings-worth. This year, consequent upon the enlargement, there has been an entire revision of the contents; and all information has been brought down to the latest date. The appeniix, in view of the Queen's Jubilee, includes a carefully prepared summary of the chief events of her Majesty's reign— it is in fact a history in little, and is accompanied by a valuable chronological table. Politicians who are still in the thick of debate on the Irish question will be glad to see that there is a synopeie of both the Home Rule Bill and the Irish Land Bill, as introduced by the Gladstone Government. There is, of course, the usual trustworthy " information respecting the Government finances, pepulation, commerce, and general statistics of the British Empire throughout the world with some notice of other countries, &c:' The almanac is simply a necessity to those who wish to keep posted as to what is going on in theworld, and in this respect is useful to the Member of Parliament and to the humblest elector. TER JUBILEE NAVAL DISPLAY.—The naval display. at Spithead on the occasion of the Queen's Jubilee will eclipse any spectacle of its kind ever witnessed before. The evolutions of the fleet will last for several days. The Reserve Squadron will assemble at Spitbead at the end of May, a month earlier than usual, in order to take part in the manceuvres. • At a meeting, on Monday, of the Birmingham public jubilee committee, it was announced by the mayor that her Majesty bad altered the date of her visit to Birming- ham, previously arranged for May 14th, to SOl2lB date towards the end of March. Wednesday, the 23rd, waS rentioned as probable.* HEAVY DAMAGES AGAINST A RAILWAY ComPAmr.—At Leeds Assizes, on Monday, in an action to recover compen- sation for injuries sustained in a collision on the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire railway near Bolton in September last, the jury awarded to Abraham Mitchell, brushmaker, Halifax, £750: to his wife, £5O, and to his daughter £lOO. making a total of £9OO. All three plaintiffs had suffered more or less severely from the accident. lesocvsecir AND RENT.—A special meeting of the Man- chester Chamber of Commerce was held on Monday to consider a resolution brought forward by Mr. R. C. Richards, declaring that the "claim for priority in regard to rent in insolvent estates is inimical to the true interests of commerce," and asking for such a change in the law as shall "place all creditors in the same legal position." After considerable discussion the resolution was rejected by 18 votes to 11. Daiwa AND CRIME.--Sentencing Gomez Leek, at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, to nine months' imprison- ment for a violent assault on his mother-in-law, Mr. Justice Hawkins said the prisoner was a man of superior education, and had occupied a good position, but brought himself into a deplorable condition by drink. Excess of drink was at the root of at least 75 per cent, of crime; indeed, if he said 90 per cent, of all crimes was due directly or indirectly to drink he would be right. Istrostso ON A PEEIC—At Pontefract, on Saturday, .Tohn W. Wilson was committed to the Sessions Court on the charge of attempting to obtain money by false pre- tences from Lord St. Oswold, Nostell Priory. The pri- soner, it was alleged, had written asking for relief as a 4 resident of the borough which Lord St. Oswald's son, the Hon. R. Winn, represents in Parliament. A post- office order was sent to York to the address given, which was a false one, the prisoner at the time living at Pontefract SHOT FIRING IN bOLLTERTES.—The Barnsley magistrates on Monday committed Willianc White, a miner, recently employed at Wharncliffe Silkstone Colliery, near Barns- ley, for two months' imprisonment in default of paying e for firing a shot in a colliery in February last year without authority. The prisoner, who absconded soon after the offence, fired a shot unknown to the manage- ment in a part or the workings where 50 men were employed, thereby putting their live in peril, and sub- jecting the owners to serious risk. • SERIOUS RAILWAY MIS/lAP.—As the Great Northern express from King's Cross was passing WerringtonJunc- tion near VeterbOrough, on Monday, some platelayers noticed that the " slip " carriage in rear of the train had become detached. They signalled to the driver, who at once applied the brake and stopped his engine. The detached carriage, follossing at considerable speed, dashed into the rear of the train and caused great damage. Several passengers seated in the carriage were hurt, one or two sather seriously, but all were able to proceed to their homes.

TUE PRICE OF A KlSS.—Edward Nelson, of The Priory, Lewisham, was on Saturday fined at the Greenwich' police court £4 and £1 casts for kissing a governess in his service. It was stated in evidence that on the night of January 21, after the complainant had retired to rest, the defendant came to her room, dragged the bedclothes from her face, and kissed her twice. She threatened to alarm the household if he did not leave the room at once.
He left, but the following day he twice attempted to kiss her in the schoolroom. For the defence it was urged that the case was entirely trumped up, Notice of appea was given.

THE SUPPOSED POISONING BY A NURSE.-012 Monday, Mr. Molesworth, the district coroner, resumed his inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Mary Ann Finley, who died at Castleton in February, 1886. The body had been exhumed with the sanction of the Home Secretary, it being suspected that the woman had been poisoned. Several witnesses who had known the deceased gave evidence, as did also two insurance agents in whose offices she was insured. The medical and analytical evidence not being yet complete, the inquest was ad- journed for a fortnight. THE SALFORD GAS COMMITTEE'S RESIGNATION DE- MANDED.—A public meeting of the burgesses and rate- payers of Salford, convened by the Mayor in reply to a numerously-signed requisition, was held, on Monday, in Salford Town Hall, to cor.sider the position of the Gas Committee in relation to the revelations made in the Lever libel case. A resolution was unanimously adopted calling upon the members of the Gas Committee to tender their resignation in order that the committee might be reconstructed. The various speakers expressed strong disapproval of the action of the members of the committee in not resigning before now. Mr. Joseph Shaw, a member of the ass Committee, defended the conduct of the committee, but stated that, in accordance with the wishes of the meeting, he would resign his pssition on the committee.'

EXECUTION OF THOMAS BLORTIAM AT LETO/INTER--. On Monday, Thomas Bloxham, aged 62, was executed in Leicester Prison, for wife murder. Last November, the prisoner shot and cut the throat of his wife, and at the trial alleged that she committed suicide by agree- ment with him. Ile maintained an unconcerned demeanour till Saturday, when he was visited by several friends and his children. On Sunday he broke down again, and received the ministrations of the chaplain very gratefully. On Monday his spirits had revived; however, and he walked firmly to the scaffold, bidding the warders farewell just before the bolt was drawn. Berry allowed a drop of aft. 6in., and death appeared to be hasiantaneonS. A considerable crowd assembled out- side the prison- DRI/TRIICTIVH FIFE AT AN , OPERA HOuSE. The Northampton New Opera House was burnt early on tiunday morning. It had been occupied during the week by Mr. Balsir Chatterton's Company, which had a suc- cessful run. The house was left in apparent safety on Saturday night, but soon after midnight the stageman found a fire raging behind the wings. lie at.once raised an alarm, but it was some time before any firemen could be summoned. In the interval an effort was made to extinguish the flames by means of a hand fire ex- tinguisher belonging to the theatre. It was then dis- covered that the gas was escaping, and that it was im- Possible to get to the meter. Later on when the flames had a firm hold of the rear of the building several fire- men arrived with the steam engine, but it was then evi- dent that the building could not be saved. In about two hours the roof fell in. The dry inflammable contents of the building were speedily consumed, and although the gallery and front of the house were saved, the remainder of the theatre was destroyed. The building was erected only three years ago. • BREACH OF TIM Mil:Es At the Dolton Police-court, on Monday, Harry Scowcroft, owner of the Itosehill collieries, and his manager, Noah I Jones, were summoned for contravention of the Mines Regulation Act, for insufficient ventilation of mines, and allowing use of naked lightt in the workings, where an explosion took place.—Joseph Dickinson, Chief Inspector of Mines, prosecuted.—lt was stated that on January 24th, the fireman, in going his rounds in the Doe mine, found gas in the working place, and the manager. instead of withdrawing the men, who were using naked lights, placed another collier to guard the place with a safety lamp. An explosion occurred, and two men were injured, one so badly that he was unable to appear as a witness.—One witness for the prosecution stated that the foreman in charge of the working place where the gas was, took the top off his lamp just before the explo- sion occurred.—The defence was that every precaution was taken.--Scowcroft was discharged, and Jones was fined £.5.

FRAUDULENT TRADE MARKS.—Deputations from the Sheffield Town Council and the Cutlers Company and the Federated 'rrades' Council of Sheffield waited on Lord Stanley, at the Board of Trade, on Saturday, to urge the adoption of stringent regulations against the fraudulent marking of goods. The Mayor of Sheffield and the Ma.ster Cutler having spoken, Mr. Mundell°, followed, and said the question was a national one. The false marking affected 'hot only the home but the export trade. There was abundant evidence of German firms selling their own goods in Germany as , Sheffield: made goods. A strong measuroof prohibition was re- quired. Mr. Stuart Wortley, M.P., and othets, having spoloan, Lord Stanley said he admitted the necessity for legislation on the subject. The Government favoured proceeding by amending' the Act of 1862. In twain). portant points the views of the deputation would bemet in the Government Bill, viz., in proceeding summarily instead of by indictment, and of throwing the burden-4f, proof on the prosecutor. The appointment of a Royal Commission would involve a long delay. He therefore urged them to support the Government Bill.

The presentation of illuminated addresses to eighty- nine persons who had formed the exploring party after the great colliery explosion at Bedford in August last took place in the Theatre Royal at Leigh on Saturday, the chairman of the Local Board presiding.

GOOD NEWS FOR VOUTATEER9.—LOrd IMITIS'S COM- mittee has agreed to recommend an increase of five shillings per head of efficients in the Volunteer grant, with allowances for range expenses in certain cases. The allowances to officers are also to be-increased con- ditionally.

MONDAY norm's DWISION.—In the division in the House of Commons, on Monday 'tight, on Mr. F...%lemunt's amendment to the Address re:rattling Scottish ease 4 the ininonstv was made tip of 54 Gladstonian Liberals, tttrve Liberal bnionists.and 41 Nationalists ;while the malority wee composed of 167 Conservatives. and L 3 crhoniet Liberals, including Lord Hartington and Sir Bent's, James.

At Manchesier, on blontlay, Neville Tripbw, a prMate in the 3rd Hussars, was charged with shooting another privates named Shepherd, with intent to murder. Dur- ing a dispute about some coppers die prisoner fetched a gun and aimed at Shepherd, who knoCked down the barrel, when the prisoner shot him in the thigh. His injuries were very severe, and he is not yet out of danger. The prisoner was remanded. _ _ _

FATAL COLLIERY Accupaxr.—Two men were killed by an accident which occurrea on Saturday evening at Bettisfield Colliery, Bagillit, Flintshire. The men, named Roberts and Pritchard, were working overtime, and when descending the pit with materials were suddenly precipitated from the cage, a depth of no yards. The remains of the men were found to be a shapeless mass. The deceased were both unmarried men.

George Whitehead, belonging to the High Rip Gang, was sentenced' on Monday by 7ustice Hawkins, at Liverpool, to five years for stabbing, on the Aintree Race- course, Edward Sebborn. Sebborn had given evidence against the gang in the local police court, and before stabbing Sebborn he wastheard to say, "We have only one life to lose: let us stand to it." Judge Hawkins felt bound in the interests of society to pass a most severe sentence. _ _

GLADSTONE.-Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone attended divine service at Hawarden church on Sunday morn- ing. The right hon. gentleman read both the lessons in excellent voice. It is stated that Mr. Gladstone is en- gaged upon another classical work on Homer. It is thought that he may consider it necessary to take part in the deliberations of the House of Commons upon the procedure rules, and he will therefore go to London early next week.

An action for breach of promise, in which a Miss Shaw was the plaintiff and a man named Robinson the defendant, came before the Under-sheriff and a jtlry at the Leeds Assizes on Saturday for the purpose of assess- ing damages. The plaintiff, who was represented by Mr. J. E. Barker, ib engaged in a school at Sheffield, and the defendant, for whom Mr. Kemp appeared, Is a lawyer's clerk at Hull. The facts connected with the case were na stated, and by arrangement a verdict wasrentered for the plaintiff for £7O, including costs. A 'Dour Commcroß. KILLBD.—On Saturday evening a ticket collector named Thomas Henry Townson, em- ployed at the Knowsley-street Station, Bury, of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, was attending to the 6-40 train from Manchester, when he heard another train approaching from the direction of Heywood. Apparently thinking, however, that it was moving in the opposite direction, he jumped off the platform. The train, which was going to Bolton, caught him, knocked him forward, about 15 yards, and injured him soseverely that he died before medical assistance could be procured.

TIIE ADULTERATION OF BEER.—HEAVY PENALTIES.-- At the Westminster Police Court on Saturday, 15 sum- monses, taken out at the instance of the Inland Revenue authorities against licensed victuallers in the neighbour- hood of Pimlico and Westminster, for selling beer adulterated with sugar and water, were heard. Mr. T. D. Dutton and Mr. T. Maitland, solicitor to the Beer- sellers' Protection Society, appealed for the defence, and pleaded guilty in all the eases. Mr. Partridge imposed penalties in §ix cases of £3O each, in four cases £25, and in three 'l2O each, The magistrate 'renta.rked that if brewers sent out their beer too strong, publicans a/ext, instead of adulterating it themselves, to leave it to the custorders to dilute according to their liking.

div.p: "Oar Earth and its Story" is the title of an impor- tant new serial work by Messrs Cassell which is being issued in monthly parts. With part 1, to hand there is fresented a large tinted plate, printed separately, entitled "Icebound." The work is edited by Dr. B. Brown, F.R.G.S: It is tobe adorned with maps and illustrations, while it will furnish the latest scientific knowledge. Another important work is a new and re- vised edition of Cassell Universal History, with about , 800 illustrations. There is also a large presentation plate with the first part of this issue. It is an engrav- ing of the celebrated picture of" Awaiting the Ver- dict." Of the " Universal History," it is not too much to say ei at a thorough study of it is an edttca- , don in itself.

" Scribner's Magazine" &or Febtuary surpasses the first number, which is saying a great deal. The article on "The likenesses of Julius Car is admirably illus- trated; and the same mey be said of Wkshbarne's Re- miniscences of the Siege and commune of Paris. "The Residuary Legatee " is the title of a new novel which promises well. " Another leading feature is "The story of a New York House" by H. C. Runner; it, too is capitally illustrated. "The Era Almanaek," conducted by Mr. Edward Ledger, is a mine of information as to matters relat- ing to the stage. The great feature of the present issue is a series of dramatic incidents, related in their own handwriting by the leading actors and act- resses of the day. It is in every way "a palpable bit." We have to hand part 27 of "Ward and Lock's Technical Journal and Industrial Self-Instructor." Amongst other things dealt with, there is a paper on "The Principles of Mechanics,' and another on "The Geometrical Draughtsman" each with fora. illustrations.

Mr. John Heywood, Manchester, has issued a pam- phlet by Mr. Herbert, on " The House of Commons in the past, present, and future." Its object is to ex-, pose the anomalies of the present system of represen- tation, and to urge a scheme of proportional represen- tation which is well worked out. Part four is to hand of the new edition of tbe History of Lancashire. There is every evidence that Mr. Croston, as editor; is doing his work thoroughly.

Cameron. Mr and Mrs Carbutt, Mrs P Robinson and family, Mr and Mrs Ogden, Major and Mrs Litton, the Misses Ridg- way, the Rev G F Reynolds, the workmen of Messrs Ry- lands Brothers, Mrs Broadbent, Mr and Mrs Long, Alderman Baron, Mr Joshua Raw!Jason, Mr Daniel Drew, Mr William Berry, and the members of the 'Burnley Unionist Execu- tive Committee, Mr and Mrs Geeenall, Miss A Ridgway, Mr and Mrs Causton, Mr and Mrs J White, Miss Dundas, Mr and Mrs H Bleakly, Mr Michael Glazebrook and family, tbe servants at Massey Hall, Colonel and Mrs McCorquodale, Miss Dora Rylands, Mr and Mrs Tom Roberts, Mr and Mrs James Nichelsan, Mr and Mrs James Tinsley, Mr Charles Adamsons the Silent Temple Lodge, Burnley; and Mr Toff, gardener at Massey Hall. PUBLIC REFERENCE. On the magistrates (Messrs R. Houghton, A. C. McCor- quodale, C. Pilkington, and W. F. Goochltaking their seats en the bench at the Newton Petty Sessioris on Saturday. the Chairman, rising from his seat. said: Before commenc- ing the business of this court this morning, I wish to say a few words in referenee to the death of a gentleman who al- though not often attending here is very well known is the county as a county magistrate, and in Cheshire as well as here. The magistrates very mach regret the loss occa- sioned by his death, whose interment takes place to-day. I am sure we all feel his loss, not only as a magistrate but in other respects. PULPIT REFERENCES IN BURNLEY. At most of the churches and .chapels of the town on Sunday suitable pulpit references were made to the late Mr: Peter Rylands. Preaching at the Holy Trinity Church the Vicar (the Rev. 3.31. D. Owen) said although many-of them differed from Mr. Rylands in many things:Jet those differences would hardly interfere with their respect for him. He did much for Warrington and Burnley and he left behind him, in the House of •Commons more especially, the character of a straightforward, steadfast, honest, hardworking Englishman. The Rev. W. J. Gerratt preached at the St. John the Baptist Church, Gannow, and said with much in Mr. Ryland's career he ditl not agree, but he could still admire an honest opponent, and a man, who with a pure mind, had the courage to 7 his conviction& / At the Westgate Congregational Chapel special refer- ences to the loss the town had suffered were road° by the Rev. J. W. Clarke, who said he knew Mr. Rvlands. personally, and he had always found him ready to render him any ,help that was within his power. He contributed to their school enlargement, and he rendered them valuable assistance during their initial difficulty with the Education Department At the Baptist Chapel, Yorkshire-street, the Rev. R. Littlehales said the qualities which characterised the life of Mr. Rylands in a special degree were honesty, useful- ness, and unselfish devotion to the general well-being and progress of society. The Rev. T. Leyland gave a brief biographical sketch of the late member, at the Unitarian Chapel. He said Mr. Rylands was a genuine Lancashire man. He was , something more than a partisan, for he was prepared to follow the leading of his conscience. He 'believed he was a true man, and was faithful iancitrue to the last. The Rev. It. Ensall also referred to the subject at the Mount Pleasant Baptist Chapel, autl said a great loss had been sustained in the death of Mr. Er-lands. In hirn an honest, a devoted and faithful servant of the people had been removed out of their midst At most of the places of worship the "Dead March" was performed upon the organ, and on all hands were neard expressions of the deepest sorrow at the death of a man who was universally esteemed. THE COBDMkt CLUR AND MR. RYLAADS. I am glad to be able to state (writes a London corre- spondent) that the following resolution has been adopted by the Cobden Club :—" The committee of the Cobden Club have received with the most sincere regret the announcement of the death of Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., who has been a member of the dub since 1869, and for many years one of the most active and earnest members of the committee, always ready to devote his time, attention and ability to the interests of the club, to the work of the committee, and to the promotion in every way of the objects for the advancement of wleich the dub Was founded. All who have been engaged in the -wprk of the club, and Mr. T. 13. Potter, M.P., and the committee especially, have had donstaeit experience of his kindly, sympathetic, and unfailing advice and co- operation. Whatever may be the judgment of Liberals as tothe later period of Mr. Peter Rylands's career, it is not questioned that in the height of his manhood he rendered aid to the Liberal 'cause. THE DECEASED MEMBER'S FATHER. In apiographical notice of the late Mr. Peter Ryland, an interesting incident is narrated. After Mr. Rylands' defeat at Warrington, in 1874, he was invited to contest the South-East Division of Lancashire, in conjunction with Mr. John Edward Taylor, against the Hon. Algernon Egerton and Mr. Edward Hardcastle. One of the earliest meetings in support of their candidature was held in the Free Trade Hall, when Mr. Taylor took occasion to relate an incident in local history in-which his colleague was not uninterested. In the year 1818, said Mr. Taylor, when Manchester Radicals were men of earnest purpose, his father, (the founder of the Manchester Guardian) fell under the lash of persecution. That was a time when to be a Liberal was to be a (marked man, and his father was one of the marked men of Manchester. He was tried at Lancaster Castle upon a criminal prosecution for libel. The Government of the day brought all its forces against him, for they desired nothing more than to be able to crush an energetic and determined Liberal. Mr. Scarlett, the great advocate, was brought down from London to prosecute, and the Judge himself was believed to be not altogether unbiassed. The accused, however, defended himself manfully. According to law as it then stood—for the law of libel was very 14rsh—probably he was guilty; but.the jury, unable to agree, remained in consultation for hours. There was one man, and at first oue only, who declared that for his part he would never convict. Be argued long with his fellow-jurors, some of whom he won over; and when, as it seemed, he could not prevail with the rest, he lay down and composed himself to sleep. saying, "Gentlemen, my mind is made up; when , you have made up yours you may wake me." That man's obstinacy in a good cause prevailed. Hours rolled by, and at length those of the jury whol would have supported a tyrannical Government gave way before the powers of hunger and cold; and in the early hours-of a winter morning they were escorted to the Judge's lodgings, where, to the delight of assembled crowds, a verdict of " not guilty" was prononnced. The accused, who was morally, if not legally innocent, was thereupon set at liberty. The "obstinate Juryman" who brought about that result was none other than the father of his (Mr. Taylor') friend and colleague, Mr. Peter Rylands.,
EITYMPS IN TEE- DIALECT. DORN'D GOOA COOARTIN' TTH" DARK. Hey, aw fancied misel a gay masher When but a oe'ergrown fella-lad, Un tni mates used to co me "a dasher"

When aw spooarted i'th' best rig aw had, A wur fairly a "goner" on the lasses— A greyt puppy i o', except bark! But,—this is good advice for o' classes ! Never gooa a cooartin' Pth' dark! Every neet, when aw'd done mi day labours, Aw'd don misel eawt spruce an' neat, Aw wur th' envy an' butt o playn nayburs. When a strutted—a dandy—deawn t' street, One wintry neet, strollin' at leisure, A met a young woman in th' Park. Hey, fooak! if yo'd miss spoylin' yor pleashur, Dorn'd go eawt a cooartin i'th' dark! 800 sed hoo wur a manager's dowther, An' wur co'd Mary Jane bi ther fooak ; Far mooat preshus than di'monds aw thowt her, An' when Sleep had fovrded id's clooak Thad neet, aw dreamt o' nowt nobbut fairies; Ther wur but one as coom to mi mark, A figure just like buxom Mary's— Thad lass as ow'd cooarted V th' dark. Aw met her theer mony a neet after, Hoo'd anus a vayl o'er her face I We cud hear seawnds o' other fooaks' Lafter, As we set in a shadowy place. • Awl! own streyt, as mi heart wur fair smitten, Mi brain wur afire wi' Luv's spark; But aw mon ha' bin mad as a kitten, To sit theer cooartin Ptle dark! Every neet for a month aw went wi' her, To thaa form bi' UP tree, dry or west. Neaw, aw'll blab yo' a saycret--Well, Weigher, Her face hed ne'er gladdened mi seet! Thad vayl wur deep black an' a thick un, Like th' geawns worn bi parson an' clerk, When aw think on't, aw know aw're a sick un, For cooartin a " darkey " i'th dark! Well, aw axed her one day to a tay do. Hoo promised hood meet me at th' heawse, "Mon aw trust i' thi word?" "Ay, tha may do," Hoo sed, tremblin' like a trapped meause. Sooa aw went, wi' sum rum for mi " footin'," For aw'd fratched o'er mi "girl" at mi wark, An' mi smiles showed her presence wur suitin' When th' lass coom aw'd cooarted i'th' dark! Wl' perswadin' hoo pood off her bonnet, An then aw fell faintin' to th' Boor. But to tell o as happened aw connut—. Aw know hoo flew rest eawt oth' door! Hood a feaw face, o' pock-marked and flobby ; An' a dumpy nooase, just like a shark; Wl' a big meawth, as wide as a lobby, Thad "angel" aw'd cooarted PM' dark! Hoo'd one eye ; hur yure grey i' sum places; Fifty year owd, aw'll bet, if a day! Aw've long worn one o'th' wost o' glum faces; Thret Park num, mi feet never stray! If yo'r wantin' a "mate" graced wi' beauty, To help yo to manage life's barque, Tek th' advice ova "mug":—Do yor duty, But dorn'd gooa cooartin' i'th' dark! JACK 0' ANN'S.

THE HorroN MCPDEll.—Currell, the man who is sup- posed to have murdered Lydia Green, at Heston, London, on the sth inst., and has since been missing, was captured by the police on Tuesday morning. The capture was effec• ted after a detective-inspector had received from Currell a pencil-note arranging to give himself up at a certain spot, but by rt detective who spotted his man when the latter was hurrying along apparently, to keep hie engagement. On Tuesday afternoon prisoner was brought up at Worship-st. Police Court, and remanded. Currell's solicitor, Mr. New- ton, declares that he has a good defence to the charge of murder, and that Carrell' father and ether friends will de- fend him to the utmost. Currell continues to protest his innocence. .

div.head: LIBERAL LECTURES AT WARRINGTON
div.p: LIBERAL LECTURES AT WARRINGTON

BY MR. JOSEPH HOWES. Each evening during the week, Mr. Joseph Howes, a lecturer who is well and favourably known to Warrington audiences, has given one of his interesting addresses to a large audience; on Monday and Wednesday, in Wycliffe Hall; on Tuesday, in the League Hall; on Thursday, In Brick-street Schoolroom; and on Friday, in the Co-operative Hall. A summary of each lecture is appended. "THE PEOPLE'S MONEY AND HOW IT IS WASTED." __

_ Mr. Howes lictured in Wycliffe Hall on Monday evening on the above subject, when the large room was crowded. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. A. Roberts, and there were also on, the platform the Rev. John Yonge, and Councillors W. Pierpoint and H. Roberts, Mr. G. Plumpton, and Mr. G.Wallington, junior. The CHArnidAlv, who was heartily received, said that the object' orthe choice of that subject was one that had been very much overlooked in most elec- torates. Some said that financial statements did not "go down" very well, but this was a subject that must command the attention of everyone who bad to pay the nation's taxes. Until the voice of the people was heard in strong remonstrance against the waste of public money, that waste would continue. He was glad to welcome Lord Randolph Churchill as a disciple of a more economical Government, and he only hoped that Lord Churchill would stand to his guns. If so, he believed that either Liberal or Tory would welcome him as a public benefactor. (Hear, hear.) That night they had to deplore the loss of one, who, in the past.. had taken no mean part in the exposure of this wasting of public money. He referred to the late Mr. Peter Rylands—(cheers)—who, from time to time had brought up question after question in the House of Commons complaining of this gross waste of public money. If Lord It:Churchill would take the! part Mr. %Tian& had taken in the past, he would do good servict. But they must not be con- tent with that, but must send more disciples of economy to Parliament, which they had got the power to do. (Cheers.) Mr. Howls, before dealing with the subject of his lecture, replied in severe terms to comments that had appeared in a ilocal paper with regard to himself. He then proceeded to say that it annually required 100 millions of money for the purpose of carrying out the arrangements of the Empire, and still not so much, 'attention was paid to the ques- tion of financial economy in the present day as was the case early in the present century. The multiplicity of work Parliament bad been cal.ed upon to consider bad to some 1 extent called away public attention, and if it was true-that there was now a tendency to return to the consideration of finance, it 'would be a very good thing. Expendi- ture was not otter increasing, but there was every likelihood of the increase continuing, unless the ; public absolutely refused to give to the Chancellor of the Exchequer the amount of money he now received. If there was to be a cutting down of expenses, they did not wish it to take place by the reduction of the salaries of third-class officials. A comme”cement should be made with the high- class officials, men who possessed titles, had large landed 1 possessions, and who received large incomes. (Cheers.) If a Government was in favour of financial reform, it was not sufficient to reduce the useful staff. He then explained the origin and growth of the National Debt, and asked whether it was wise, from a taxpayer's point of view, to go on ex- tending our territory. lie maintained that it was not, as it occasioned warfare and its attendant expenses. We should I I either have to conselidate our empire on a wise and equit- able principle, or we should have to lessen the extent of the territory in connection with the empire. (Hear, hear.) ' During the present century we had paid the National Debt twice over without reducing its bulk, except to a slight ex- tent, and the only reduction had been through a system in- augurated by Mr. Gladstone, and carried a little further by the wisdom of the late Lord Iddesleigh. It was desirable 1 that the Government should be called upon to make arrange- ments whereby there might be a permanent reduction in the National Debt, and they ought to protest against that , debt being increased'. (Hear, hear.) When Mr. Gladstone ;left office in 1874, there was a surplus of over £5,000,000. with which the Tory Government were enabled I to commence business. In that year, owing to the apathy of the people, and a great number ; of voters staying away from the polls, the Liberal party were defeated, and the Tories were returned to power. The Tories were in office the next six years, and, in 1880, when they were beaten, the expenditure had increased from £74,000,000 to £84,000,000. The Gladstone Govern- ment that succeeded the Beaconsfield Administration in- creased the expenditure from £84,000,000 to £87,000,000, bet during that time they paid £10,000,000 of the floating debt created by the Conservative Government. We 'had I now reached an expenditure of £lOO 000,000, and it would I take a long time to get back even to the expenditure of £74,000,000, because fdreign complications were still mil I band. After the question of national expenditure. the next iss importance was that of the pension list. He thought that pensions in a public department should be abolished. If a person worked for the State he should ba well paid, but the a h to go on paying pensions from generation to generation was a crime. As with the wages so with the pensions. The useful man who had done the active work received a small pension. of a department, who had not much o elo t but received laeragde one. Parliament had no practical control over the public departments and the way in which , they spent money. It had been seggested that there should be established a Permanent Finance Committee in connec- tion with the House of Commons, to go through the ac- counts of each public department, and, at the eery least, to find out the dead 'men, who were at the present time 'drawing pensions. (Laughter.) Parliament should have greater control over the public departments, and should make an investigation concerning the bead permanent offi•

dials. They as voters mast see that men were returned to Par- liament who were likely to take an interest in this financial work. They wanted more professional politicians. At the present time a committee had been appointed, and would soon commence operations, whose duties would be to make an exhaustive inquiry into pensions, general, here. ditary, and particular pensions. For that they had to thank Mr. Bradlaugh. Mr. Howes then referred at length to the lavish expenditure sin in connection with the Royal household, and said that if the people knew bow their money was spent it would be impossible for Governments to spend it in future. They knew how wars were created, and they knew what had been the cost. He maintained that neither a Prime Minister nor a Cabinet ought to have power to make war. The matter should be brought before Parliament, and before the people's representatives. (Hear, hear.) After speaking Of the expense attached to the keeping up of Dublin Castle, the lecturer concluded by saying that the remedy was in the bands of the people. They had to pay the taxes, and they had the power of sending representatives who would go in for a reduction of the public expenditure. (Cheers.) Mr. PLuarFam proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Howes for his lecture, and the Rev. J. YONGE, in seconding, ob- served that the 1874 account of the Abyssinian war had only just been put before the House of Commons. He thought snub things wanted looking into. The motion having been carried, Mr. HOWES replied, and afterwards proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding, and the proceedings shortly afterwards ter- minated.

"IRELAND :—PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE." On Tuesday evening Mr. Joseph Howes addressed a crowded and enthusiastic audience in the League Hall, Or- ford-street, on "Ireland : Past, present, and future." The chair was occupied by Alderman Burgess, J.P., and amongst the gentlemen present in addition to the lecturer, were the Rev. W. Carew, Messrs. C. S. Burgess, F. Lough- lin, T. Whitehead, M. Chambers, G. Walker, W. Stirrup, J. Mounfield, junior, D. Davies, It. Roberts, H. Whitham, C. Sudlow, J. Bromley, G. Holford, T. Weir, S. Dunbobbin, and W. Crosskill.

Mr. HENRY ROBERTS, secretary to the Liberal Associations read a letter from the Rev. Father Thompson, St. Mary's, Latchford, who said that he was prevented being present at the meeting, and added that the justice-loving people of England only required educating, and he firmly believed that once they saw the usefulness of Mr. liladetone's work they would give him that strength that would enable him to do the crowning act of his life—(cheers)—the cementing together of two hearts, the heart of England and the heart of Ireland. Mr. Roberts also read a letter from the Rev. G. E. Cutting, Wesleyan Minister, who regretted his inability to attend, but expressed entire sympathy with the move- ment to educate the people in political (details. The bands of the clock were going silently round, and they would soon point to Home Rule for Ireland—(cheers)—and after that, if it could not be before, to useful reforms for England, eix., for which every true Liberal longed. (Cheers.) The Cemeamsw, who was well received, expressed his his gratification at seeing so large a gathering assembled to hear Mr. Howes. As an Englishman, be said, he felt so strongly on the wrongs done to Ireland by England in the past, and continued in the present, that he could not stand before an audience of his fellow-countrymen without feeling shame and indignation at the condition things were in at the present time. (Cheers.) He never had known the period when there had net .been an all-absorbing question with reference to the government of Ireland, and which had been in the way of legislation for England. (Hear, hear.) They never would know a period when legislation would go on unimpeded until justice was done to Ireland. (Cheers.) Justice, freedom, and truth, demanded an equit- able settlement of this question—(cheers)—and in the end it would be obtained. He hoped that he was net too old to live to see the day when Ireland should be freed from the oppression, the thraldom, and the tyranny in which it was now held by the gaolers and turnkeys of the liberties of Ireland. (Cheers.) Mr. Howes then delivered his lecture. England had been, he said, sowing the seeds of the difficulty of Ireland for the last 600 years, and after that they should expect an abun- dant harvest. (Laughter and cheers.) During that 600 years England had been trying to manage Irish affairs, but had not succeeded in giving happiness and prosperity to Ire- land. After remarking that they believed one cause of the Gladstoniaa defeat at the last election was the want of union amongst the people regarding the true state of affairs, he said they were determined to use their best endeavours to turn back the pages of history, and fortify the people with facts in connection with this great question, in order that these who were deceived at the last elec- tion might not be swindled again, and that those who wavered might be stronger. (Cheers.). The emancipation of the Irish depended upon the action of the Irish people, as in Eoglend it depen- ded on the English. Prior to 600 years ago, Ireland had managed its own affairs, and the struggle commenced with the invasion of Ireland by Henry 11. The landed aristoc- rade, of England having obtained land in England without purchasing iesaw an opportunity in that invasion to get land in Ireland on the Same terms. Wherever the British soldier obtained a footing, the land was taken from the Irish peo- ple, and banded over to the alien aristocracy. It was re- corded that in one or two provinces the Irish people, find- ing that they were unable to repel the invader, offered to fraternise, thus holding put the hand of friendship, but the English had not the sense to take it. On the contrary, Acts of Parliament were passed prohibiting the Norman's from adopting the dress of the Irish, or intermarrying with them, and thus a barrier was, at the commencement of the struggle, erected between the two countries. When these foolish laws were passed the Irish people saw at once that they were not to be allowed to become the friends of the invaders, and consequently they determined to be their enemies. The fight was continued from the reign of Henry H to that of Henry VIII, who was the first Eng- lish king who called himself King of Ireland. He passed laws in Ireland by Englishmen, which were not oueye I in Ireland, because the Irish saw those laws meant the dis- appearance of their property and liberties, and the melan- choly struggle was renewed and carried on until the end of the reign of Elizabeth. They had before been struggling against the nationality of the Irish, and now commenced to proceed against their religion, and session after session of the British Government was engaged in passing the laws afterwards known as the penal code, the results of which remained with them to the present day. Having detailed the injustices under which the Irish at that time lived, Mr. ' Howes said that if the Irish were rebels it was the brightest trait in their character, for if they had not rebelled they would have been the greatest cowards in the world. The trade of Ireland was attacked next, and the people were driven from the country. It had been said that the Irish were vicious. Suppose it were true. England had taught them for 600 years. A period of 600 years of plunder and ' pillage, scaffold and jail, repression and forcible extermina- tion, was not likely to raise a people in the social scale. The struggle went on until the terrible famine in Ireland, and no light broke in upon the circumstances of Ireland until the close of the last century. When England and America came , to hostilities, the Irish made a demand for the liberation of ' a Parliament then sitting in Ireland from British control, but there was no demand for repeal of the union. England gave a pledge in the British House of Commons that the Irish people politically should manage their own, affairs in their own fashion—that the laws of Ireland should be made by the king, lords, and commons in Ireland, but it was soon broken. The moment that the foreign difficulties were cleared away, the British Administration set to work , W break down the liberated Parliament, which, by corrup- tion in one direction, and force in another, they succeeded in doing. Dark days set in and revolution spread itself over the land. Open demonstrations were suppressed, and consequently secret organisations sprang into existence. This went on until the middle of the present century, when at last a statesman appeared on the scene, who commenced to diverge from the old lines. That was Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) The forces against him were so great, the aristocratic power so strong, that very little could be done. He commented upon Mr. Gladstone 's various measures for the benefit of the Irish people and said that as arietocratic legislation in ree gard to Ireland had failed, now was the time for the democratic legislation to be tried. The great extension of the franchise had given to the Irish people the opportunity to make their demands in a constitutional manner. They had accepted the responsibility and made the demand, and now eighty odd members had been returned to the House of Commons who could not be silenced, and who dared not re- main inactive. If better relations could be brought about between the two countries, the people of England and Ire- land would be able to go together shoulder to shoulder to pull down monopolies, privileges, and interests, and make the Empire stronger in the future than ever it had been in the past. (Cheers.) Mr. GEORGE WALKER then proposed "That this meeting protests against the barbarous evictions recently perpetrated in the district of Glenbeigh, and calls upon the present Gov- ernment to introduce immediately such remedial legislation as will prevent a repitition of such atrocities." (Cheers.) Mr. T. WHITEHEAD Seconded the motion, which WAS car- ried unanimously, and it was announced by the Chairman that copies of the resolution would be sent to Sir Gilbert Greeualt and to Lord Salisbury. .

A hearty vote of thanks was- passed to the Lecturer, on the motion of Mr. MOVNEIELD, seconded by Mr. 01.0,113E115, and a similar compliment was paid to the -Chairman, on the motion of Mr. HOWES, seconded by Mr. LUNBOEMN. Thanks were also given to the Irish National League for the use of the room, on the motion of Mr. HENRY Ronpwrs, after which the meeting concluded. "STRUGGLES FOR REFORM."

The third of the series ef lectures given by Mr. Howes was given ir. Wycliffe Hall on Wednesday evening. Mr W Pierpoint presided, and there were also on the platform Messrs S Dunlsobbing, J Bromley, and S Davies. There Wafl a crowded attendance. .

The CHAIRMAN said he had a special pleasure in presiding over so large and important a meeting for the first time in the capacity of a chairman of a public meeting. (Hear, hear.) He was very much impressed with the ability of Mr. Howes, from the fact that the Warrington Tory paper had taken extreme pales to go out of its way to villify him. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) felt satisfied that if they felt a necessity to adopt that course, Mr Howes was very much like a thorn in the flesh. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The subject that Mr Howes had chosen for that night was one of very vast interest to both old and young. To the old men of the party he was sure that the references Mr Howes would make to the struggles that they necessarily met in the past would be of very great delight to them, and the references to the subject would be of very great encourage- ment to younger members of the party who were now coin- ing to the front in active political work. (Hear, bear.) The reform era, from 1532 to 1885, was a very notable era

"THE GREAT • ICE AGF." LECITTRE BY THE REV. IV, TUCKWELL.

On Monday evening another of the free educa- tional fund lectures in connection with the War- rington Co-operative Society was given in the Co-op- erative Hall by the Rev. W. Tuckwell, Rector of Stockton, near Rugby, the subject being "The Great ,Ice Age ". Mr. Tuckwell was already known• to Warrington audiences as a lecturer of unusual tal- ent, and consequently:there was a wiry large gather- ing to hear him, although there we're severed other meetings of more or leas attraction held in the town on the same evening.. Mr. W. Long, J:P.. had I been announced to.preside, but at the commence- ment of the meeting Mr. T. Birchall, the president of the Co-operative Society, announctd that Mr. Long was unable to be with them owing to a severe ' bronchial cold. Mr. Long had written to him say- ing he was advised by his doctor against venturing out that night, so that he was reluctantly com- pelled to ask the Committee to find a substitute to preside at the lecture.— He (Mr. Long) was very sorry that that should be necessary, not only because he thoroughly appreciated the good' co-operation had done for the people mateTiidly, and the coarse that Society had taken in devoting' a .fund to the spread of knowledge by such lectures as they would have that night, but also on the more personal ground that heliadhoped to make the acquaint- ance of the Rev. W. Tuckwell, whose good work all who were educated in liberal education must appre- ciate. ( (Applause.) Mr. Birchall then moved that Mr. Torris take the chair,, and this was agreed to unanimously. Mr. Morris then briefly introduced ,The Lecturer, who was received with warm ap- plause. The lecture throughout proved to be ex- tremely interesting, the text being illustrated by numerous drawings and lantern views. In the course of it Mr. TUCK,WELL §aia be had that night to open what sorne people thaught the most interesting chapter in the great stone.book. He had to speak of a time which though not sufficiently far oil to be unrealisable, was sufficiently remote to be imposing and of a country almost identical in contour and in outline with this England in which we live, yet containing gigantic and now extinct animals and supplying conjecture as to the origin, and evidence as to the development of the earliest man in west- ern Europe, if not upon the globe. He had. to speak to them of the great ice age. Forty, years age no such lecture as that could have been giyen., the phenomena were then present in abundance, but the key to them was wanting. These phenomena were roughly known by the name of boulders. A bould7 er was a stone-large or small, but foreign to the dis- trict in which it was found, and brought from a greateror less distance by natural and not by hu- man agencies. These boulders are, scattered all over the world and connected with them are religious and other assoeiations. Many of those large stones we readbf in the historical books of ,the, bible were unquestionably boulders. There are some famous boulders in Birmingham, and the finest collection in England is in Wolverhampton, where, for two or three miles, you walk through nothing but boul- ders. Here in Warrington they were in the very midst af a most remarkable boulder stream flowing southward from Scotland and from the lake dis- trict. He had 'seen a stone about a hundredweight in this neighbourhood, at a place called; Morley Common. At Daresbury Hall there was one, and there were others at Runcorn and on Delamere Hills, while there was an immense block at Preston Brook. All round Warrington, where they put the plough into the fields, they would find some of these stones. Boulders had been taken from the neighbourhood of Lovely-lane, and he had one ze- raarkable specimen which he got from Warrington several years ago. (Applause.) The key 4_ to these boulder stones was found by Louis Agassiz, who said that they had been brought from the localities to which they originally bonged by, glaciers, which, on being melted, dropped them whole they' are now found. This was not a lucky guess of genius on the part of Agassiz, for he had lived within sight of the Alpine glaciers, and it was from his knowledge of the action of the glaciers of to- day that he diagnosed the action of the glaciers of a past and interpreted the meaning of the boulders. (Applause.) The lecturer then, with the aid of lan- tern views, explained the origin and action of gla- ciers. Glaciers' were formed by the continual accu- mulation ,f snow on the top of mountains, the snow afteTwards condensing into ice, and by its own weight slowly forcing an ice stream, or glacier, down into the valleys below. In and on the glacier were carried pieces, of rock from the mountain, and when the glacier was melted on the lower grounds these pieces of rock remained as boulders. He mentioned that the boulders now found in England had been mainly brought from Scotland and the north by, glaciers. In answer to the question that might be asked how it was possible that at any time tliere could be glaciers in the soft temperate climate we enjoy in England, Mr. Tuckwell explained hi suc- cinct, yet exceedingly clear language, the causes and the probable period and duration of the glacier epoch in part of -.Europe. in- cluding the ' British Isles. He then referred to the remains of animals that had been found in these islands, such as the mammoth, the cave bear, the woolly rhinoceros of the cold period; the tiger, the lion, and the elephant of the tropical period; and also to the buffalo and other animals of a former temperate period. It might be asked, he said, how these animals got into England and Ireland. Well, there was no English Channel in those days, and there was no Irish Channel. England was joined to Ireland in those days. (Laughter and applause.) Lantern views of several of the animals referred to were next admirably given, and evidently appreciated' by the audience. They would ask him, he said, if they. knew of any evidence of the existence of man in those early times. They very rarely found man's bones, and he thought the reason of it must have been that men even in the earliest time either burned or buried their dead, and they knew that when men were buried soft earth was a great decomposer. That seemed to him to account for the fact that they so rarely found human bones, but they found some- thing more unperishable than human bones; they found human tools or implements. Geologists had divided man's history into four periods,the old stone period, the new stone period, the bronze period-, ind the iron period ; land it was a fact that they found the rude chipped flints which belonged to the earliest age of man, side by side with the bones of the most ancient extinct animals. With the aid of specimens, drawings, and lantern views a number of very interesting relics of ancient man, rude stone, polished stone, and bronze implements—were then described, and the places at which many of the more notable of these relics were found were also alluded to. In conclusion, Mr. Tuckwell said that great were the mysteries which lay in their path, great was the joy of penetrating them. He did not envy those who, in the search found not something greater still, who failed to discover and to proclaim ifs the outcome of scientific labour that the master secret of creation was to do homage to the wisdom of the Creator. (Loud applause.) _ The CHAIRMAN said he thought they would all agree with him that they had never heard a scien- tific lecture of so much interest, and given in so racy a style, as that just given by' Mr. Tuckwell. (Applause.)—Mr. T. BIRCHALL moved a vote of thanks to the leoturer, and this was seconded by Mr. H. WHITHAM, and carried by acclamation. Mr. Tuckwell having responded, the proceedings con- cluded; a large number of people, however, re- maining behind to view the numerous geological specimens and relics of early men Mr. Tuckwell had brought with him.

THE RECENT TOWN'S MEETING IN WARRISGTON. Sir,—l think all who are wishful that the Lending Lib- rary should be freed, and there are more than some of our fence-sitting members of the Town Council seem to think. will agree with you that Alderman Harrison has a very un- friendly way of showing his friendliness to the object they have in view. Our Deputy-Mayor (or is it ex-Deputy- Mayor ?) evidently feels a little despite against the recent toein's meeting which so emphatically declined to be influ- enced by his Jack-in-the-box series of speeches against the library movement. Not having succeeded in " nobbling " er bamboozling the meeting, I see he has been doing his best to belittle it in the Council. But whatever gloss Ald- erman Harrison may put upon that meeting there are two or three facts in connection with it that should be kept in mind. First of all it was a Town's Meeting called in tne usual way ; then, whatever may be said to the contrary, it was well attended as town's meetings go; and last but not least it was heartily and thoroughly, beyond the shade of a doubt, in favour of a really Free Library. Alderman Harrison says there were none of the large manufacturers at the meeting, but what of that ? Has a thing that is good for the town not to be done because the large manufacturers are two indifferent or too well provided for themselves to help in bringing it about? If the public affairs of the town bad to depend m the large manufacturers, it seems to me, they would soon fall into chaos. If the being a large manufacturer is the only source of authority and considera- tion in the town what about a very large majority of the Town Council and even Alderman Harrison himself? The truth is this bringing forward of the objection that there were no large manufacturers at the meeting is just a symp- tom of that peculiar friendliness (!) Alderman Harrison feels towards the movement for freeing the library. It should also be remembered that the meeting Alderman Harrison depreciates was called to consider in what way the Queen's Jubilee could best be celebrated, and it was unanimously of opinion that the freeing of the library would be the best way of doing this in Warrington. Now, unless we are to have a mere money-bag Jubilee in this town, the wishes of the classes of people represented at the Town's Meeting and who form by far the greater part of the, population, must be fully cousidered.—Yours, &o.

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND ITS DOINGS.

Sir,—! think I shall turn Tory; you Rads. want to get along too fast. Bless us all ! At the rate you are going at the Reformers' occupation, like Othello's, will be gone. Now let me, Mr. Editor, put a plain question to you—ls it not far better that we should have something to strive for, than have that something already in hand ? I take it, and I speak from experience, that the mind ora Radical is SO constituted that it is always seeking further developments and never satisfied with things as they are. That is there is no peace for the Radical unless he .is at war with some thing or some person. What a happy state of things we should have had to-day but for the passing of several measures in the House of Commons, and one Act alone, the irst Reform Bill, has led to troubles innumerable. During the agitation for the bill, its opponents were, and justly so, indignant that the people should presume to do more than obey the laws already in existence, for, said Lady Harrowby, "What does it matter what the people think, or what they express, if the army was to be depended upon." The mistake is, sir, that the people have, unfortunately lest their original state of innocence,and their eyes being opened, they now presume to suggest laws, and make laws, altogether ignoring the maxim laid down by a once famous bishop, via, that" be did net know what the mass of the people in any country had to do with the laws but to obey them." The people have got their reform acts, ballot boxes, free library acts, and so on, and now they seem to say- - And next I'll hurl upon the rubbish-heap The cradle that has lulleel me long to sleep; And, warming. to my work, when .I've begun,

help; myself in hr more ways than on-e." And now, Mr. Editor, what are the things to which we are going to help ourselves? And what are we going to hurl upon the rubbish heap? Mr. Editor, I could do with you at my elbow just now to caution me. I feel so much like rushing into trouble, and this all through the cheap press—another Radical mistake. I have read your report of the proceedings et our Town Council ; I have also read a lot of stuff about a famous Hunterian process through which one of our neighbouring towns has for some years been struggling, and I have come to some strange conclusions, may be of a gaseous nature. Suppose I put a question to the audi- tors, who are, in the words of Alderman Davies, "in the service of the ratepayers." What did the said alderman mean by asking that It be "an instruction—nay, a direction to the auditors of the borough, that the gas accounts should be audited?" The " hear, hears," twice repeated, seemed to give great satisfaction to the worthy alderman. Still more satisfaction will be given to ratepayers if an explana- tion is given. Allow me to say here that I shall not allow the" sleeping dogs to lie," and before leaving this subject allow me further to suggest that the auditors be respectfully invited to say how far it is true that in scarcely a single case are the departmental accounts kept separate. I am not very much enamoured with the way in which two or three of the Councillors keep on year after year mak- _

. . ing spasmodic efforts at reform. Councillor Dixon is, I think, the chief of sinners in this. Why does he not get all his facts well in hand, and, defying all dirt throwing," throw so brilliant a light on the gas question as to even penetrate the H green shade" worn by Councillor Fran- combe, and extinguish Alderman Burgess's candles? And now, Mr. Editor, allow me to thank you for your article on the Free Library question. You have shown how it can be done, and now that the movement has got into the IpPriosition stage there can be no doubt of its ultimate suc- cess. But sir, I assure you there is no need for either your euu4-sted economy or Alderman Harrison's timid support. Whit we want is the strong hand of a strong man, deter- mined to utilize the resources already at hand. I have been satisfied fot seine years that the institution in Bold-street is not made the best possible age of; that its potential powers are not even dreamt of by those who have taken up its management from the dilettante point of view. The management of the instii.ution differs in no respect from the management of everything else in the town. 'Therein the werk is lett in the hands of the "classes." Don't imagine for a moment that the masses are likely to ever lay claim to the stupid French phrase, .• Liberty, equality, and fraternity." All the liberty we have any right to is the liberty' to pay rates and taxes, and to be permitted to earn sufficient for Our employers, so that they may be enabled to pay theirs, and have a few luxuries besides. This done we . shall be qnite satisfied to know that the reading room com- bines and contains all the blessings Alderman liarrieon says ;it does. In the "fullest acceptation of the term" the library is free to those who can pay. You can also "resume the reading of a book whenever you please," that is, if no noselse hal got kold of it. What rubbish to talk like this As well tell the reople that the reading room is a place Where the classes mingle with the masses, and that the re- public of lettere has its seat within the building. And now, sir, allow me tra congratulate Councillor Roberte on his straightforward speech respecting the Art Gallery. I shalt go a littlts further, and state distinctly, it is a fraud on th,, public, that as yet it haa not done six- pennyworth of teal good to the inhabitants of Warrington. I went to the trouble a short time ago of testing one of the largest works in the town as to evidence of the interest taken in the Art Gallery. Not one ser cent of the workmen had ever been within its walls, and a vety large number were ignorant of its exist-nce. I have no objection to the Art , Gallery, but art moat be the handmaid of literature, and not its despotic mistress. One word in conclusion, I find I cannot possibly tumble 4

I myself into that kind of Toryism which belongs to the 1" reit and be thankful" frame of mind, nor can I under- stand why, if we are to do the Jubilee trick in Warrington, the transformation scene should not find a fitting stage al- ready constructed in Bold-street.
COLIN CLOUT.

div.head: CONDITION OF THE WORKING CLASSES.
div.p: THE CONDITION OF THE WORKING CLASSES.

Sir,—l am afraid "Cohn Clout" bas misunderstood me in my last letter. I apprehend that he thinks lam want- ing in sympathy for working people. If so, he is greatly mistaken. My sympathies are entirely and alsolutely with those whose lot it is to earn their daily bread with the sweat of their face. My contention, however, is that notwith- standing all the disadvantagel under which they at present labour, they are surrounded with greater comforts and luxuries than the working classes were at the beginning of the century. I mean, of course, taking them as a whole. Progress has not been continuous or uninterrupted. There have been years of clouds as well as of sunshine, there have been losses as well as gains; some classes of the people have suffered severely, and some have greatly advanced: but if we take the nett result, and contrast the present material con- dition of the people of this country now and fifty years ago, ' we shall find that the improvement ad round has been very great. There are many facts, such as the increasing con- sumption of food and clothing, and the large amount of money invested intayings' Banks, &c., to prove this. There , is some agent at work—quietly and silently—which is slowly but surely eliminating, from our midst perperiam and crime, and even drunkenness—the great bane of our country —is coming to be looked upon as discreditable by all intelli- gent workmen. I attribute this to the better position of the people, brought silent largely since the introduction of "new and improved machinery." "Cohn Clout" sneers at Mr. Mackenzie'a book as ancient history. Perhaps he will allow that an article written last month is tolerably modern, and that the writer, Professor Leone Levi, has some slight pretensions to being an author- ity. If he will condescend to allow this, I will tell him and your readers what the professor says on the subject. After speaking of the large productions of the country dur- ing the last fifty years, he says :—" Since labour is one, at any rate, of the chief agents of production surely the peo- ple of the United Kingaona must have been very busy in doing all this, even allowing for the increase of machinery, since even machinery must be supervised and guided. And if they have been so busy they must have had their proper wages or their due share of what they have helped to produce. This is not the place to enter into the rates of wages is the different industries, but it is well known that, as compared with fifty years ago, the earnings of the labour- ing classes have greatly increased, and that their total aggregate income is far greater than at one time was ever imagined. Doubtless at times the demand for labour is slack, and the number of the unemployed increases; but, apart from exceptional occurrences, there are many evi- dences of the improved condition of the people as a whole. One result we see in the increasing quantities of the neces- saries of life they consume. For instance, in 1840 there was scarcely any foreign bacon and ham consumed. In 1885 there was consumed as much as llilbs her head. In 1840 there was consumed less than lib of foreign butter; in 1885 7ilbs. In 1840 there was consumed lilb of tea per bead; in 1885 slbs and more. Evidently tie people have more means at their command, and they live more comfort- ably. Their houses are also much better. Agricultural cot- tages are more numerous, the houses et the working classes in towns are better built and better furnished. In truth, conveniences and comfcrts are placed within the reach of alma,t every one. Wall paper, gas, and water are greatly diffused, fire irons, kitchen pots and pans, and beautiful drawings and pictures are all cheap and available, and the people exhibit a better taste in the furniture of their homes, and more relish for what is elegant and beautiful. Nor must we forget that the working people have more time at their command and more facilities for recreations and amusements, of which they avail themselves to the full. Indeed, the whole course of legislation has been of late years favourable to the working claeses. The factory laws, the laws relating to mining, the abolition of the combination laws, the Masters and Servants Acts, the Employers' Liability Acts, have all been passed in their interest, an evidence, surely, that their voice has become much mere powerful in the State."

But " Colin Clout" says "it is of no Ils3 to make com- parisons between to-day and yesterday," and straightway marches us off iato very ancient history indeed, compara- tively. Well, now, what .are the actual facts as to these very "good old days?" Lard Macauley—l suppose he ie another ancient historian—says that under the Plantagenets the peasants were degraded to the levahof the swine and oxen which they tended. Another writer says that the re- sult of inquiries into the manners and customs of the mid- dle ages is to inspire all thinking minds with sentiments of gratitude that the clouds of the dark ages have passed away. But to pass on to the Elizabethian age—the age when Eng- land was called " Merrie England"— and we will join Chaucer's merry travellers, and will seek "Colin Clout." the shepherd, and hear him pipe his pastoral lays. Well, sir, what's the result? "There are light and wonder in the faces of men, and new melodious speech on their lips and great purposes in their hearts, and latent energy is bursting forth in a thousand forms of activity." It was in very truth a marvellous age. The people were, as "Cohn Clout" says, free spoken and well fed. Food was cheap and wages were good. Beef and pork could be bought at a half-penny or three farthings a pound; a fat lamb might be had for a shilling, a goose for fourponce, aad a hen for two- pence. Listen; Oh, ye topers—beer was one penny a gal- lon—wine eightpence. The wages of artisans were about sixpence a day, labourers fourpence. The penny was about equal to a shilling of our currency. If there was not material comfort in the homes of the working-classes, it was not for want of means. But the style of livinz was gen- erous, and poverty followed close on plenty. Still, the peo- ple were characterised by the "broad, rosy health" that waits on labour.

The other side of the picture is not so attractive. There was much severity, much coarseness, much trifling with justice. "The gallows rose gaunt in the towns, the village green was the scenes of the whipping post and the stocks, the village pond was the drowning place of old bags who professed witchcraft, political crimes were freely expiated at the block on Tower Hill. The sanitary condition of the land was deplorable. The peasentry were huddled together in unwholesome dwellings. Hospitals were few. Fierce diseays carried off periodically tens of thousands of the in- habitants." How does this contrast with our conntry of to-dav ? Not- withslanding all our drunkenness and crime and physicial discomfort and wretchedness and overcrowding and disease, England to-day—socially cmsidered—is vastly in advance of England under Elizabeth. Well, sir, I think I had better take " Colin Clout's " ad- vice and bottle up and wait to hear what Mr. Morris has got to say, or I must fear that I shall trespass too much on your spice and the patience of your readers. Otherwise I should like to take up in detail the other remarks of "Cohn Clout." JOHN GANDY. Warrington. February 9th. 1887.

div.p: WARRINGTON IN FLRMARY AND DISPENSARY.

In connection with the Working-men's Committee of this institution the annual meeting of represen- tatives from the various, works in the town and neighbourhood was held in the Mayor's parlour at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon, when there was a good attendance. Major Litton was elected to the chair.—Mr. Z. Armitage, the honorary secre- tary, said that the total contributions during the past year had been .C 367 Is Bd, as compared with £478 13s Cid for the previous year. Five sources of income in 1885 had not yielded anything this year, the athletic sports and the concert had not yielded such good returns as before, and three or four firms had given considerably less money.—The CHAIRMAN : That is owing to a great extent to the depression of trade.—Mr. ARMITAGE said he sup- posed it must be accounted for in that way. The expenses in connection with the collection of the money, for Hospital Sunday and the contributions at the works had been .£l4 98 lid, lees £1 Is 5d interest. The expenses last year were .£l3 4s 10.—Mr. JOHN ROBERTS said that he was convinced that the workueople of Warring- ton bad taken a great interest in-the Infirmary, and had done their best towards it. (Hear, hear.) He ,thought, however, that possibly a little more might be done in organising weekly subscriptions, and, if so, he thought that at the end of 1887 they would not find themselves much behindhand. At carious times he had opportunities of going through the Hospital and making inquiries, and he could say that, with the exception of one case where there was a slight complaint, everyone who had been in the institution were per.. feetly satisfied with their treatment. (Hear, hear.) —The CHArnmAx said that as far as the Infirmary was conceraed be was sure it was satisfactory to ii oonnected with it to hear such a good account of was then decided that all the representa- tives present should be appointed a general com- mittee, with power to add to their number, and the , following were selected Worm the executive com- mittee :---Mesers. John ,Berts, W. A. Lloyd, J. Potter, W. Fielding, John Griffiths, Thomas Knight, J. Scattergood, Thomas Barton, J. Hartley, George Jones, B. Budge, John Taylor, George Gill, Arthur Miller, John H. Wareing, Thomas Wadsworth, and Samuel Ross.—On the motion of Mi. AnntrrAGE, Mr. John Roberts was unanimously re-elected chair- man of the Executive Committee for the ensuing year, and it was resolved that collections be made, as before, at the end of May and the end of Novem- ber.—This concluding the business before the meet- ing, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. ARmrrioß, who, acknowledging the compliment, 4id that he thought they had got hold ot a good method in putting the matter of subscribing in the hands of the workpeople, through their own 'repro- sentatives. Directly the working-men took the matter up a change was seen. He then prOposed a vote of thanks to the honorary k medical officers, to the Mayor for the use of the room, to the chairman, &c., the passing of which brought the meeting to a close.

BURNLEY ELECTION. On SatUrday night, at a meeting of the Burnley Liberal "300," Mr John Slagg was adopted as the Glad.stonian candidate, to contest the seat vacant:by the death of Mr. Rylands. At a meeting of Liberal Unionists it was decided to request Mr. J. 0. 5. Thursby, a son of the High Sheriff, and a Conserve- .tive, to allow himself to be nominated as a Unionist. Mr. Thursby also received a requisition from the Conservative party, and has consented to become a candidate: Mr. Gladstone has written a letter— strongly supporting the candidature of Mr. Slagg; but, on the other hand, Lord Hartington recom- mends the Liberal Unionists to vote for the Tory candidate. The polling takes place to-day -(Satur- day). • Mr. Slagg, Libel al candidate, in his address, which was issued on • Monday, declares that, recognizing his abundant and glorious services in the past, his unrivalled experience and matchless grasp of states-. manship, he still had faith in Mr. Gladstone, and, further, he has faith in the people and, among them, the Irish people. He has confidence that, in according to Ireland a qufficient and generous mea- sure of self-government, we should not fail to secure the contentment, welfare, and affection of her people. Mr. Thursby, the Conservative candidate, appeals to the electors solely on the mainten- ance of the legislative union between England and Ireland

The election campaign proper opened at Burnley on Monday night, when the first meetings were held in support of the respective candidates. On Tuesday, both candidates continued their campaign. Colonel Saunderson' M.P., spoke at a meeting in I support of Mr. Thursby. Mr. Slagg addressed a i largely-attended meeting n the afternoon, and two crowded meetings in the evening.' On Wednesday Mr. Slagg held , three large and successful meetings. He WM supported at one of them by Mr. Robert Leake, M.P., and at each a re- solution approving of his candidature was carried amid manifestati • : of enthusiasm. The. Liberal Unionists held a eeting in the evening, which was presided over by Mr. Alderman Baring, and was ad- dressed by Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., Colonel Saunder- son, M.P., the Hon. A. D. Elliot, M.P., and Mr. Thursby, the Conservative candidate. A resolution pledging those present to support Mr. Thursby was put to tbe meeting and 'declared to be carried, but there was a large opposing element present. Several meetings were held on Thursday evening, and on Friday morning the nominations were made. Mr. John Slagg, 39, Hertford-street, London, merchant and bleacher, and Mr. John Ornierod Scarlett Thursby, Bank Hall, Burnley, were nomi- nated. Both parties express confidence as to the` result of the polling to-day.
