div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A meeting of Ministers will be heldlo-day (Saturday) for the purpose of considering the Egyptian question and other foreign matters of urgency. A number of agricultural labourers made an attack upon a Primrose League meeting at Mannington. Dorset, on Thursday night, the windows being broken acd the people assaulted.

The Rev. E. Lock, vicar of Selside, near Kendal, fill down dead whilst walking to the parish scleool, on Fri- day morning. The body was found in the road by a rural postman. EXTEMORDINARY DEFIANCE.—The hearing of the charges to Ireland against the New Ross Workhouse rioters have been adjornmed for a week. When the police attempted to take the prisoners to the Court Rouse the six women stripped themselves naked and defied the constables.

EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE—On Friday morning at Dud- ley, near Newcastle, a man named R. Boak, who was sus- pected of having shot Mr. Bell, a local farmer, went out at eight o'clock, set his gun against a hedge, attached a boot lace to the trigger, bared his breast, and shot himself. The suicide was witnessed by a man who dared not interfere The deceased was a single man. ALLEGED MEADER OF A flusnamo.—At Leicester, on Friday, Ellen Kinsley. aged 52, was charged with the mur- der of her husband, John Kingley, the day previous. The pair had quarrelled on Wednesday night, owing to prisoner's drunken habits, and she afterwards admitted that she threw two caps at him. cutting his nose in such a manner that he bled to death. She was remanded for a week.

div.head: SISTER SHOT DEAD AT NEWTON.
div.p: A SISTER SHOT DEAD AT NEWTON.

A shocking tragedy occurred on Friday ramming, at Park. side, near Newtou-le•Willows. William Jenkinson (19), porter at Lowton Junction station, was handling an old dis- used gun in his father's kitchen, and plkyfully aimed at his eldest sister, aged 22, through the window. The gun ex- ploded, and the full charge entered her temple. She exclaimed "Oh my!" and immediately dropped. Or. Maple, Golborne, attended at once, but life was extinct. The mother witnessed the heartrending scene. The police ap- prehended the brother immediately. The deceased was a cripple.

div.head: GERMAN ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE GERMAN ELECTIONS.

A Central News telegram' dated Berlin, Friday. states : According to the official North German Ga:ette to-day, the Reichstag to be elected on Monday next will be again dissolved if the Govenment does not obtain an absolute majority.

div.p: THE POPE AND I PALI'.

Roma, FRIDAY.—At a meeting of cardinals yesterday the Pope declared that his acts were in no way intended to in- jure Italy. bat iC was absolutely necessary to arrive at a settlement concerning the position of the Pontiff.

BULGARIA.—The report on the Address was brought up by Mr. A. Balfour. The Address was read by the Clerk at the table.—Mr. LABouctrarn then moved to amend the Address in respect to affairs in Bulgaria. He condemned the action of the present Government in regard thereto. Be objected to the action of her Majesty's Government in tak- ing steps to support the Prince Alexander, and quoted at length in support of his argument extracts from the Blue Book and other official papers. He insisted that the policy of Lord Salisbury had been to strike up war against Russia.—Sir R. FERGIISSON defended the policy of the Government, and justified the moral and diplomatic support being given to Prince Alexander.—The debate was continued by Mr. Bryce, Mr. W. H. Smith, Sir W. Harcourt, Lord John Mancers.—The amendment was then put from the chair and negatived without a division. [LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: EXAMINER, S A TURDA, FEBRUARY 19, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, S A TURDA, FEBRUARY 19, 1887.
WIFE MURDER AT BURY.

On Thursday afternoon, at Bury, Walter Wood, a machine litter, of Bolton, murdered his wife by cutting her throat. The deceased woman's maiden name was Emma Ford, and she had been twice married. Prior to her first marriage she had had an illegitimate child, who was present at the time the woman was murdered. It appears that the mur- derer( came to Bury to fit up some machinery, and there made the acquaintance of the deceased.' They were marrieda few months ago, but as they lived very uncomfortably together the deceased re- turned from Bolton to Bury to live with her mother. It is said that the husband, who had writ- ten several letters to her, made an appointment to meet her on Thursday afternoon. Be that as it may, they did meet, and went for a walk through some fields towards Iluntly Farm. Suddenly, the man seized his wife and cut her throat almost from ear to ear in the presence of the child above referred to, who screamed, upon which the mur- derer ran away in the direction of Heywood. The poor woman staggered to the house of a Mrs. Kay, next to the farm, and said, "Oh, do lay me down, because I am dying." A medical man was sum- moned, but Mrs. Wood died in a few minutes, though not before she had told her husband's name and said he had murdered her. The deceased was about 30 years of age. Wood has not yet been appre- hended.

tip to three o'clock on Friday nothing had been heard of Woodi.but the police are pretty confident that they will ultimately be able to arrest him un- less he has oommitted suicide, which is not con- sidered probable. The inurder was committed through jealousy, as the deceased refused to live with him.

THE PENKETH ABKCTION CASE. A charge of assault, arising out of what is known as the Penketh abduction case, came before the magistrates at Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday. Charles Crookes, a fashionably- dressed maq, was summoned for assaulting Mary Hayden Crookes, on the 2nd of February last. Mr. Davey appeared for the complainant, and Mil. P. Davies for the defence.—Mr. Davey said that the case was the natural sequel to some proceedings which had already been taken in the Chancery Div- ision, and which, he thought, it was desirable he should lightly touch upon.—Mr. Davies objected to anything being said in respect to matters not in dispute in 'relation to parties other than the par- ties to that action.—Mr. Davey then said that on the day in question, at about two o'clock in the afternoon, Mr. Dignum, father of the prosecutrix, who resided at Penketh, answered a knock at the door of his house. His grandchild, the little daugh- ter of the prosecutrix, ran out at the time, and was immediately seized by a man—the husband of the prosecutrix and the father of the child. Mr. Dignum struggled with him, and prosecutrix and her sister, Miss Dignum, hearing a noise, came out. The husband of the prosecutrix then handed the child to the defendant, his brother, who made off with it in the direction of Sankey. Prosecutrix followed, and tried to get the child back, but the defendant refused to give it up, pushed her, and " butted " against her with his head. That was the assault complained of. The prosecutrix, Mr. Dignum, colliery agent,and Miss Dignum,gave confirmatory evidence. During the hear- big of the case Mr. Davey mentioned that an action had been taken in the Chancery Division to recover possession of the child, and an order had been made that it should be given up to the mcither.—Mr. Davies said he believed that the child was with its father in Spain. He contended that the defendant was acting under his brothees instructions to get possession of the child, and set up a claim of right to test whether the Bench had jurisdiction.— .After consideration the magistrates came to thcf conclusion that an assault had been committed, and imposed a fine óf 10s and costs.

WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION. ' The annual meeting of the members of this as- sociation was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Luncheon-room at the wirks of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Company. The president, Mr. E. K. Muspratt, was in the chair, and there were present —Messrs. 'T. S. Timnus, .T.P.t G. Pilkington, J.P., R. Cook, E. Carey, J. M. Wareing, and LW. Deacon, hon. secretary.—The Hon. Secretary read the report lof the Executive 'Committee, which referred to the Railway and Canal Trnffic Bill of last year. which was ultimately withdrawn.—After allusion to the unsatisfactory condition of the entrances to the Canal and Dock, the report dealt with a clause on the London and North - Western Railway Bill, the object of which is to increase charges. A petition had been lodged On behalf of the association against the bill. The Railway and canal opposition account had closed with a balance to the credit of £234 Is 2d.—Mr. T. S. Timmis moved the adoption of the report, and Mr. Cook seconded the motion, which was carried unani- mously.—Mr. Carey moved a resolution authorising the Executive Committee to oppose the London and North-Weste,rn Railway Bill in Parliament. —Mr. Pilkington seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously, and it was afterwards resolved to ask the assistance of non-members of the Association. --Mr. T. S. Timmis moved that the best thanks of the Association be accorded to the president and hon. secretary for their previous services, and that they be re-appointed for a further period of three years. Therservices of these gentlemen, he said, had been invaluable,—Mr. Cook seccinded the mo- tion. and it was carried with acclamation.—The Chairman and Mr. Deacon hading replied, the meeting terminated.

div.head: "JUBILEE CONCERT" AT WIDNES.
div.p: "JUBILEE CONCERT" AT WIDNES.

The Welsh Presbyterians, of Widnes, have decided to celebrate the Jubilee of the Queen in a most practical fashion. They intend. if possible, to clear off the debt which at present exists upon their place of worship in Milton-street, and their first effort towards this desired con- summation was made on Monday evening. Under the able management of Mr. John Davies a "Jubilee concert" had been arranged,and that the title bestowed was deserved was the earnest enjoyment d isplayed by the large audience that crow- ded the Volunteer Hall,ef the choice ballads and classical ex- cerpts rendered by a company of efficient vocalists.—Tbe duties of chairman were fulfilled by Mr. H. Wade Deacon. who made an appropriate speech in opening the proccdings. He commented upon the fact that there was no general desire amongst the inhabitants of Widnes to celebrate the Jubilee by any public subscription, and applauded the man- ner in which his Welsh friends Intended to honour the oc- casion. The debt upon the chapel amounted to £lOO, and the pastor, the Rev. E. Jones, had informed him that the managers bad received the promise of £25 on the condition that another £25 was raised during that year. (Applause.) But they would not be satisfied with producing the sum of £5O. Tney had determined upon the liquidation of the entire debt, and also upon taking the important step of dis- pensing with the small grant they had hitherto re- ceived from a general fund in aid of their mission, and becoming self-supporting. (Applause.) He wished them every success. (Applause.) The first item on the programme was given by the Liverpool Standard Quartette, consisting of Messrs. J. T. Sydney, W. Griffiths, M. E. Williams, and T. G. Fargher. Their performances were marked by precision, great tunefulness, and power, rind on two occasions an eccore was loudly demanded. Madame Williams, of the Royal National Eisteddfod, a favourite with Widnes audiences, sang " When the heart is young," " A bird in hand," and" Let me dream again," in which she displayed her accustomed command of her fine soprano voice, and she was awarded a cordial recall. Madam Emilie Young, of the Leeds and Manchester concerts, also made three ap- pearances before the audience, and with the vocalisition of A true and gifted artiste sang " The better land," " Tit for tat," and " Never again.' She had to respond to an enthu- siastic encore in her first and third efforts. Miss Maggie E. Morgan, of Grassendale, who is the possessor of a pleasing mezzo soprano voice, sang with mach taste "When th ivy is in flower" and" The lost chord," but a want of ease in her deportment detracted from the effect of her

otherwise capiial performances. Herr March, principal rbass of the Liverpool Opera Company, contributed " Nazereth," "The heart bowed down," and "I fear no foe." A vocalist of natural ability with a powerful voice of good quality, Herr Morch did not reach the expectations of the audience, probably through the foreign accent of his pronunciation. A tenor with a pure light tenor voice, Mr A H White, of Liverpool, rendered with cultured taste and expression an excerpt from Handel, Pin- suti's "Last Watch," and "Sweetheart," and he narrowly escaped a recall in the last-named song. Mr J Busfield gave two clever performances on the violin. Mr B D Rod• gers, of Liverpool, is a huineurous vocalist of more tuan erdinary ability, and he convulsed the audience with laugh- ter by his songs and sketches. Mr Tl' Ford, organist of St Cyprian's, Liverpool, officiated as accompanist in capital style. The National Anthem by the whole of the artistes brought a most successful concert to a conclusion.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

C.E.T.S., PM/SCOT Baca.—The usual monthly meet- ing of the senior branch of the Band of Hope, in connection with the above, was held in the Houghton-street school- room, on Monday evening. The attendance was very good and Mr. James Case occupied the chair. During the even- ing Mr. John Case gave an address. The meeting closed in the usual way after an excellent programme had been gone through.

A LICENSING DIFFICCLTY.—Before Messre. B. Bright and W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Albert Gerson, of Liverpool, applied for the transfer of the license of the Hare and Hounds. Tarbock, now held by Margaret Pearch, a widow. In answer to the Bench, appli- cant said be had given up a !jeepse he had held at Liver- pool, the magistrates there having granted ite transfer to his wife. Is answer to Mr. C. Spencelev (clerk), the appli- cant added that his wife had applied for the transfer at the sessions held a fortnight ago. The Bench censidered the application an unsatisfactory one, and refused to grant it. PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS.—At these sessions on Tuesday there was an exceptionally small number of cases for dis- posal. The magistrates present were Messrs. H. Bright and W. L. Evans. John Mercer, a labourer, of Prescot, was summoned for cruelly working a boree,but Inepector Morton, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, withdrew the case, as the animal had been alaugh- tered.—Joseph Roby, a labourer at Prescot, was summoned at tee instance of Mr. William Bullock, rellevice officer, for neglecting to contribute to the support of hi 3 father in the Union Workhouse at Whisten. The case was a 4 journed to give the defendant an opportunity of paying. ‘VATCIT TRADE.—The Fraudulent Marks Bill now in print contains clauses for the protection of Le watch- making industry of the country. Any person desiring to get watch cases hall marked at any of the British Assay Offices will be required to state where the movement for the cases has been manufactured, so as to stamp the watch with the name of the place of origin. Mr. T. P. Hewitt, of Prescot, suggested to the Board of Trade the desirability of tte Custom Authorities being empowered to seize goods cdming into this country with marks calculated to lead the public to believe they were ef British manufacture. Mr. Broadhurst asked for a Royal Commission to be appointed to make searching inquiry into the whole subject. It is to be Lisped he will be successful.

div.head: BOARD.OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: BOARD.OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the.--IVeac--o—t• Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present—Mr. John Lowe (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. Wm. Tyrer, josedh Jackam„ Wllliain G. Ashton William Middlehurst, James Fisher, John Whalley, John L owe Charles B. John- son, James Ranson, William Swift, Joseph Ellison, Joseph Griffiths, John Leatherbarrow, John W. Warding, James Buckley. and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF RETURNS.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 498 inmates of the Workhouse this week. 492 last week, and 508 in the corresponaing week of last year. Miss Lee, of Huytoo, and Mr. John Leathersarrow, had for- warded a number of books and periodicals for the use of the inmates, and the thanks of the Visiting Committee had , been accorded to the donors.

PAUPER LITNATICS.—The Local Government Board wrote informing the Guardians that they had paid to Mr. C. C. White, treasurer of the Union, the sum of £1,845 Sc, being the amount payable from the grant made by Parliament in respect of the coat of maintenace of pauper lunatics in county and borough licensed houses for the year ended 29th September last. POSTAL FACILITIES.—Mr. Welsby, the postmaster at Preruot, wrote asking for the sanction of the Guardians to a letter-box being placed in the bend of the boundary wall of the Workhouse, opposite "The Dragon," and near the fingerpost. The pest office would undertake to remove such box on receiviug and giving three months notice, and to make good any damage to the wall.—The Clerk stated that he was in correspondence with the postal authorities to have a postal-box placed in the wall so that the inmates would be able to post their communications without leaving the Workhouse premises. HALF•YEAR'S Eariattilra.—The Clerk submitted an esti- mate of the probable expenditure by the Guardians during the half-year ending 29th Sept, 1887 (27 weeks.) The following were the amounts : In-maiatenance £2,000, out relief £4,000, children In schools £1,500, lunatics in asylum £2,250, salaries of union officers £l,OOO, salaries of assist- ant overseers £6OO, workhouse officers' rations £2BO, Assess- ment Committee expenses £3OO, school fees (non-paupers) £5lO, vaccination expenses £2BO, registration expenses £220, extra medical fees £5O, printing, advertising, &c. £l5O, establishment charges, Workhouse, etc. £l,OOO, county rate . £6,060, and 10 per cent contingencies £2,080. total £22,880. He stated that the expenditure for the half-year ending I September, 1886, was £21,850. The increase was occasioned by the fact that they had to provide for 27 weeks, while in the former period they had only 26 weeks expenditure.— The Rev. Dean Finegan moved that the estimate be ap- proved, and Mr. Ellison seconded the motion, ,vhich was adopted. CRUELTY TO CHILDREN.—The Clerk reported the receipt of circular letters and publications from the Liverpool Society for the Prevention of cruelty to children, and said he was in communication with the solicitor to the society

with the view of prevailing upon the Local Government Board to give the Guardians permission to contribute three guineas annually to the funds of the society. THE WOOLTON RELIEVING OFFICER.—Mr. Thomas F. Hill, guardian for Wootton wrote to the Clerk, under date 15th inst., that be would feel greatly obliged if be could forward the more frequent visits of the relieving officer to Wootton. It was most inconvenient for the poorer people that they could only see Mr. Bullock on Saturday, and con- sidering that Wootton was the district having most outdoor relief in the Prescot district, be did not think it right that every one who required temporary assistance should be compelled either to walk to Prescot or wait until Saturday to see the relieving officer. They were at present having an epidemic of measles (in a light form), and he and Mr Tuson were frequently asked for medical orders, &re., which Mr. Bullock had to cover. He suggested Mr. Bullock should be seen at Wootton at least two days in a week.— Father Prest complained very bitterly about what he termed the neglect of the poorer classes in the village, and threatened to write to the Local Government Board.—Owing to the absence of Mr. Hill, the letter was left over for con- sideration at a meeting of the Board when Mr. Hill was present.
This was the only business.

WARRINGTON. CADISHEAD AND IRLAM CRICIUM CLUB. - The annual concert of this club was held in the Wes- leyan School, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. An Interesting programme was well aone through by the following :—Messrs. W. and Pi Sharpies, Miss Marion Evans, Mr. J. J. Sut- cliffe. Mr. A. Ramm, Mr. Cecil Berle (encore), Miss Martin.

ST. PAUL'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— OnSaturday evening the membersof this society and their friends partook of an enjoyable tea in one of the schoolrooms. An interesting musical entertain- ment was afterwards given, the chair being occupied by the vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson. Votes of thanks were accorded to the Chairman and the ladies and gentlemen who had taken part in the entertain- ment, and altogether 4a very pleasant evening was spent.

THE DISTRIBUTION OF INDECENT L/TERLTURE. At the Borough Court on Thursday, a man named James Cross, alias Thompson, was brought up on a charge of distributing indecent literature. Evi- dence was given by P.C. Plumley to the effect that he saw the prisoner distributing, improper pamph- lets, and Chief Constable Hunt remarked that it was becoming very common, particularly on mar- ket days, for men to distribute- such literature on the outskirts of the borough and near the railway stations; they ran away when they saw a police- man. Many complaints had been received. Pri- soner, who gave an address in Gerard-street, Liver- pool, was sent to gaol for 14 days without the option of a fine.

WAr nwonxs COMPANY.—The half-yearly meet- ing of the shareholders of this company was held at the offices in Cairo-street, on Wednesday afternoon, Lord Winmarleigh presiding. There were also pre- sent—Sir Gilbert Greenall; M,P., and Messrs. J. Mar- son, J. C. Parr, P. Stubs, W. Fairhurst, J. Geddes, T. W. Mellor, J. Shaw Green, J. W. Booth, T. Briggs, H. E. White, Rev. W. Kenworthy, E. J. Nicholson (law clerk), and J. Ross (secretary.) From the re- port of the directors, which was adopted, it ap- peared that the revenue account gave a balance, including £537 38 5d brought from last half-year, of £3,513 18s Bd. The preference charges amounted to £BB6 10s, leaving a balance of £2,627 8s Bd, out of which a dividend of 5 per cent. per annum on the ordinary share capital was recommended. £752 8s 8d was carried forward. The reserve fund amoun- ted to £3,617 10s. Lord Winmarleigh, Mr. James Manson, and Mr. William Fairhurst were re-akpoin- ted directors of the company, and Mr. W. Silcock, junr., was iv-elected auditor. Votes of thanks to the Committee of Management, and to the chairman, concluded the meeting. , THE APPLICATION POE A NEW TRIAL.—At War- rington County Court, on Thursday, his Honour Judge. Ffoukes gave his decision in regard to an application made by Mr. Riley at the last sitting of the court, for a new trial of the case in which Walter Liptrot, shoemaker, Newton, was sued for damages in respect to injuries caused to the eye of Percy Mellardy, by the throwing by defendant of certain small nails or " sparrowbills." Particulars of the case have been previously, given. His Honour had his decision for considerativ of the ground of the application which stated that the judge ought to have left it to the jury to say' whether the defendant "acted unreasonably in throwing the nails at the plaintiff in reply to plain- tiff's challenge asking defendant to see if he could hit him. • After explaunlig his reasons at consider- able length, his Honour said that he could not grant a • new trial, but would allow Mr. Riley? if he wished, to appeal. Mr. Longton, who appeared for the defen- dant, then asked -tor the costs of defendant in con- nection with defending the application, but his Honour thought that defendant should forego the costs, as plaintiff was ceoainly entitled to some sympathy. MUSEUM FREE LECTURES.—The third of the series of these lectures was delivered in the Lecture Room, Museum-street, on Monday evening, by Mr. G. W. Webster, F.C.S.; .subject, "Seeing, not believ- ing; a chapter on optical illusions." In the absence ' of Mr. T. G. Rylands, who was linable to be present, ' Alderman Sutton took the chair. Mr. Webster said that by the term optical illusion he wished to be 1 understood as meaning -those incorrect or imperfect judgments of the qualities of an object of which the mind was conscious through the organs of sight. There was an old proverb that" seeing is believing," but it was scarcely possible to imagine an apothegm 1 less to be depended upon,' for it was his experience that the exact reverse is far the truer. Innumera- ble facts of everyday observation, the \ aspect of the heavens, of the fields, of .the buildings and streets around us, the countenances of our friends, the garments we wear, are very different indeed from what we imagine them to be either id size or pro- portion. The importance Of exactness in observa- tion need not be dwelt upon, and yet he felt justi- fied in stating in the majority of cases where we depend upon visual perceptions it *as only what he might call their ordinary human experiences that enabled them to make a correct observation, and whenever the usual order of things was at all upset they at once began to fall, into most ridiculous errors in their perceptions of the sizes, shapes, colours, or distances of objects when they attempted to ex- amine them. The lecturer gave numerous instances of optical illusion, his explanations being greatly aided by the use of diagrams. Throughout, the large audience, which filled the room, manifested a deep interest in the sttbject. GOLBORNE-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL.—The an- nual congregational tea party in connection with this place of worship was held on Thursday even- ing in the schoolroom. There was a fairly good attendance, the tables being attended to by the following ladies, Mesdames Baxter, Gough, B. Few, Dodd, Patrick, Longshaw, Green, Hall, and Lee. After tea a well-attended public meeting was held in the chapel, the pastor, the Rev. E. Moore, presi- ding. In his address the chairman said they had had a fairly satisfactory increase of members during the year. They had had some losses from removals and other causes, but on the other hand compensa- ting gains. The various agencies connected with the church had been vigorously worked with satis- factory results, and the friends looked forward to the future with hopefulness and encouragement. Mr. Moore also referred in feeling terms to the death of Mrs. Hall, one of the oldest members of the church.—ln his report, which was submitted, the treasurer (Mr. William Bamford) stated that they closed the chapel accounts for the year with a balance in hand.—An excellent musical progranime was afterwards rendered. Mr. W. H. Wallington sang "The' three beggars," "Four jolly smiths," and, as an encore, sang "The little hero.' "Should be upbraid," was sung by Miss Riley, who also made a successful appearance latir in the evening, Miss Mary Podmore rendered in a manner that was much enjoyed, the song "Watching the embers ;" and Mr. Patrick, "The song of the old. bell." For her execution of the song, "Katie's letter," Miss H. Fieldhouse was deservedly encored. A violin solo was admirably executed by lir. G. Shakeshaf,t, who likewise gave a selection of Scotch airs. The choir, under the leadership of Mr. T. G. Lee, gavb several 'selections, which were warmly appreciated. 'Mr. G. Riley played the accompaniments with *his usual ability. It should also be mentioned that an elo- quent address'on the various aspects of Christian work was given by the Rey. J. G. Raws, of Man- chester. A vote of thanks to the ladies, performers, *etc., moved by Mr. E. J. Hall, and seconded by Mr. Few, brought the proceedings to a close.

BOROUG II OF WARRIN GTON. VIC CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AELMALS Aors. 1878 To 1886. • THE RABIES ORDER. NOTICE IS HEREBY' GIVEN. that at a meeting of 'the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington. held at the Town Ball; en Wednesday, the 16th day of February, 1887, the said Local Authority made the Regulations followlug, that is to say:- 1. These Regulations shall cmimence and take effect from and after the let day of March nest, and shall con- tinue in force until the 31st day of March next, unless sooner revoked or altered by the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington, 2. No Dog shall be allowed to be, in any street within the Borough unless securely and properly muzzled, so as to prevent it from inflicting injury with its teeth, or unless led by a chain or leash, under the control of some person. 3. Any Dog found straying or at large in contravention of the above Regulation shall be seized by the pollee and detained until the owner has claimed it and has paid all expenses connected with such detention. 4. Any Dog which the police bye had in their possession for three clear days without being claimed by the owner, and all expenses paid by him, shall be des- troyed. Any person offending against the above Regulations will be liable to a penalty of £2O. Dated the Nineteenth day of February, 1887. WM. KY. BROOK. Town Clerk.
